Summer in Zagłębie.

(The difficult sanitary situation of Zagłębie's residents. An improvement should be brought about.)
And here it has appeared, the dear, beautiful summer; here it warms us with the burning sun, which so refreshes people's health. Thanks to the sun's rays the human being comes alive; wherever he may be, he is drawn by a hypnotic force to the longed-for sun. The animals and birds in God's little world come alive, plant life begins to blossom freely and broadly, the green carpet begins to weave itself out and gives off various colours and hues, and the delights of life breathe a spirit of life into everything that lives, breathes and grows under the open sky.
As soon as we catch sight of summer, the world is lit up. Nature shows itself in all its greatness and beauty; little children begin to move about freely like summer birds, old people begin to breathe more freely after the long, cruel winter with its great dark nights. In short, everything comes alive, everything blossoms and awakens and develops under the loving rays of the sun, under the singing and twittering of the birds and under the aroma of the plants, which give off so much fragrance for the living creatures under the blue skies.
But every virtue also has its flaw, every good side also has its bad side. The sun and the heat are indeed good in the village and in the forest, in the mountains and by the sea, where one can protect oneself from it when it begins to become dangerous. Quite different, however, is the case in the city, where the sun burns and glows and the high walls that block everything do not let the refreshing breeze in and shut out the fresh air; and it is then that the sun begins to become dangerous, and because of the heat the air becomes stifling and city people cannot breathe. City dwellers living in the conditions mentioned begin to look like skeletons; the blood is sucked out of them and their strength grows weaker.
Well, if one lives in towns where there are gardens and fields and enough open spaces, one still manages somehow; but if one lives in towns such as, for example, Zagłębie, it is impossible to get through a hot, dry summer.
Statistics in Poland show that the largest number of people leaving [for holidays] come from Zagłębie and Łódź, and this is understandable, because in those towns the air is dangerous. People live in compact masses, in narrow, cramped streets, in densely built tall houses that let no air in; on top of that we are surrounded on all sides by factories with tall chimneys, which emit choking gases that poison the air. Gardens and fields are nowhere to be seen. It is a good thing that in recent years the local governments have begun to see to it that there is a little greenery in town; otherwise a Zagłębie child might think that greenery is manufactured like all other products in a factory.
The hygienic and sanitary conditions are also very bad: for example, to this day the sewerage question in Zagłębie is still not a settled matter; there are still no gardens, we have no parks where one could cool off[?] and rest bones worn out by a whole day and a whole winter of hard toil; even benches are not to be found in town.
Moreover, the streets are in a terrible state; it is not enough to say they are not clean — they are badly neglected, dirty and dusty. When a car or a tram passes through the central streets it is impossible to stay in the street; one must hide in a gateway. A cloud of dust then comes, so thick that one cannot see the other. It is surely intolerable to leave in such a condition streets where people walk and stroll and where the traffic is relatively heavy. No better is the sweeping of the streets: it is done when the traffic is in full swing. Where has one ever seen such carelessness, such negligence?
Why shouldn't the streets be watered several times a day? Where has it been heard of that instead of watering the streets the population should have to eat dust whenever it strolls along the street? Can it not be arranged that the streets be watered with hoses several times a day? Are these really such large and costly expenses that a town cannot afford them for the sake of its citizens' health?
Here we stop over trifles, often over ridiculous questions, debating them as though they were first-class matters of life — while the most important and most pressing problems are not considered at all.
If two or three people stand in the street, the policeman speaks to you far[?] from politely, and it goes so far[?] that if you have a "piamakel"[?], or if a housewife has taken it into her head to put a pot out on the balcony, you can be fined for it on the spot; whereas if a sewer opening in the street is not covered and people can break their necks, or other similar things from which various accidents occur — that the police do not see, that bothers nobody, and for such things nobody is responsible.
There are very many absurdities for which people are held liable, while the most important disorders are ignored.
One must, once and for all, know first of all how to distinguish between more important and less important disorders; they must be classified and attended to according to their importance.
First and foremost our city fathers must remember that the summer months have now begun, and summer in Zagłębie is by no means an easy matter; therefore care must be taken that we live in better hygienic and sanitary conditions than until now.
True, one cannot deny that a great deal has been improved over the last several years; but that does not mean that everything is already in perfect order, especially when there are such cardinal defects that cannot be tolerated.
Order in the streets must be established as quickly and as well as possible. The dust in the streets is unbearable; it is enough to walk through the street once and one has to go home to wash. That is how dusty one gets when a tram or a car passes by, which is no rarity here.
Surely summer, which everywhere is a paradise for mankind, need not be a hell for the residents of Zagłębie. Well, for those who can leave Zagłębie for a couple of weeks it is still bearable; but what are those to do who cannot even dream of it? Is Zagłębie really to remain for them an unbearable place where one can find no place of rest? One must surely see to improving whatever can be improved; what can and must be done — with good will a great deal can be achieved.
One must not forget that the population of Zagłębie lives in a narrow box, blocked on all sides, which neither air nor a refreshing breeze can reach. The box must be repaired; the boards must be cut back a little to make it possible for the sun's rays, the life-giving air, to get in.
Y. Sh.
Lorry carrying textile goods for Zagłębie robbed.

On Wednesday late in the evening a lorry belonging to Łódź forwarding agents, who were transporting textile goods (manufaktura) to Zagłębie, set out from Łódź for Będzin. When the vehicle was on the narrow highway beyond the Tuszyn forest, a passenger car suddenly drove out of a side road, and several persons armed with revolvers jumped out of it. Threatening death in case of resistance, the attackers demanded that they be handed the goods.
The lorry's passengers were frightened; one of them at first wanted to resist, whereupon a bandit put a revolver to his temple and forced him to give in.
The attackers then, lightning-fast, set about transferring the goods from the lorry to their passenger car and vanished with goods worth a considerable sum.

Our Panorama

(“Messianic times.” — The Jews of Pogoń make peace. — Hasidism overrides the Sabbath. — Moshe Kapoyer [“Moses Upside-Down”] runs the show. — Hefker petrushke [a free-for-all]. — Two towns with one complaint. — Everything stays as it was. — A new danger of war. — A gabbai who hands out slaps.)
— Messianic times! The Redemption is near!
That is what I cried out on reading the good tidings from Pogoń. Can one even call it good tidings?! It is a great event in world history: the words of the prophet Isaiah, “the wolf shall dwell with the lamb,” are being fulfilled; the hatred among one's own is ceasing, and peace be upon Israel.
In truth, one has to admit that were it not for America, the peace would never have been concluded, for many “kingdoms” had previously intervened so that the battles between the “beit-midrash-ists” and the “shtibl-ists” should be stopped, but the interventions had the same effect as appeals at the tax offices: the public files complaints and the bailiffs [?] search for “chametz.” Only when the Pogoń kehilla heard that an American delegation was coming — a delegation famous for its dollars — did it, the kehilla that is, acquire great respect, put down “the cannons with the rifles,” and on Sunday, 4 May, the Pogoń kehilla — made peace with itself..
So that this great event should not be forgotten by the historian of the future, we present the following important points of the peace agreement:
1) In the distribution of the contribution [war levy], the opposition shall be represented by four delegates, corresponding to the “four principal categories of damages.”
2) The geographical map of the beit midrash shall be altered so that the minority receives a neutral zone..
3) [On the Sabbath of] the portion Tazria-Metzora [the leprosy portions], the aliyot shall be given to the “fine Jews”...
And 4) the peace must be ratified at “the season of the giving of our Torah” [Shavuot]...
———
The Gerer Hasidim in Dąbrowa also possess a mighty “power,” which deserves [?] to become famous throughout all the dispersions of Israel.
Until now it was known that among the Gerer there are various “antiques,” but lock-breakers, and on the Sabbath at that?! — that really is a “rare phenomenon”...
And it came to pass, when the Dąbrowa Gerer Hasidim came into the shtibl last Sabbath, they saw a lock hanging on the door with a “little note”:
— “Rent not paid — so pray at home.”
But a “sharp” Hasid was found who ruled that — “Hasidism overrides the Sabbath.” He recited “Vihi Noam” 7 times, the lock fell to its knees, and the door opened..
———
The Gerer Hasidim of Pilica are very great “stringent ones”: even in matters on which the local rabbi says “permitted,” they say “forbidden.” They do it not out of piety, but out of... hatred.
The dispute in Pilica has made a name for itself “all over the world”; everyone, young and old (except the Agudas HaRabbonim of Poland), knows that the local Gerer Hasidim have set upon the local rabbi and inflict harsh torments on him.
The rabbi says “day,” the other side says — “night”; the rabbi rules that the eruv is in order and one may carry — the Gerer shout: no, don't carry!..
As our correspondent assures us, things have gone so far that if the rabbi issued a proclamation that men, women and children must eat at least 3 times a day, the Gerer would do the opposite...
— The Moshe-Kapoyer folk..
———
Moshe Kapoyer has also barged into the Będzin synagogue, where he has been running things for a very long time already. Whatever existed in the synagogue — has ceased; all the customs have been changed; in a word, Moshe runs the show..
And when Moshe Kapoyer runs the show, everything is forgotten; they even forget to say a Mi Sheberakh for those who fast on Monday-Thursday-Monday, they do not say Av HaRachamim, and
— it's hefker petrushke [a total free-for-all]..
———
The Radomsk Hasidim of Będzin (second category) and the same Hasidim in Dąbrowa both have one and the same complaint. The former want to know what the halakha is when two persons — two people — want, want to lead the prayers before the ark: this one says — one shouts “I want,” and that one says — and the second also shouts the same?
And the Dąbrowa people have this complaint against us: you write — they claim — from everywhere and about everything that happens, so why have you taken “a mouthful of water” and don't write about a Jew, a Hasid, who took a fancy to evicting an heir, and since the eviction was to take place precisely on the Sabbath, this fine Jew ruled that eviction “overrides the Sabbath”; he ran from the court to the bailiff [komornik], from the bailiff to the inheritance, and at the very end, at the last “tekiah,” the curtain came down and..
— everything stayed as it was, as it is said: “a bargain remains a bargain and..”
———
In the synagogue in Old Sosnowiec, too, they are once again back “at the old.” The “political horizon” in this house of prayer has clouded over again, and a new “danger of war” looms...
The cause was the gabbai, who insists that during the Torah reading there should be an “armistice.”
At this “insolence” the worshippers throw off their tallitot and their jackets and roll up their sleeves...
———
The gabbai of the Strzemieszyce beit midrash hands out, besides aliyot, also... slaps.
He made his start with the shammes: he served him a double portion, two slaps at once..
The gabbai's slaps will have an echo far, far away — all the way to the judges of the Sosnowiec district court..
In These Hard Times

[Będzin — economy and taxes; opinion.] (How are public problems understood among us? At long last one must look with open eyes.)

Must one really tell how great the economic ruin is now? Must one really say what a hard situation we find ourselves in? Must one really explain to oneself how great and harmful our situation is now? It would seem that one need tell oneself nothing, one need say nothing to oneself, for who does not know how bad things are in his own pocket, who does not know whom the shoe pinches?

Whoever thinks so is mistaken. We can say quite surely that none of us knows how bad it is, none of us takes stock of how we look in reality and wherein the tragedy of a people lies. We do not want to look reality in the face; we do not want to understand that wind and air and fooling ourselves can bring salvation to no one.

Against what are we saying this? Why has it come up for discussion[?]: it is like this — when we consider how we react to unheard-of[?] injustices, how we remain indifferent to our most painful questions, at such moments we come to the conviction that we are far from understanding our tasks, that we do not even try to want to understand what we lack, what we could have improved.

And at precisely such worst moments one must be conscious and guard one's positions. At such a time the citizens must stand on watch and prevent the government from taxing them with higher tax obligations; it goes without saying that it is ridiculous even to think of such things, for how can one raise taxes at a time when it is generally known that a standstill reigns in the country in every field — but when one does not reckon with reality, there is no point. The citizens can no longer bear that at such a time we ourselves do not guard our positions.

How far we remain indifferent and apathetic to all our most painful questions may be characterised by the polemic that has developed in the columns of our paper.

A citizen who was wronged in a tax assessment writes a letter to the editors saying that our assessors do not properly fulfil their tasks and cannot be Jewish representatives. The latter answer that they can insist that the wronged man take their place, and then they will find themselves in a more pleasant situation, because they will then be able to put various questions to him in the tone of accusers.

That is how such serious questions are dealt with! When an individual is wronged, he feels hurt and decides to react to a phenomenon unfavourable to him. In this way painful national problems are exchanged for private, petty questions and answers, as if this were a matter for a select few.

By contrast, not long ago Mr. Selekt[?] published here an article entitled "The Dangerous Disease", in which the author treats the tax question in all its seriousness and concludes that we have fallen so low that one man looks to "hack into"[?] the other — so that they should know — if that is healthier for him. It would seem that the degradation has already reached its culminating point, and yet no one reacted to such an unheard-of phenomenon.

A second fact: a few weeks ago the "Izba Skarbowa" [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce considered appeals concerning the income tax [podatek dochodowy]. Sosnowiec sent a representative there and a great deal was reduced, whereas Będzin did not send its representative at all, so that there was no one to speak for the wronged, and hundreds of appeals were not considered at all.

That is how public moneys are treated, that is the sense of responsibility of many of our representatives, who take it upon themselves to defend and fight for the people's interests.

And here too the public saw no crime, and therefore the fact was hushed up, as if nothing had happened, as if everything had been settled in the best order.

One asks: in what manner are public problems dealt with, how do we react to them, and what is done if the representatives do not understand and do not properly fulfil their tasks? Do we among us discharge our duty to the community, to the people, if criminal deeds are not properly reacted to? May one leave everything so ownerless at a time when the Jewish population finds itself in such hard conditions of existence?

Why then should the representatives not stand under the control of the economic and professional associations, and as soon as they do not submit to the directives of the institutions, the latter should call them to account, and before them they would also have to render an account.

The same applies to individuals: when they are wronged, they must turn to the association, in which all of life must be reflected.

If one does not want to abandon everything, if we do not want to go under completely, if we want to exist somehow, we must begin to shape public life differently. For we see that in tax matters the individual's question is a zero; there the community decides — if it is well represented, sometimes more and sometimes less is achieved, whereas when it is not represented or badly represented, we have failed on all questions. We have seen this more than once already, and we see it constantly with every mistake that is made.

And therefore, therefore we must have representatives who will be responsible to the community, and the community should elect them and send them in the name of the population.

The concentration of the representatives as well as of the members must at all times take place in the association, towards which all must bear responsibility at the same time. For this purpose a life together is required, a brotherly life of the representatives as well as of the members.

That is the only way out that can improve the economic situation, not only in the field of tax defence but also in the field of trade, where the members should be taught to trade and earn, to calculate and organise themselves, and to be people on a par with others — and then the unheard-of lawlessness, which is making giant strides forward, will cease.

That is what we must remember in these hard times.

R. Let.
Meirl the Water-Carrier

[Hasidic tale — Aleksander Hasidism.] (A story of how Chaim Rifiner and Meirl the water-carrier were helped by the "Yismach Yisroel" of blessed memory, by way of a jest...)
(A Hasidic tale.)
By Ben-Tsiyon Grinboym.

It is well known that each of the rebbes ("good Jews") had his own particular ways, and in each "court" different customs prevailed: a different procedure for receiving a greeting (sholem), a different style of conducting the tish, different habits in the inns. In a word: one could tell that this was such-and-such a court, because there such-and-such a rebbe presided.

The Aleksander [Aleksandrów Łódzki] Rebbe of blessed memory, the "Yismach Yisroel" [R. Yerachmiel Yisroel Yitzchok Danziger], had a way of helping Jews "by way of a jest"... That is just how it is put — by way of a jest. What is meant is this: he used to clothe his intention and his advice in a witty saying. Not for nothing is he called "Yismach Yisroel" ("Let Israel rejoice") in the Hasidic world; his manner was to receive the needy with joy, and as the rebbe — so his Hasidim.

Among the intimates in Aleksander, the Charzhitsers [?] are known to this day; they were, incidentally, the court singers, merry Jews, keen Hasidim and witty phrase-makers all at once.

Once R. Yisroel Charzhitser [?] of blessed memory came to the "Yismach Yisroel" and asked his advice about a match. He has a young man, a fine scholar, who is already ripe for the wedding canopy, and he is looking for a suitable match for him.

The old Rebbe of blessed memory answered him:
"Do it with Moshe Rifiner! He has a virtuous Jewish daughter."

Needless to say, so it remained. Before anyone could say what or when, the preliminary terms (rashei prakim) were drawn up — in Aleksander itself, as it happens, since both of them, R. Yisroel Charzhitser as well as Moshe Rifiner, used to sit in Aleksander quite often. And indeed, within a short time the wedding took place.

The young couple lived very well. After the years of kest [board at the in-laws' table] the father-in-law set the young son-in-law up in a business beyond Warsaw. The business went well, there was a livelihood in the house, and all would have been well, were it not that the young man, Chaim Rifiner, was, heaven spare us, "lacking a face" [so printed — probably for "lacking sons"].

A year went by and another year, and there was no child. The young man wants a son, but the wife is barren. He is greatly grieved by it, but he says nothing — after all, the old Rebbe of blessed memory had been the matchmaker; what is there for him to say!

But now ten years had already passed since the wedding, when according to the law one may even give a barren wife a divorce. So Chaim Rifiner got up and travelled over to Aleksander — well, he would hear what the matchmaker would say...

Having arrived in Aleksander, one of course goes first to receive a greeting. The attendant lets him into the greeting room and he hands in a kvitl (petition note). Next to him stand other Jews, perhaps a minyan, perhaps more. For in Aleksander the custom is different from Ger [Góra Kalwaria]: in Ger they let people in to the rebbe only one at a time, whereas in Aleksander they let in even two minyans of Jews at once — such is the practice there.

The Rebbe looks through his kvitl and says nothing. Then he looks through the kvitl of another Jew. It was Meirl the water-carrier from Głowno. For forty years he had carried water in the shtetl, supplied Jews with well water for the Sabbath, and also supplied the Aleksander shtibl in Głowno with clean water.

Now, heaven spare us, he had suddenly become frail, and the doctor had forbidden him to carry water any longer, since it smacks of mortal danger.

So Meirl the water-carrier stands and pleads:
"Gevald and outcry! For forty years he has supplied Jews with water for washing the hands, for mayim acharonim, for cooking kosher food, for Sabbath and holiday meals — and now he is to be left, God have mercy, without bread. How can it be — is this the Torah and this its reward? If he had at least fifty roubles, he would buy himself a little cart with a horse and go on carting water."

Chaim Rifiner, in turn, has his own complaint, and pours out his heavy heart:
"The Yismach Yisroel himself was the matchmaker, and here he is ten years after the wedding — and nothing. Neither child nor calf [idiom: 'nothing at all']. Well, until now he has kept waiting and hoping. After all, the old Rebbe of blessed memory told him to make the match; but now, according to the law, he can wait no longer!"

The old Rebbe of blessed memory hears out the distress of both and is silent, but one can see a smile hovering on his lips. What the meaning of that smile is — that they already know in Aleksander.

Suddenly the old Rebbe of blessed memory speaks up, by way of a jest:
"Listen, Chaim, oy va [?], a good idea has occurred to me. Your wife wants to carry and cannot, and Meirl the water-carrier wants to carry and may not [pun: Yiddish 'trogn' means both to carry a load and to be pregnant]. You know what? Give Meirl fifty roubles so that he has the means to buy a horse with a cart; then he will have someone to carry for him, and your wife will have the merit to carry."

And so it was. It did not take long at all before Chaim came running to Aleksander with the good news: his wife had borne him a son, and they named him Pesach.

Chaim Rifiner already dwells in the dust, but his son, Pesach Rifiner — to distinguish between the living and the dead — is to this day a keen Aleksander Hasid, and on every holiday he turns worlds upside down in Aleksander with his merriment and joy.

Not for nothing does he understand a jest — for his soul, too, came down into this world only by way of a jest...

Natan Szpigel

[Art — exhibition in Katowice.] (From the art exhibition in Katowice).
Szymon Rotenberg.

What is art?
It is not at all easy to answer that. There are so many definitions that simply a chaos of concepts arises. Almost every artist, every art critic has a different concept of art.
Szpigel belongs to those artists who know that the spirit they seek is found within themselves, and from there they must drive it out onto the canvas. He speaks to us through the language of the line, through its rhythm, through its plasticity and through lyrical precision.
Take, for example, his oil painting "The Old Woman". It is a perfectly finished masterpiece. Both in composition and in the handling of colour it is "a chef-d'oeuvre" of painterly perfection. The vibration of the colour tones is so fine, so ethereally light, that we are simply seized by the noble, quiet "pianissimo" of the colour chords.
The same can be said of "The Woman Knitting". There too calm and cosiness are poured out, and one feels that the old woman is knitting into the sock the secrets[?] of a long life gone by.
"The Green Dress" is a wonderful achievement of being able to manipulate the brush so finely and with such ease, with such discretion to pass from the fat, deep green tones to the brightly shining ones.
Special attention is deserved by Szpigel's various painted fish. He has succeeded in fixing, besides their fine elasticity, also their slipperiness and liveliness, and the impression arises that the fish are leaping out of the canvas. In some places he managed to obtain such a magical, brightly shining colour that it creates the immediate impression that the colour phosphoresces.
A very great artistic victory Szpigel achieved in his watercolours. He has proved that he can paint in watercolour and at the same time remain emotional. It is simply astonishing how easily he masters the great technical difficulties that watercolour work raises; he displays a masterly technique and creates wonderful gleaming colour chords.
Watercolour painting is actually the road the artist must travel in order to return to oil painting. It is the best school for perfecting oneself, because with watercolour the artist, at the moment he lays on the colour, must have thought out well in advance what he wants, since he can no longer manipulate with the brush, as is the case with oil paints.
What the artist's relation to his creations looks like is best characterised by the following conversation.
To my question why he had placed some of his paintings, which I consider among the best, in such an inconspicuous spot that they are hard to notice, he answered me that each time people come and look at his paintings, he silently prays in his heart that it should not, God forbid, occur to anyone to buy these paintings, because they belong to his pampered darlings.
This relation of the artist to his work shows us clearly that for Szpigel painting is more than a practised art; for him it is a cult, a divine service.
With such a religion of art, we wish to hope, Szpigel will attain on his further artistic path that height, that perfection, for which "Apollo" endows the artist's works with the height of eternal values, of eternal power of attraction, of immortality.
Ignacy Hirszfang

[Art — exhibition in Katowice.] We usually regard rich manufacturers, or simply profiteers, as exploiters; that an artist should be an exploiter is hard even to believe, and yet one can say it of the painter Hirszfang, who takes from nature with full hands pieces of life, pieces of light, and packs them onto his canvases with such grace, with such verve, that it simply captivates us and it is hard to tear oneself away from his paintings.
Hirszfang's paintings have a magnetic power because they are not overworked, and therefore they breathe with such dewy freshness.
Hirszfang is a lyricist who sings out on the canvas his splendid soul-melodies and brings his lyricism to a quite high level.
His still lifes breathe with such vitality because Hirszfang looks at a still life as at a living thing, and he translates it into forms that once again evoke in us the illusion of life.
Hirszfang's self-portraits confirm once more that he is a painter who stands on a high artistic level. If a portrait is already a good touchstone of talent, this can be said all the more of a self-portrait, since a good self-portrait succeeds only for a painter who views himself quite objectively. He must be able to abstract himself as a stranger and be free of projecting subjective moods.
This, however, is very difficult, because there is always the danger that the painter will try to make himself more significant and more interesting than he is in reality. In a self-portrait the painter is at the same time: the client, the model and the artist. It is not easy to hold together these three, each of whom wants something different. Therefore the self-portrait is decisive when it comes to passing judgement on the artist's talent. Whoever is able to paint himself can, without doubt, also paint others.
One must not forget that absolute objectivity in a painter is almost impossible, because the painter always leaves traces of his own self on the painted canvas. If the painter is intelligent, temperamental, then all who sit for him take on a part of his intelligence or temperament. While he portrays others, he unconsciously depicts himself as well.
About the attitude of Jewish society to art in general and to Jewish art in particular, a great deal could be written. It is complete ignorance, the lack of the slightest understanding for Jewish plastic art — not only among the masses, who do not react to art because of the specific conditions in which they are brought up and in which they must live, but even among the intelligentsia, who are accustomed, for the sake of "bon ton", to talk about the various trends and to interpret the various "isms" in art — if among them there is, unfortunately, no relation at all to Jewish art and artists.
Because of this it very often happens that Jewish artists must create in a foreign camp, where there is a warmer environment for art, which is absolutely necessary for the development, for the existence of art, which, like a delicate, noble tropical plant, must wither and finally die in a cold, unspiritual atmosphere.
For those who love joy in life, mastery of artistic technique and aesthetic taste — for them the paintings of Szpigel and Hirszfang can be the source of emotion, of true joy of life, the oasis in the desert of everyday monotony, which represents the greatest danger, causing physical and spiritual degeneration.

[Feuilleton — humour; foreign passports.] By Y. Aberzhanek.

(Complaints of a man whose wife is getting ready to travel abroad on a 100-złoty passport)

Do you hear — if I had the say, if I had the say, I would dissolve the Sejm. Out with the Sejm, and enough! I've had enough of it already. Enough chattering [?], enough going round in circles [?]. I forgo their good fortune. I've had enough of the babble [?] of the "nebekh" speeches and the "revolutionary" speeches of the P.P.S. — if I had the say. Do you hear — if I had the say, I would dissolve the Sejm.

In truth, what do I get from the Sejm? Nothing but troubles and blows; wherever there's a trouble, wherever a calamity, wherever a decree — it comes from the Sejm.

But all the decrees until now were not as terrible as the latest decree! I mean the passport decree. In case I had too few troubles, they have favoured me with a brand-new [?] trouble, a spanking-new plague — with 100-złoty foreign passports.

Don't think [?] — I see how you stare at the 100-złoty passports. Perhaps you are even pleased that "foreign" passports have become cheaper; I say only one thing: for me the 100-złoty foreign passports are a misfortune, a trouble, "a plague not written in the Torah". For me your good luck is a great misfortune. This new passport decree is turning me grey and old before my time.

It doesn't make sense to you. You don't understand what I have to do with the cheap foreign passports? And why I am going grey and old because passports have become cheaper?

To blame for it is first the Sejm, and then — my Keyle Gnendl..

As you probably already know, my Keyle Gnendl is a great saver, and how much she thinks about thrift you can see from her clothes. The first woman to go out into the street in a little "décolleté" [?] dress was my Keyle Gnendl — she saved herself a whole metre of fabric.. When big décolletés went out of fashion, she found a solution: she cut away half a metre of fabric at the shoulder...

As you know, I live in two rooms with a kitchen. What does Keyle Gnendl do? She lets one room to two bachelors [lodgers]; and since she wants to save on light, she does not light the lamp in the flat, and whole evenings she sits in the bachelors' room — a sure sign [?]: a saver, no question about it...

That's Keyle Gnendl for you. All she looks for is how to save. She saves fabric on her clothes, she saves on light and on rent — a real woman of valour...

Well, that's good, isn't it? What could be better? One would think every husband would wish for a thrifty wife. But the trouble is that my Keyle Gnendl's savings come out of my head, and even more — out of my pocket.

What it means to have a thrifty wife I only found out last week. Jews, men, hear a story and take a moral from it — how to run away from a thrifty wife.

It was last week, when the angel in charge of the weather made it up [?] with the spring sun. The women let themselves out into the street like summer birds. When the "fair sex" went out on the Główna [main street?] to show off in their new "wiosenki" [spring outfits], while the spring sun stole [?] in through the window panes, my Keyle Gnendl says to me:

— Do you know what, Osherl, what has occurred to me?

— And what has occurred to you? I ask her.

— It is high time, she says, to think about thrift. These days one has to be a little more "oszczędna" [thrifty]. Golden banknotes [?] don't hang off you nowadays; one has to think how to save.

— Well, I say, by all means — you tell me, how can one save?

— I mean, she says, regarding the "letnie mieszkania" [summer lodgings]. You get blackened and gloomy all summer, it costs "mammon" and "damim" [a fortune]. For a "dziura" [a hole] in Bystra or in Ojców one stuffs the peasants' sack — what good is it? What do you get out of it, and what do I "skorzystać" [gain] from it — isn't that so, Osherl?

— May I have such a year, I told her, as how [?] right you are. What do I get out of it, and what do you "gain" from the "summer lodgings"?!

— There, you see, she goes on, now an idea has really occurred to me, how we can both "gain" and also save.

When I heard "save", my blood at once ran cold [?]. I understood that her "saving" would come out of my head, and even more — out of my pocket.

— Let me hear, I say, what does this saving consist of?

— Very simple, she says, you know that a passport for abroad costs, with all the "dodatki" [extras], a hundred altogether. Rather than hang on the peasants' necks [?], rather than settle somewhere in a "dziura", surely a foreign passport for a hundred is better. You'll have peace, you won't have to haul [?] the suitcases every Friday onto the trains and buses, and I will "przy okazji skorzystać" [benefit on the occasion]... I'll take my liver abroad. Why shouldn't a German professor make the acquaintance of my liver? When a passport cost 500 zł. I had to drag myself and my liver around the doctors of Zagłębie and Katowice, but for a hundred I can surely show up with my liver in Berlin too...

I saw that I had fallen into a nasty trap. I understood that my Keyle Gnendl's "saving" would again come out of my head. The passport — a hundred; the railway won't carry my 100-kilo Keyle Gnendl for free either; and what about half a dozen "zagraniczne" [foreign-style] dresses, slippers [?] and little hats, besides "all the other vegetables".

I tried to talk my Keyle Gnendl out of her "saving plan": it isn't proper, I said, a Jewish woman alone in a foreign country — what will people say?

Of course Keyle Gnendl got her way. When she has said "abroad" — it's abroad. Once she has decided to export her liver to Germany, it's a lost cause.

This is where the main course really begins. As you know, to get a foreign passport one needs a Polish passport, and which Jew (read: Jewess) already has a Polish passport? So one has to go and take out a Polish passport — and here is a new trouble again: for a Polish passport one needs a "metryka" [birth certificate], and which Jew (read: Jewess) already has a metryka? So one has to run and take out a metryka — and here is a fresh trouble again: to obtain a metryka one needs a "wyciąg" [register extract]. Now go and find out where, in which town, Keyle Gnendl was born — and how should I know, when she herself doesn't know either.

So now I really am running from town to town. Here the Russian registration books are missing, there she was never born at all; they send me from one magistrat [town hall] to the next, and she still has no wyciąg.

Now I have one request of the Master of the Universe:

You are a merciful God, You have already shown so many miracles — show a miracle now too: let it turn out that Keyle Gnendl has not been born to this day... let Keyle Gnendl not get a "wyciąg"...

Do you hear — if I had the say, I would chase the Sejm apart, and basta. I forgo their slaps [?] and their new passport decree...

Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Acharei Mot-Kedoshim)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.
Parashat Acharei-Kedoshim.
—o—
a) Acharei Mot, Kedoshim, Emor.
The names of these three consecutive portions form a complete verse: "After death — holy, say" (Acharei mot, kedoshim emor) — after death one says of the deceased: he was holy... While he lived, everyone spoke ill of him, "forbidden to speak"; but after his death he suddenly becomes a saint in everyone's mouth, and everyone boasts of a connection with him.
Folk saying.
* * *
"When a sage dies, all are his relatives" (Shabbat 105).
In life, "bread is not to the wise": the sage dies of hunger and nobody so much as looks his way. He seeks relatives — but everyone hides from him, everyone edges away. But when the sage dies and the danger of having to help him out with something vanishes — then: all are his relatives; everyone becomes his kin, everyone shows that he was his relation. What harm is there in it? Money one won't have to give him anyway any more...
Malbim.
b) "After the death of the two sons of Aaron" (16:1).
One of the reasons why Nadab and Abihu perished was "that they did not take counsel with one another": each had convinced himself that he was already so great that he no longer needed his brother's advice and help. "Each his censer" — each had his own censer, each took everything on his own responsibility.
Tanchuma.
c) "And let him not come at all times into the holy place" (16:2).
The Dubno Maggid came to a rich man on a matter of charity. The rich man, a learned man besides, said to the Maggid: I give enough charity; on the verse "and he who does charity at all times" the Gemara (Ketubot) expounds: this is one who supports his sons and his household — whoever provides a livelihood for his wife and children, that is called charity at all times, at every moment.
To this the Maggid replied: "And let him not come at all times into the holy place" — with such charity, of the "at all times" kind, with such charity one cannot come into the holy place.
d) "That the land vomit you not out" (18:28).
The meaning of the verse is: although the Land of Israel vomited out the earlier nations when they were sinful, you Jews, even when there will be "when you defile it", even if you are not properly pious — the Land of Israel will not vomit you out, because you are her children.
Melekhet Machshevet.
* * *
The Holy One, blessed be He, says: "I would rather that My children be with Me at home (in the Land of Israel), even though they do not do My will as they should."
Yalkut Reuveni.
"You shall be holy" (19:2).
When Jews do not make Kiddush — when they do not fulfil the commandment "You shall be holy" — the gentiles make Havdalah over them: they are kept away from all sources of livelihood.
Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin.
f) "You shall be holy.. every man shall fear his mother and his father.. turn not to idols" (19:2, 3, 4).
Each of these verses ends with "I am the Lord", because they refer to three categories of Jews. The first: the holy, the very pious — upon them comes the endorsement "I am the Lord", meaning a documentary certification that they are Jews. The second: "every man shall fear his mother and his father" — upon those whose whole Jewishness consists only of honouring their parents: well, they too are Jews, and upon them too comes the signature "I am the Lord". The third: the real assimilationists, whose whole Jewishness consists only in "turn not to idols" — in not converting; of them too it is said "I am the Lord": they too are Jews.
Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin (according to Rabbi Yeshaya Zlotnik).
g) "You shall not steal" (19:11).
In the Ten Commandments the prohibition "You shall not steal" is in the singular — thou shalt not steal. Here the prohibition is stated in the plural, "you [pl.] shall not steal", because it is addressed to the "fine" Jews, whom one does not usually address with the familiar "thou" but with the polite "you" (to a respectable Jew one does not say "thou" but "you", or "he"[?]) — the Torah says that even such Jews must not steal, and a special prohibition is needed for it.
Rabbi Baruch Mordechai of Shedlitz [Siedlce][?].
h) "Love your neighbour as yourself, I am the Lord" (19:18).
Rabbi Naftali of Ropshitz [Ropczyce] related that when he was a small boy, his teacher taught him that when two letters yud stand side by side, level, it is a Name — God's name. The little one made a mistake and called the two dots ending a verse in the Chumash (:) a Name as well. The teacher told him: when two Jews ["yidn", also the letters yud] stand level beside each other, it is a Name; but when one sets himself above the other, it is nothing..
When there is "love your neighbour as yourself" — you hold the other Jew equal to yourself — then it is "I am the Lord", it is a Name; but if you set yourself above him, it is nothing..
Ohel Naftali.
—o—
Avot, Chapter Three.
a) "And there are no words of Torah between them" (3).
"Two who sit" — when two scholars sit "and there are no words of Torah between them", the Torah is not shared between them; each sits apart with his own little Torah, isolated, distant — that is a "seat of scoffers"; such Torah has no value.
Tosafot Yom Tov.
b) "Three who ate at one table" (4).
"Who ate" is phrased in the after-the-fact (bedi'eved) form, because one need not eat together, but individually.
"And you shall serve the Lord your God, and He will bless your bread" — with "service", meaning prayer, the plural is used ("and you [pl.] shall serve"), because one must pray in a congregation; but with "your bread" it is singular — because eating should be done individually..
Midrash Shmuel.
* * *
On the Sabbath before the meal one invites the angels and greets them: "Peace be upon you, ministering angels", and at once bids them farewell: "Go in peace". Why does one dismiss them so quickly?
Because when one is going to eat, one says even to angels "go in peace" — go in good health..
Folk saying.
The Balfour Month in Poland

(Sent by the Central Committee of the KKL [Jewish National Fund] in Warsaw.)

The Action Committee decided at its last session to collect 5000 inscriptions in the special volume of the "Golden Book" (Sefer ha-Zahav) dedicated to the memory of Balfour. The Jewish people must show the whole world how much it values and reveres the name of the great deceased, who publicly proclaimed the building of the Jewish National Home and realised this proclamation of his with the Balfour Declaration, which was turned into an international document that serves as the basis for all our political and colonisation work in the Land. Through these inscriptions, through erecting an eternal monument to Balfour, the people will express its strong faith and deep reverence for the realisation of the Declaration in its full breadth [?] and scope. Besides its monetary value, this campaign of ours also has great significance as a demonstration of our Zionist forces and a revelation of our will to realise our aspirations to establish and consolidate our National Home. All of world Jewry is stepping forward to carry out the Balfour campaign, and Polish Jewry will of course take its proper place.

In connection with the above, the Directorate in Poland has proclaimed a Balfour Month, which will last the whole month of May, until 5 June. The Lag ba-Omer campaign and the pledges (nedarim) [?] at Shavuot will be carried out in favour [?] of the Balfour campaign. Throughout this whole period public meetings will be organised, popular assemblies in Balfour's memory and large popular collections for inscribing Balfour in the "Golden Book".

At the centre of the Balfour Month will stand the great popular collection, which will take place on Lag ba-Omer over 3 days, from 15 to 18 May, Thursday, Friday and Sunday, when signatures and donations for the inscriptions in the Balfour volume of the "Golden Book" will be collected on special forms.

A detailed circular has been sent to all KKL committees throughout the country, which must already now place the necessary orders for the material and found the joint Balfour committees.

Express trains do not stop at the Będzin railway stations / Dr. Gottlieb's lecture — on the 24th of this month / Mi-sheberakhs at the cemetery..

In the previous issue of our paper we brought the news that the new timetable has been put together so „logically“ that the express trains would not stop at the Będzin railway station.
Everyone naturally treated this news with scepticism; nobody believed that such crazy things could even occur to the authors of the new timetable.
But the unbelievable is a reality: from Wednesday at 12 midnight onward the express trains do not stop at the above-mentioned station.
The memoranda and telegrams of the Magistrate [town council] and of the merchants' institutions have had no effect whatsoever so far.
On this question we conferred yesterday with representatives of the Supervisory and the Municipal Council, who stated that one must wait until the 24th of this month, when the president of the Railway Directorate in Warsaw returns from Madrid, and then it may perhaps be possible to bring about that the express trains be held at the station for at least one minute.
—o—
Dr. Gottlieb's lecture — on the 24th of this month.
Yesterday the women's organisation „WIZO“ in Będzin received a telegram from Dr. Gottlieb, that he is coming to Będzin on the 24th of this month to give a talk entitled[?] „My impressions in America“.
The lecture will take place in the „Nowości“ theatre.
—o—
Mi-sheberakhs at the cemetery..
Yesterday, on the day of the first yahrzeit of R' Nachum Cukierman of blessed memory, a tombstone was set up.
Rabbi Friedberg spoke about the significance of a tombstone and the great merits of the deceased..; Cantor Żutowicz[?] sang the appropriate prayers, and the president of „Ahavat Chesed“ ordered the cantor to make a „Mi-sheberakh“ for each member of the family, and above all „ba'avur she-nadar“ [„because he pledged“ — i.e. a donation]...
This „brilliant“ act naturally aroused bitterness in everyone..
A theft at the Będzin „Urząd Skarbowy“ [tax office]

In the night from Wednesday to Thursday the lock was torn off the storehouse in which the requisitioned [distrained] goods of the „Urząd Skarbowy“ [tax office] in Będzin are kept.
The damage from the theft is not great.

This week a conference took place at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, at which the Interior Ministry's draft on the supervision of meat processing was discussed.
A number of Christian butchers from Będzin and Sosnowiec took part in the conference.
Of the Jewish representatives who had been invited, none was present.. G.[?]

A young man has disappeared.
On Sunday the nineteen-year-old Szturner[?] left his parents' flat in Old Sosnowiec and disappeared.
Despite all efforts the young man has not yet been found.

A fire in Wolbrom.
In the night from Tuesday to Wednesday a fire broke out in Piltzer [Pilicka?] Street in Wolbrom.
5 houses burned down.

Killed at work.
On Saturday a 32-year-old woman worker was killed by electric current at the „Huta Bankowa“ ironworks in Dąbrowa.
On Monday a 45-year-old miner was killed at the „Paryż“ coal mine.

Injured by the tram.
At the Będzin railway station there is an elderly character still from the old times — the mute Christian, a well-known drunkard. On Sunday he was strolling in the middle of Małachowskiego Street. At that moment a tram came by, which gave him a strong blow and badly injured him.

A gang of pickpockets arrested.
This week the Sosnowiec police carried out a „lustration“ [spot check] in the cinemas[?]. The „lustration“ gave a very good result. Arrested were: Herman Szajer[?] (Bernów[?]), Simcha Liberman (Radom), Abraham Lafman (Kraków) and Icchak Goldberg (Częstochowa).
The arrested men are known as „qualified craftsmen“...
Fearing the police, bandits jump into a canal.

[Sosnowiec — crime; police.]
Yesterday at about 7 in the evening the following incident took place in Sosnowiec:
On Third of May Street [ulica 3 Maja] card sharps "took to work" a Silesian [Ślązak], from whom they took his whole couple of gulden [colloquial for złoty].
When the Silesian, seeing his ruin, demanded his money back, he received "as a bonus" [a blow] with a knife.
At that moment a policeman passed by; the bandits started to run away and went into a deep canal not far from the church [cerkiew].
A larger detachment of police and firemen tried by various means to catch the bandits, but at the time this issue went to press the result of the chase was not yet known.

Parents' Conference at the Jewish Girls' Gymnasium with the Participation of Former Senator Dr. Braude

[Sosnowiec — education.] (Sh—kh) The Jewish girls' gymnasium in Sosnowiec, which after hard toil and work by a group of devoted idealists headed by Dr. Meladista[?] was raised to a very high level (as confirmed by the latest inspection of the school inspectorate), is now threatened with ruin. The reason is an eviction which the landlord of the house where the school is located has obtained against the school.
The school's situation at the present moment is so dangerous that in the very next few days it threatens to be put out on the street. The various interventions of respected and influential persons have so far produced no result whatsoever. Having no other way out, the management was compelled to invite the founder and curator of the Jewish gymnasia, former Senator Dr. Braude of Łódź, in order to consult together with the parents on how to find a way out of the situation that has arisen.
The conference took place last Thursday evening in the hall of the Merchants' Association (Kowalska[?] 2).
City councillor and president Dr. Meladista opened the conference, greeting the very distinguished guest, who founded the type of Jewish gymnasia to which the Sosnowiec gymnasium belongs. In brief strokes the speaker then gave an overview of the thorny path the school has travelled during its existence. "These have been 8 years of hard and devoted work," concluded Dr. Meladista, "and now, when we have already brought the institution to a proper level, we are threatened with ruin — and that because of a premises question."
Dr. Meladista gave the floor to the distinguished guest Dr. Braude, who delivered a two-hour lecture rich in content on the education of the Jewish generation then and now.
"Twenty years ago," the lecturer began, "we did not yet know of a special Jewish gymnasium. The Jewish father who sent his child to a gymnasium had from the outset resigned from Jewishness, because the child, finding itself in a foreign environment and receiving a foreign education, quickly assimilated. There were cases where children were sent to foreign schools deliberately, for a purpose. The father thought that when the child finished the gymnasium with a certificate from a Christian school, it would have open doors in the world. The sad reality, however, showed something different. A Jew who wanted to blot out his Jewishness did not succeed so long as he had not had those few drops of baptismal water on him. It is the greatest sin of Jewish parents that they give their children to non-Jewish schools, for when learning in a Jewish school the child also receives a Jewish education, founded on the old, glorious Jewish tradition."
Turning to the matter of Sosnowiec, the lecturer drew an analogous comparison between the two cities of Łódź and Sosnowiec.
"I have spent the last years," the distinguished guest continued, "in the factory city of Łódź. Łódź perhaps arose a few decades earlier than Sosnowiec, but it too is a new city without traditions. Yet Łódź has created, and keeps creating, hospitals and various social, cultural and philanthropic institutions. And what has Sosnowiec accomplished during the whole time of its existence? True, there is a Jewish hospital — but that was created by the old generation, the assimilationists; and even the gymnasium, which ought to be your finest institution, was not created by you either. One cannot merely live and spend oneself in commerce just in order to get rich. The only Jewish institution, the Jewish girls' gymnasium that exists in your town, is to go to ruin — and for what? Because of a few rooms? Is this not a disgrace and a shame for Jewish Sosnowiec? I have not come to preach morals to you, but where is humanity? The gymnasium should long ago have had a building of its own. I want Jewish public opinion to feel that this affair utterly degrades the honour of Jewish society."
Dr. Braude's lecture, rich in content, made a strong impression on those assembled and was listened to with the greatest attention. The audience gave Dr. Braude long-lasting ovations.
Then alderman (ławnik) Dr. Pruks[?] took the floor and gave a short but very successful and in places moving speech. Advocate Pruks greeted the guest as one of those from whom he had learned a great deal. "The very distinguished and esteemed Dr. Braude," said Dr. P., "surely does not know me, but for 25 years I have been drawing from the well of wisdom of the learned Dr. Braude." Dr. Pruks proposed that they immediately set about forming a committee whose task would be to settle the matter as quickly as possible.
Further speakers were Messrs. S. Warman, Lubelski, president L. Zendel[?], Jungster, Grandapfel[?] and Rabbi Hager.
Dr. Meladista replied to all the speakers, and a committee was formed which includes Messrs. Rabbi Hager, Advocate Pruks, president L. Zendel, Y. Saks, Broner, M. Rajner, S. Lubelski, Lajzerowicz, Raman and Binkowski.

Impossible Possibilities
(The Railway Ministry plans that the express trains shall not stop in Będzin)

[Będzin — transport and railways; article.]
Upon my life, there was an uproar a week ago Friday: almost a whole day the editorial telephone rang, everyone asked for an interpretation, an explanation of the notice printed in our paper that from 15 May the express trains would no longer stop in Będzin. Many wondered and could not understand what this was supposed to mean; some thought it simply could not be, that it was a thing of impossibility; one even asked whether it was not a first-rate April Fool's joke that had not made it into the issue in time and that the young typesetter had now put in by mistake. That it was correct news, an accomplished fact, never entered anyone's head; nobody could imagine it.
What does this mean, everyone asked himself, all at once — that not a single express train will stop, neither in Old Będzin nor in New Będzin? What will one do when one has to get off at Będzin? Ah, it cannot be understood — what does it mean, one will not be able to come to Będzin? You must have heard wrongly and not understood properly — so everyone tried to explain it to himself, that the news could not match reality; and it took no small effort with each and every one until, willy-nilly, he had to digest the unbelievable news.
Of course we are not at all surprised that the inhabitants of Będzin were beside themselves when they read the strange report, which is, after all, incomprehensible to everyone.
And a real piece of work began for the Magistrat [city council], the Chamber of Commerce and the economic associations, which are sending memoranda, petitions and delegations to the Railway Ministry pointing out the wrong decision. As we write these lines we do not yet know whether all this has had any effect and how far the arguments have been listened to. The decision will find its place in the chronicle, which will tell us the outcome of the comic report.
But this does not interest us. Would that it had not interested the above-mentioned institutions either, and that they had left things as they are [?]; for if the Railway Ministry believes that Będzin should be erased from the timetable — as if that were an honour for Polish culture, such an old historic town where Polish kings built castles, palaces and fortresses — then why should we interfere here? For us the very thought is enough: that someone wants to turn a town into a village.
It is interesting that some twenty-odd years ago, when we belonged to Russia and, owing to a combination of interested persons, a railway station was built outside the town, and Petersburg — which, it goes without saying, never took any notice of Będzin — ordered that the express trains should stop only at the so-called "New Station", it was already then achieved that they should also stop in the town. And now, 20 years later, when Poland is independent and when the capital is so near to us and knows what role Będzin plays both in history and in the present, they manage to treat such a town with such disregard that it borders on comedy. In Petersburg Będzin existed outside the town, at the New Station; in Warsaw the town exists neither at the New Station nor at the Old one — in a word, for the Railway Ministry Będzin does not exist. Well, can that be understood? Can one imagine so much that is comic and ridiculous?!
We believe that Będzin will later be put back into the new timetable, but that is not the point; what interests us is only the thought: how can one imagine that a train should run past a large town and not be permitted to stop.
And what sort of town is Będzin? First of all it is the oldest town of Zagłębie, with a great and rich past; at the same time it develops constantly, so that at present, when the government gives almost no help to construction, not only houses but whole streets are being added, and it counts some 50 thousand inhabitants. Będzin is the crown of Zagłębie. Here are the powiat [district], the starosta, the police headquarters, the 23rd regiment of the army; besides, a large and rich surrounding area of factories and coal mines, and in the town itself trade plays, after all, a great role. What enormous sums does the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office] draw in Będzin from the local merchants?
Besides, we know how great the bustle is at the station in Będzin when a train arrives; it seems that from Sosnowiec to Częstochowa you will not see another station with such lively traffic as in Będzin. So it will turn out that at a station such as, for example, Tychy [?], where surely not even two persons get on or off, the express will stop, while past Będzin it will rush like a meteor. Upon my life, nothing invented!
Now the new station building is being built here, which costs several million złoty. So what is it needed for, if not a single express train will have to stop for it? Evidently the right hand does not know what the left is doing.
As is known, every express train carries the mail; so how is Będzin to send it off and receive it? It turns out, then, that either in Dąbrowa or in Sosnowiec — and if not, it will have to lie there for a few hours until it is sent on by another train; this may therefore cause the postmen to deliver the mail a whole day late. Upon my life, that is what you call progress!
We know from old times past that Russia was called the land of impossible possibilities; we knew that whatever is not at all possible can become possible in Russia. And here in Poland — could one ever have imagined that old, well-ordered towns, which keep building up and developing constantly, should suddenly be turned into villages by the railway directorate? Is this not impossible possibilities?
Let us imagine that a foreigner wants to travel to Będzin — he will not be able to find the town, because on the map he will have Będzin, but in the timetable not. He will therefore have to get off at the nearest station and then travel on to us. He will picture to himself that he must travel to a village, to a godforsaken place where no railway goes; and when he enters the town and sees the wide streets with the 4–5-storey houses, with the trams and cars and human bustle, he will be beside himself; he will not be able to understand how [?] backwardness is combined with progress, antiquity with the latest mechanical inventions.
And if such a European asks us for an explanation, what will we be able and obliged to answer him? Will we be able to tell him that we find ourselves in the land of impossible possibilities? And if not, what answer will we have to give him?
And if we have no answer for him, let it at least be recorded for history that in the year 1930, in the Polish railway directorate, the town of Będzin was erased for the express trains that rush past us into the European cultural world.
Y. T. [?]
Jewish Children in Schools of Their Own

(A letter from Kraków.)
In a short while Jewish Kraków will celebrate the opening of the new building for the Jewish gymnasium. Through the effort and help of Kraków's own philanthropists a fine 3-storey building is going up, built according to the new pedagogical and sanitary requirements. It is worth noting that construction of the building began this past winter. The gymnasium belongs to the "Society for Jewish Elementary and Secondary Schools", which has recently set itself the goal of expanding and developing the Jewish school system in Kraków. The latest sad events in the university cities of Europe. The latest events in Jewish life in the Diaspora and in Eretz Israel have clearly shown that we must raise a national generation that will understand its duties. That can only happen in our own schools, in schools conducted in a Jewish and national spirit.
In Kraków there is now also talk of creating a vocational school for Jewish youth. Such a school is very necessary, because the surplus among the intelligentsia, and especially among the Jewish intelligentsia, has already clearly shown that we must create our own vocational schools, which will train intelligent and good craftsmen. The new building of the Kraków Jewish school organisation should make it possible to expand the school in this direction.
What a building of its own means for a school we know well. Premises of its own — that is the elementary condition for a school's existence. We can say boldly that the building which the "Yavneh" received in Będzin has secured the school's existence and a sure development for the future. But beyond all that, receiving a building of its own is of great value in that the school will at last be rid of the Jewish landlord who "understands" so well the necessity of a school of our own and "helps" it at every step. The latest proof of this we now have in Sosnowiec. It is unbelievable that a Jewish landlord should come out with such doggedness against the only Jewish private gymnasium in Zagłębie. In Będzin one man comes and builds a splendid building, gives the school new strength to live and develop, and in Sosnowiec another Jew comes and undermines the foundations of the other school. It sounds like a paradox, but it is the sad reality.
The population of Sosnowiec should take as a model the new school building rising in Kraków. One must have good will, one must take the matter seriously, and there will not be a single person who, understanding the importance of a school of our own for Jewish youth (excepting those who know how to throw it out), will not come to help according to his means. To what happened recently in Sosnowiec the whole Jewish population must respond — and finally understand that there is one single salvation, a salvation that will secure for the school, once and for all, an independent development:
Build a school of your own for your children!
Eliyahu Gertner.
A Little Feuilleton — The Fourth Moment

The Fourth Moment.
There are three moments — Max Nordau once said — when the greatest sage feels like an idiot: when the barber shaves him, when the tailor fits him for a garment, and when someone praises him to his face.
When the barber shaves him — how so?
He sits in the chair, helpless as a child, and the barber daubs soap lather over his face with the brush as much as his heart desires — he can even treat him to a portion of lather in the mouth, and the other must keep silent; he dare not open his mouth, for he will only make it worse...
When the tailor fits him for a garment — how so?
The tailor turns him this way and that like a dummy, and he has to let himself be — does he have a choice?..
When someone praises him to his face — how so?
Just imagine: someone pays you a compliment that you are clever, a sage, and you smile contentedly.
But just try, on the contrary, to catch a glance in the mirror at that moment, and you will see how clever you look with that smile...
Were Max Nordau alive now, however, he would surely say that there are not just three moments, but all of four — for instance, the moment our deputies are living through now.
A deputy — no small thing!
He is, after all, the greatest sage of all sages — he is elected so that, at his own discretion, he may elect a president, arrest [?] a minister — and he indeed makes use of this wisdom: what he wants he does, when he wants he gives...
But what do our deputies look like at the present moment? They have mouths but speak not...
Neither alive nor dead: to the Sejm they cannot come for fear — they must wait until they are called — and to the voters they cannot come for shame.
What can they tell the voter, when they do not even know whether they will be called at all.
Never has a deputy earned his pension so honestly as at the present moment, when he, the sage, has to play the role of a fool...
And not only the deputies — even our own local town councillors are now living through the fourth moment.
Who does not remember the uproar and the chase after the seats on the eve of the town-council elections?
We thought, and they thought.
We thought that through them we would become masters over ourselves, over our town; and they thought that through us they would rise to greatness — their voice would be heard...
But how does it look now?
Does not our Jewish town council look just like our Polish Sejm? Are not the councillors in the same situation as the deputies? Their situation is perhaps even worse, for the deputies at least get money for their "trouble" — and what do the councillors get?
They sometimes get invitations to come to "Małachowskiego Street", but they have as much say there as the deputies have on Wiejska Street — and neither these nor those can tell us, the voters, anything; they are now living through the fourth moment: they have mouths but speak not..
Here and there no one has a word — because "it is Acher [the Other]". What he wants he does, when he wants he gives..
Onkelos.

Philanthropy or Collectivization

[Sosnowiec — free-loan societies and social welfare; opinion.]
(On the margin of the recent conference of the free-loan [gemilut chasadim] societies)
In connection with the recent conference in Sosnowiec of the gemilut chasadim (free-loan) societies of the Kielce voivodeship, some reflections come to mind which I would like to share with the readers of the newspaper.
No one who has taken a little interest in, or got to know, the aims and work of the free-loan societies, who has had the opportunity personally to help in the development of the institution and to help it, or even those who benefit from the society, will deny that the societies carry out very important public work, and that not one but [printed "gur", for "nur"] tens and hundreds of Jewish families have been saved by it from hunger and ruin. Very right, however, were the words of the chairman of the conference, the president of the Jewish community of Częstochowa, Mr. Goldsztajn, who remarked that one must not forget in this that, thanks to the free-loan societies, the number of petty traders and peddlers is growing — people who work very hard to earn a dry piece of bread. It cannot be otherwise, because that is the proper aim of the free-loan societies. On the other hand, the societies from time to time support Jewish artisans, buying them tools for their work. The speaker also mentioned the right to work for the Jewish masses, and the state and municipal posts that are completely closed to Jews.
We must not forget, however, that the Jewish people does not consist only of petty traders, peddlers, merchants and artisans. Besides, there are also such craftsmen who do not know their trade, the so-called "partacze" [bunglers] — the Jewish people does not consist only of such elements, as some activists of the free-loan societies may imagine. Our general aim must be that the Jewish people should not consist of these hardly productive or entirely unproductive elements; rather, one must strive to make the Jewish masses productive. This aim, incidentally, is already inscribed on the banner of the Zionists — in the Zionist sense, of course. We must remember that for 10 years the organization ORT has been working throughout the Polish Republic; it has created a network of institutions where one can properly learn a trade: a number of trade schools, summer courses for artisans, for master craftsmen and for master craftsmen [sic, repeated], and also for adults who want to learn a craft; thousands of craftsmen have benefited from these courses. The work of vocational education borders on another problem — bringing Jews into small and large industry, so-called industrialization. First place in this respect is held by ORT in Łódź, where it maintains a school-factory to prepare workers for the various branches of the textile industry. Similar school-factories exist and are being founded in other towns too. ORT procures machines and implements for Jewish workers and artisans. The third part of the work with which the ORT society is engaged is work on the land: in hundreds of places ORT has brought help to Jewish settler-farmers and gardeners who were ruined during the World War; later ORT created among the Jewish settlers a network of cooperatives for field workers and gardeners. The ORT society also mediates in the shipping of machines from Americans to their relatives in Poland, and lately it has developed a broad campaign to supply machines and tools to the declassed Jews in Soviet Russia.
About all these things nobody speaks here in Zagłębie; nobody talks, nobody has any interest in getting involved with the JEAS organization, whose aim is planned help for Jewish emigrants emigrating from Poland and other countries — to give the emigrants moral protection and also to give them vocational and language preparation for emigration. Finally we must also say a few words about TOZ, whose branch has existed here in Sosnowiec for several years, but the interest in it on the part of Jewish society equals zero, and because of that it cannot develop properly. And yet, if one took into account the important tasks, the splendid aims and the great work that ought to be accomplished even in Zagłębie; if one reflected even a little on the fact that the aim of the TOZ society is to prepare the Jewish masses for a new life under new living conditions, where a great reserve of physical strength is required, where a physically healthy life is necessary; that TOZ creates a healthy, not hunchbacked Jew; that TOZ has cured thousands of Jews sick with tuberculosis, that it has cured thousands of children who were sick with favus [scalp ringworm], and thereby many of them were given the possibility to emigrate — we shall come to the conclusion that the work of the Sosnowiec and Będzin public activists is limited entirely to the work of free loans or orphanages.
One cannot say that this work is not useful; but it is a drop in the ocean, while the most fundamental tasks are neglected; everything that represents the future of the broadest Jewish masses in Poland, who are threatened by pauperization, has been neglected.
Recently all the above-mentioned institutions, together with the CENTOS society (union for the protection of orphans), have united and created a united committee, which has set itself the aim of conducting a propaganda campaign under the motto: "Reconstruction and Self-Help". The union came about with the purpose of coordinating the work. The campaign must embrace all strata of the Jewish population, since it is non-political [? printed "a politishe"]. The mark of the campaign is the economic, physical and social reconstruction of the Jewish masses.
A little energy and work — and one can achieve a great deal.
Dr. K. Trapojer [?].
