A Prezes

[Humour — feuilleton.]
A prezes [chairman] —
What sort of creature is that? What kind of talent must one have in order to be a prezes?
What must one know?
What must one possess?
Must one be clever? Educated? Well-read? Intelligent?
Must one be a writer? A diplomat? A philosopher?
No! A thousand and ten thousand times no and no!
So who can be a prezes?
I will answer you: every person living in the world can be one.
He need only possess something that not every plain person possesses.
When a person — it makes no difference whether he is a whole, a half or a scrap of a person — merely possesses that very "something", he can be a prezes, a chairman, or, as some [—] Yiddishists call it: a "benklman" [bench-man].
What, then, is that "something" that a prezes must possess?
We will explain it to you. And if God has blessed you with a good head with brains, you will understand me very easily.
Let us begin!
When a young man, for instance, wants to become a bridegroom, what must he possess?
He must first of all be a young man; a handsome one, a clever one, a father's son [of good family], not a card-player, not a drinker, not a dissolute fellow; have charm, intelligence and, above all — be a good earner, have money in the bank and love a girl.
When a young man possesses all these excellent virtues, such a one can quickly become a bridegroom.
It is the same with a girl: if a girl is getting on, let us say eighteen or nineteen, or twenty, or even twenty-five years old, and she is not ugly, not a fool, lively, cheerful, capable, well-read, she does not drag about every night with other young men and she has brains — indeed, such a one can very easily get a fine young man, marry and become a mother. And later, when the children marry too and have children of their own, such a girl becomes a grandmother.
Now let us go a little further:
When a Jew wants to become a melamed [teacher of small children], he must know how to teach children, hand out a smack now and then, have a lot of patience, a healthy heart, [?] lungs, and must also know how to go hungry.
Such a Jew can in time become the greatest melamed in the world.
The same goes for all other professions:
A watchmaker must have sharp eyes, a lot of time, must poke about in the works of watches, make out the tiniest little screws, much smaller than a pinhead.
And besides that he must actually understand the craft.
A tailor must have a stomach that will not demand any food, and have a wife with seven children and a mother-in-law in the house, and not have a decent apartment.
A cantor, on the other hand, must have a voice, be a good singer, understand the meaning of the words, have a good post, get his wages on time and not give a hoot for his choir-conductor.
Otherwise he cannot be a cantor and have success.
A musician must possess a good ear, a fine feeling to catch the subtlest sounds.
A poet must possess a rich imagination, fiery wings, a broad heart, a still broader soul, and be surrounded by a lot of pretty girls.
It makes no difference which girls: brunettes, blondes, redheads or — others.
So long as they are girls!
Then the poet can create his "immortal poems".
Then he can sing of the mountains, the rivers, the forests, the Godhead, love and everything together.
And as you know, or do not know, with all poets love stands far higher than the Godhead.
Although the Godhead is in heaven and love is on earth.
A writer, on the other hand, must possess rich thoughts, know the craft, have a clean handwriting, must know how to "oysleynen" [?] well and must live [in peace] with all editors and publishers.
And on top of all these great virtues he must absolutely have talent.
Without talent he is a nothing of nothings: a disease, a beast.
With speakers it is the same.
A speaker must possess a mouth, a tongue and brains.
On these three pillars rests the whole art of oratory.
Besides these three pillars a speaker must know when to stop.
In stopping lies great wisdom, much greater wisdom than in beginning!
Any Jew who has a mouth and a tongue in his mouth can begin a sermon, but not everyone can end a sermon.
We have speakers who talk and talk for whole hours and say nothing; they do not want to say what they are talking. And there are such as say nothing and say a great deal and finish at the right time, and then again there are such as speak before fire and before water [i.e. before anyone at all] and do not know when to finish.
Such speakers should be shot! Simply shot!
The sooner, the better for the listeners and the healthier for himself.
The bottom line is, as that joker from the "Kibitzarnia" [the kibitzers' club] said:
Before a person is born, an angel comes flying and gives him a kiss. If the angel gives him a kiss on the head, he grows up a man of brains; if the angel gives him a kiss on the throat, he grows up a singer; if the angel gives him a kiss on the hand, he grows up a fiddler, or a boxer, or a beggar, or a thief, a man with "long fingers"... And if by chance the angel gives him a kiss on that place which is needed for sitting, he grows up a chairman, a prezes, as it is called.
A prezes, with whom no person can compare himself.
In other words: it has nothing at all to do with us; it depends entirely on the angel — if he kisses the right spot, there is born — a prezes.
B. Kovner.
The Tax Pains

[Poland — taxes; opinion.] By A. Tiktin.
The whole world of industry and commerce in Poland is writhing in pain and groaning heavily under the yoke of the taxes which the Sejm, with its "kosher" hand, has laid upon its neck. Everyone, almost without exception, agrees that the high taxes are undermining the foundation of our economic edifice; everyone agrees that it cannot go on like this. The government itself also agrees that our tax system must undergo a radical reform, and... people bustle [?], they fuss, they write and erase and write again. Whether anything will ever come of it is hard to predict. As the Frenchman says: whoever lives will see.
The tax screw was tightened after the war in many states that were financially ruined by the war. Here it presses harder than anywhere else: first, because we are poorer than all the others; second, because to the large state and municipal taxes the Sejm "in hors" [?] added a whole series of social taxes which in other states, richer and more cultured than ours, have not yet been introduced. Thanks to this peculiar practice the Sejm hurried to introduce them, and one cannot say that they contribute to the development of industry in the country.
But while in all states the fiscus applies only those means that can lead to the collection of the taxes, our fiscus applies means that can only irritate, hurt and ruin the taxpayer and bring him to the point where he cannot pay a single grosz of tax.
Which of us does not know what injustices and illegalities the bailiffs (sequestrators) commit in the course of their work!
Not long ago I had occasion, while walking along Kołłątaja Street, to see how a bailiff angrily threw the goods of a ready-made clothing shop onto the cart. The white walls of the surrounding houses turned red with shame at the sight of such scenes...
Appeals lie for years before they are examined. Meanwhile the poor taxpayer's last few groszy are taken from him, and when the appeal is finally examined, it often happens that the appellant has already forgotten what he wrote. And how are the appeals examined? The so-called representatives of the public sit, with very few exceptions, like mutes; the chairman waves his hand to signal that the matter is settled, and 90 percent of the appeals remain without results.
In the legal world it is known that whoever claims money must prove that it is owed to him. As long as 2000 years ago Jewish law ruled: "the burden of proof lies on the one who seeks to extract from his fellow"; if he brings no proof, the law said: "leave the money in the possession of its owner"; the same law also exists today in their [the gentiles'] codes. In taxes, however, it is demanded not that the party making the claim prove that it is owed, but that the party from whom it is claimed prove that it does not owe. This is an unheard-of inversion of concepts, to which everyone silently agrees. Hand on heart, one can say that 90 percent of the appeals are fully justified, only nobody takes them into account at all: they are not even considered in theory! Their full content is not even accurately conveyed by the chairman to the members of the commission: there is simply nobody to take up the grievance [?] of the unfortunate taxpayer. The lower official, who even knows privately that the appellant is right, has no courage to put in a good word for him, lest he be suspected of taking money; and indeed the tax officials are changed like gloves. Instead of giving them the opportunity to become thoroughly acquainted, on the spot [?], with the economic situation and the course of business of their "customers", other officials are appointed each time, with whom the taxpayer must every year start cramming a new "portion".
Muhammad said: poverty is my honour. In our present "capiscalist" age one cannot say that it is a great honour, but poverty is no disgrace either, especially here in Poland, simply because there is nobody to be ashamed before — we are all paupers. So it is the most natural thing that our pauper, the taxpayer, comes to ask that his tax be spread into instalments; he himself has no banks to borrow from — such as there once were, there are none today — so he turns with such a request to his adversary, the tax office; and he does not ask for favours (łaski), he agrees to pay interest for the time. In the world of commerce no merchant refuses such a request when he sees before him an honest client. In the world of podatki (taxes), however, it is viewed differently. The naczelnik (head) of the office, who knows the taxpayer better than the Izba does, once one has finally earned the privilege, after a three-hour [?] wait in the queue, of seeing his radiant face, answers cold-bloodedly that he has no authority for this, and that one should apply to the Izba Skarbowa (Treasury Chamber). At the Izba Skarbowa they already do him the greatest favour when they allow him to pay the tax over six months; one has to apply to the Ministry, and the taxpayer cannot apply to the Ministry, because that would take a long time, while the bailiff with the cart has no time to wait — so the taxpayer torments himself in bitterness, squeezes out of the business, if it can still be squeezed, the last few groszy that still remain in it, or else he runs up debts over his head, pawns himself, pays three percent a month, covers the state its debt, and remains a superfluous pauper.
Oh, Old Age...

(Idle chatter into the world at large) — by Graf Kali [„Count Kali“, a pen name].
Why have such sad thoughts occurred to me now — you ask? Just when spring has come and outside May reigns in all its splendour and glory?
May, dear brother, it seems, has a great deal to do with my pessimistic mood..
It annoys me terribly with the Master of the Universe: why did He create the world so that every year it renews itself, becomes young and fresh again, full of hopes and expectation — while human springtime comes no more than once?
Why shouldn't man keep pace with time? According to Professor Albert Einstein, a person ought to stay young forever. For Einstein says that time is a relative concept — so how is it that my hair grows greyer from year to year — nothing relative about it!..
Old age — that is one of the ugliest, most loathsome things in the world. And all the greatest inventions put together, along with Marconi's newest electric apparatus — are not worth a pinch of snuff if no remedy is found against old age...
My friend, a Zagłębie industrialist, owns a million dollars, though he won't admit it — and he has a business such as I wish on everyone who wishes me well — I meet him in the street: he walks along and groans..
What can such a man groan about, when he lacks no livelihood, thank God, his children are all provided for in wealth and honour, the business is doing „prima“ — so what is he groaning about?.. And the answer: h a e m o r r h o i d s [„meridn“]..
Oh haemorrhoids, oh haemorrhoids.
It's an illness Jews suffer from,
in war and in peace alike..
It's an illness that comes from sitting
among a people that keeps on going...
To be ashamed of haemorrhoids
one must not, God forbid, no..
On the contrary — it's a great pedigree:
whoever has haemorrhoids
will sooner receive ordination
as a communal leader here in town..
In all those institutions
who sits up there at the top?
The biggest haemorrhoid-sufferers [„meridalnikes“]
set the fine tone there...
And just to spite us, outside it is May... the birds sing songs of praise, everything lives and rejoices. And man, the crown of creation, with his million dollars in his pocket and his desire to live and enjoy — walks about, poor thing, on the green, May-embroidered carpets and groans about his haemorrhoids...
I ask you: is that fair?
Or, let us take even an old writer, one of the great men of yore, who in his time took the world by storm... Hundreds of articles were written about him, not to mention the banquets held in his honour — they are beyond counting.
Along come young „shneks“ [whippersnappers], good-for-nothings, barely out of children's trousers, and say:
Who? He? [printed „ר׳?“ — probably a misprint for „ער?“] Old... banal... worn out... one can't read him any more...
Hush! What more do you need? Take an old woman... she never did anyone any harm... wouldn't hurt a fly on the wall... and still nobody loves her... or perhaps, eh?
Perhaps you love an old woman?
— Not I...
And therefore I say that people like Steinach [Eugen Steinach] and Voronoff [Serge Voronoff], who devise means to make man stay young forever — deserve to be elected as dozores [board members] of the new Jewish kehilla in Będzin in the elections that will take place soon...
Oh old age! Oh old age!
Ugly, disgusting and cold —
yet, gentlemen, wonder of wonders,
everyone wants to grow old...
Young, beautiful, tender women
also grow old, poor things,
black curls turn grey,
hot eyes turn cold...
But one thing in women
stays forever fresh and young,
tireless to the grave —
and that is indeed — their tongue...
Who Says of Us That We Are Paupers?

[Satire — poem; taxes.]
Who says of us
that we are paupers,
who says of us
such a terrible lie? —
Why, it ruins for us
the firm, the name;
we will, God forbid,
get no credit.

Who says of us
that we are going under,
that beneath us
the ground is shaking —
the story is a lie,
we are really well-off;
I will back it up for you
with a few totals:

A baker-woman, Zlate,
a cellar, a narrow one,
a pauper, it seems,
that is easy to recognise —
only it turns out
that at Zlate's
the takings no doubt reach
into great millions.

They assessed her tax
from her turnover,
and there in figures it was
raised up [?],
that Zlate sells
a "little billion" every single day
of wheat rolls
and little rye loaves.

Oh, should you perhaps ask
a little question:
where in Zagłębie does one get
so very many eaters?
The answer is simple:
what are you asking? what do you know?
The assessment commission —
it surely knows better!
* * *
Reb Yosl, a shopkeeper:
when into his little shop
two customers come in,
the third already stays outside —
and he seems a pauper,
a little shop, an empty one,
darkness in the till,
the shelves sparse.

But, apparently,
our eyes can fool us;
it turns out,
according to a clear reckoning,
that here in the little shop
Reb Yosl made a turnover
of heavy millions
last year.

And should you ask a question:
goods worth millions —
where on earth
did they stand here in the little shop?
What are you asking? what do you know?
The assessment commission —
it knows for sure
from what and from where.
* * *
Reb Feitel, a tailor,
a workshop, a narrow one,
a little boy
helps him with the sewing;
Reb Feitel rarely sees
a customer before his eyes,
and he seems a pauper —
yet he is a substantial man!

But the assessment commission
knows for sure
that Rothschild at Feitel's
may polish the boots —
Feitel is worked to the bone [?]
with work — suits
he sews day in, day out
by the tens of dozens.

Oh, a question arises:
would there be in all of Poland
enough people
for so many suits?
What are you asking? what do you know?
The assessment commission
took it from reliable
sources!
* * *
A Jewish woman, Feige,
she deals in poultry,
she goes with her basket
and carries [it] to market.
A dwelling — a grave,
poverty, darkness,
and mouths [to feed] aplenty [?],
growing, knock on wood.

Well, what a catch!
This genuine rich woman
they laid on the table
and began to thunder:
she deals in poultry!
A good business,
one may place her among the hundred-
thousanders!

You say: so many fowl
to buy —
in Poland the population figure
is small!
What are you asking, what do you know —
why, in the "Toyshand" [?]
such information
is found in the books!
* * *
Who says of us
that we are paupers?
Who dares
to tell such a lie?
Here, ask out of curiosity
the assessment commission —
it knows for sure
what Jews possess.

Why, it assessed,
and why, it measured,
why, it sought
to know the very truth, —
the assessors are,
after all, people of integrity,
with unsullied hands
and a clean conscience.
D—l.
The Awakening East

[World — India, British imperialism and Palestine.] It began about 7 weeks ago. Gandhi, with 80 of his closest followers, came to the seashore and started boiling salt. In doing so they broke the salt-monopoly law, which forbids private persons to extract salt from the sea.
By this deed Gandhi showed that he was passing from passive resistance, which rests mainly on "non-cooperation", i.e. not taking part in any office and boycotting everything that is English, to active deeds against English rule in India.
It goes without saying that Gandhi's boiling of salt could have no practical significance, but the little salt boiled out was enough to become the symbol, the banner of the uprising that has flared up in India.
Finally, after an understanding with MacDonald's "Labour government", the Viceroy of India arrested Gandhi — whom the same MacDonald had freed from prison barely eight years ago.
Gandhi's arrest acted like a spark in a powder keg. An uprising broke out in India, spreading ever more strongly and constantly seizing new areas. The newspapers bring figures [of] killed and wounded on both sides, which in reality must be much larger, since it is not in the interest of the English censorship to give the correct figures.
England, which maintains in India altogether some 70 thousand soldiers, bases her rule on the stirred-up strife[?] between the Mohammedans and the Hindus.
The uprising in India bears more than a local character. It is highly probable that it will engulf the whole English colonial possession, already exhausted by the inhuman exploitation of the English imperialists.
During the World War, when the wire entanglements proved too weak a fortification against the German guns, millions of coloured people from the colonies were recruited with the help of the magic formula "freedom for all oppressed peoples", and out of them a living wall was made that was to take the enemy's bullets into itself before they could reach the warm bodies of the French and the English.
When it was necessary, the black-skinned became the saviours of culture, the defenders against German barbarism — and now the same people are oppressed in a brutal manner, and every demand to introduce the promised "freedom" is rejected on the pretext that they are not yet ripe for it.
The imperialist powers come with the hypocritical argument of civilisation. They claim that for a people to become independent it must stand on a high cultural level, and therefore the peoples must first be civilised and only afterwards presented with "freedom". But together with the pseudo-culture, together with the pseudo-civilisation, they drag in all sorts of crimes and bring healthy peoples to degeneration.
A people like the Hindus, which thousands of years ago — when on the British island people still ran around naked, lived in caves and ate roots — already possessed the deepest philosophy that human thought has created: this very people the English enslaved by force and robbed of its enormous natural treasures, in which India is so rich.
Slavery in the colonies has supposedly been abolished, but servitude has remained. A native is regarded as a beast, and perhaps even worse.
That this is so is made clear to us by the following articles of South African legislation, which read:
"Every male native between the ages of 18 and 60 must pay an annual tax of about 220 guilders if he has not worked for a white man at least 3 months in the year (Art. 8).
Every native working for a farmer must have a written contract for at least 3 years. 3 months a year the native must work entirely for nothing (Art. 3).
If the farmer sells his estate, all contract rights pass to the buyer (Art. 5)."
Almost the same regime is conducted by the English everywhere. They stop at nothing; all means are kosher to them when it is a matter of the benefit of "Albion".
Towards the Jews, too, they have applied this tactic. When it seemed to them that Jewish sympathies might perhaps be of use to them, they plastered[?] the two-thousand-year-old wound of a people with the "Balfour plaster", which they are now tearing off again, thereby enlarging the constantly festering, hardly healing wound. The hopes for the Land of Israel, which have been cherished by a whole people over thousands of years for religious, national and social motives, are being brutally trampled by MacDonald's "Labour government", in whose time the sad bloody events in Palestine were organised, and which were later justified by the famous "Shaw Commission".
And as if that were not enough, the English government has recently sent Sir Simpson, a former official in India, with a mandate to Palestine to investigate various questions, chiefly of land policy and immigration.
It is not hard to foretell that Sir Simpson's report will not be favourable to Jews, since in Palestine he will consult the officials there, who for years have been conducting an anti-Jewish policy and who were the spirit that inspired the "Shaw Commission".
For thousands of years we have indeed been the guinea pigs on which a whole world, all the peoples, have carried out the most varied, most horrifying experiments, in the name[?] of God and of the devil, without asking us whether we agree or not.
But to such cynicism as the policy of the English government has reached, no policy of any other state whatsoever has yet reached.
Gandhi's arrest is strengthening the Indian freedom movement, because the road leading to Gandhi's prison has become the "Golgotha", the way of suffering of the Indian people. Tens[?] of thousands of Hindus make pilgrimage to the place where their "prophet" is imprisoned, and they sing religious prayers which have in the Orient the same significance as revolutionary songs in Europe, and which cause the fire of the ever-growing uprising to blaze up — and who knows whether the blood of the English soldiers will be enough to quench this conflagration.
To make clear what Gandhi's relation to India and to Hinduism looks like, we shall let the "prophet" himself speak.
He writes: "I cannot describe my feeling for India more vividly than by comparing it with my feeling for my wife. She moves me more than all the women in the world, not because she is perfect; I know that she has more faults than I see, yet there is the feeling of attachment. The same is my relation to Hinduism, with all its faults and limitations. No music in the world enchants me as much as the music of the 'Gita' or the 'Ramayana' — the two books about which I can boldly say: I understand. I know well about the sins that defile the Indian temples — yet they are dear to me. I am a reformer from the depths of my heart, but I do not deny any Indian superstition."
So think millions of Hindus, because Gandhi is the conscience of India, and all his actions can therefore be regarded as the deeds of a large part of the Indian people.
S. Rotenberg
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings and remarks on this week's portion (Behar-Bechukotai)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings and remarks on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and edited by Y. L.
Parashat Behar-Bechukotai
—o—
a) "And if a man has no redeemer, and he himself becomes able and finds sufficient means to redeem it" (Lev. 25:26).
Such is human nature: when a man has a rich relative, a redeemer, he is lazy and unproductive. For why should he create and toil bitterly when he has a rich uncle who will bail him out anyway — and so he remains forever a pauper and a beggar. Says the Torah: "And if a man has no redeemer" — he who has no rich redeemer and is left to his own lot — "and he himself becomes able and finds sufficient means to redeem it": he will find himself a livelihood, a way to redeem his inheritance. When one does not rely on rich relatives and works oneself, God helps. Melekhet Mahshevet.
—o—
b) "And if your brother becomes poor... you shall support him... that he may live with you" (Lev. 25:35)
There are rich men who could have done much good with their wealth, helped many unfortunates, but their stinginess will not let them; yet when they stand on the threshold of death the stinginess vanishes, and they leave a will in which they designate larger donations for charitable purposes. But such charity bequests most often come to nothing; they are lost. That is what the verse says: "And if your brother becomes poor, you shall support him" — if you wish to do good and help your poor brother, do it when — "that he may live with you" — while he is still living with you; while you are alive, give charity, rather than leaving charity bequests from your deathbed. Yalkut Peninim.
—o—
c) "Interest and increase" (neshekh ve-tarbit, Lev. 25:36).
Interest has a double name: neshekh and tarbit. For the borrower it is neshekh ("bite"), like the bite of a venomous snake. The snake lets its poison in only at an unnoticed spot, in the foot for instance, and the poison penetrates deep, deep into the blood until it reaches the brain, and all at once it kills the whole body. Earlier no one noticed the little bit of poison, and suddenly it appears at the very center of the body, and there is no rescue any more. For the lender, however, interest is tarbit ("increase"), because his wealth grows from day to day. Kli Yakar.
* * *
The wife of the Maharshal [R. Solomon Luria] was engaged in lending money at interest. Her husband, the Maharshal, comes in and sees that the household things are dusty; he says to her: this is "avak ribbit" — the "dust of interest" (avak is also the Hebrew word for dust). She answers: it is a different dust, it is "avak lashon ha-ra" — the "dust of slander". (She lent only under a heter iska [a permit for a partnership arrangement], which by law is not "avak ribbit"; therefore in her sharp wordplay she labelled his remark "dust of slander".)
* * *
Two friends, both professional moneylenders, sit at a table and chat. One says:
I acquired my whole fortune through the first loans, because the first time one may lend to anybody, since the first time everyone pays back, reckoning that they will get a larger loan in return.
And I too — says the second — made my fortune through the first loans, back when I myself was a pauper, and it was not I who lent to others but I who borrowed from others; back then I borrowed from all the moneylenders for the first time (and the first time, after all, one lends to anybody) — and promptly did not pay back.
From the mouth of the people.
—o—
d) "You shall not rule over him with rigour (be-farekh), but fear your God" (Lev. 25:23 [so printed; should be 25:43]).
The Torah says: "You shall not rule over him be-feh rakh" — "with a soft mouth" — because there are those who flatter and speak politely to their workers, and meanwhile exploit them terribly, all under the mask of a "soft mouth", of gentle talk. Birkat Avraham.
—o—
d [so printed; should be e]) "And you shall eat the flesh of your sons" (Lev. 26:29).
According to the Midrash, the curses of the Rebuke will in the time to come be turned into blessings. So how will such a curse as "and you shall eat the flesh of your sons" be interpreted?
— Very simply: "and you shall eat the flesh of your sons" — you will eat meat at your children's homes, because nowadays many pious parents may not eat meat at their children's homes...
From the Rebbe of Sadigura [?].
—o—
f) "And I will scatter you among the nations" (Lev. 26:33)
This is the most terrible curse of the Rebuke. Precisely when you find yourselves "among the nations", in exile among the peoples, precisely then, when common unity is needed, precisely then there is division among Jews; precisely when you are "among the peoples" you are "scattered and divided" — that is the most terrible of all.
Or Pnei Moshe.
—o—
Avot, Chapter Five.
a) "The sword comes into the world because of the delay of justice and the perversion of justice"
In wartime two merchants once come to hold a din Torah before a rabbi. Because of the war the goods have risen a hundredfold, and on that ground a dispute arises between them: each wants a bigger share of the profit. The rabbi speaks up: the biggest profit is surely due to me, for I am the direct cause of the war, since "the sword comes into the world because of the perversion of justice" (because of the twisting of justice war comes upon the world) — so the war is on account of me..
Sihat Hullin.
—o—
b) "Which is a dispute for the sake of Heaven? — The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. And one not for the sake of Heaven? — The dispute of Korah and all his congregation"
For a dispute for the sake of Heaven the Mishnah presents two partners [?], Hillel and Shammai. So for the dispute not for the sake of Heaven it should also have been "Korah and Moses" — why then does the Mishnah change its wording and write "Korah and all his congregation"? Did Korah conduct a dispute with his own congregation? He quarrelled only with Moses — so it should have been "the dispute of Korah and Moses"?!
— That is precisely the best sign of a dispute not for the sake of Heaven: when those who conduct the disputes also have no peace among themselves, for none of them grants the other anything; only in order to fight a Moses do they unite, but among themselves too strife [?] reigns. A dispute not for the sake of Heaven is the dispute of Korah and all his congregation: the Korahs quarrel with their own congregation as well, and only their disputes with Moses hold them together. Noam Elimelekh.
—o—
c) "The brazen-faced to Gehenna, and the shamefaced to the Garden of Eden" (25)
There are those who are brazen-faced "to Gehenna" — when it is a matter of a sin — whereas when it is a matter "to the Garden of Eden", a matter of a mitzvah, they suddenly become bashful, shamefaced...
Nahalei Devash.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Jewish Councillors Propose Reducing the Speed of the Trams

[Będzin — city council.]
Monday's session of the city council passed quietly. The gallery no longer stormed and sang "Czerwony Sztandar" ("The Red Banner") as it had last Thursday.
Of the items on the agenda, it was decided to buy 57 square metres of land from M. Chajnsztok for the purpose of widening Modrzejowska Street.
The proposal of the Jewish councillors that the city council intervene with the tramway management so that the trams should not run through the town at such speed was sent to the commission for general affairs. Apparently the non-Jewish councillors are not frightened by the fact that such running of the trams brings sad results...
Then a series of items of the revenue budget for 1930/31 was adopted in second reading.
The total sum of the anticipated revenues amounts to 2,133,103 zł.
Hush, Hush, Don't Make a Fuss — the New Shochet Will Be the Fifth...

[Będzin — kehilla and ritual slaughter.]
When the question of engaging a new shochet (ritual slaughterer) became topical, the local Aleksandrów Hasidim were against it, fearing that it would be an attack on the shochet R' Yisroel Moshe.
This was taken into account by those who, so to speak, run the kehilla's affairs, and they, the leaders, decided not to fall out with the Aleksandrów Hasidim and to engage a fifth shochet.
The decision was conveyed to one of the most respected local Aleksandrów Hasidim, to whom it was explained that "the public should keep quiet". Everything stays as it was, and a fifth shochet will be appointed...
— The fifth wheel of the kehilla wagon.
Invitation from "Shomrei Shabbat" to the Kehilla Board

[Będzin — kehilla.]
The world union "Shomrei Shabbat" in Berlin has invited the local kehilla to come to the congress which will take place in the month of August in Berlin.
Lectures by Dr. Gottlieb in Zagłębie

[Będzin, Sosnowiec, Dąbrowa — lectures; Zionism.]
As we have already reported, this Sabbath we shall have as our guest the well-known speaker and feuilletonist Dr. Yehoshua Gottlieb, who will give a lecture on Saturday afternoon at the "Nowości" on the subject "Impressions of America".
The distinguished guest has delivered this lecture in a number of towns, and everywhere it passed with the greatest success.
Dr. Gottlieb will also discuss the present tense situation in Eretz Israel.
— The same lecture will be given this Saturday evening in Sosnowiec at the "Hotel Polski".
— On Sunday Dr. Gottlieb will visit Dąbrowa, where at 11 in the morning he will give a lecture at the "Menus" [?] cinema on the subject "The Present Situation in Zionism".
Bookkeeping Department at the Merchants' Association

[Będzin — commerce.]
A bookkeeping department and advice office for members has been opened at the local Merchants' Association under the direction of Mr. Fajerman [?].
In the department merchants will be given bookkeeping advice, and commercial books will be kept for a minimal fee.
Będzin Goes "Forward"...

[Będzin — railway and post.]
As our readers know, when drawing up the present timetable the railway management abolished the stopping of the express (courier) trains at the local station. But the "wisdom" of the railway management goes still further: because the trains do not stop, the postal connection is also cut off in certain cases; for example, the post to Warsaw, which is not sent off during the day, remains lying until the next day...

[Będzin — trams; lost property.]
A lady's sweater, a pair of scissors, a briefcase, a bag with pieces of butter, a woollen shawl, a bag of yellow leather, a black walking stick, men's underwear, leather gloves, a gold ring, a purse with 5 zł. 75 gr., a man's shirt, a lady's handbag.
A Protest Meeting Against the Immigration Decree for Eretz Israel

[Będzin — Zionism; Right Poale Zion.]
In connection with the present situation in Zionism, the Right "Poale Zion" are arranging this Sabbath at the "Kursal" theatre a lecture by Mr. Israel Ritov on the subject "Who Will Win?!".
Because of the tense mood now prevailing in Jewish circles, as well as the popularity of the speaker, the lecture has aroused interest.
Break-in at a pharmacy warehouse.

During the night from Friday to the Sabbath the back door of Mr. Danziger's pharmacy warehouse on Małachowskiego Street was broken open.
The "guests" picked out the best perfumes and other valuable goods.
The damage amounts to about one thousand złoty.
An Esperanto activist has died.

On Wednesday the chairman of the local Esperanto society, Izydor Serczarusz [?], passed into eternal rest.
At the open grave Dr. Weinzieher, Icchak Kozłowski and M. Rozen spoke, describing the deceased's activity in the field of Esperanto.
Demonstration of the unemployed. Panic among the merchants.

Throughout the whole week crowds of unemployed gather every day in front of the magistrate (city hall) and in the surrounding streets.
Today, Wednesday, the number of unemployed assembled was very large. When the police saw that a huge demonstration was forming, they began to disperse the crowd.
The unemployed then went into Magruszewer [?] Street with singing and uproar. This caused a panic among the merchants, who began to close their shops, so that within a short time almost all the shops on the street were shut.
The demonstrators, escorted by foot and mounted police, marched through as far as the slag heaps.
No serious incidents occurred; only one window pane was smashed at Mr. Agista's [?].
A Jewish daughter from Radom comes to Sosnowiec to marry her lover.

A few weeks ago 19-year-old Ester Fiszer suddenly disappeared from her parents' home.
Miss Fiszer had for a long time been acquainted with a Christian young man, one Szemiankowski, who worked in Radom as a dental technician. Fiszer's parents paid no attention to Miss Fiszer's acquaintance with the young man, until a fiery love flared up between the couple and the enamoured pair decided to marry. But knowing that Ester's parents would not allow it, the couple came to Sosnowiec in order to take a "ślub" (wedding) here.
When Ester disappeared, darkness fell upon her parents — they began running about, searching, but — Ester had vanished.
Then the desperate parents informed the police that their daughter had stolen various articles from them and had disappeared.
The police, having received information that the missing girl was in Sosnowiec, notified the local police about the theft, and on that basis Ester Fiszer was arrested here. But after she had been questioned by the investigation office, she was released.
Protest by the kehilla against the calendar reform

At the meeting of the Va'ad ha-Rabbonim (rabbinical council), held on Monday in the premises of the Jewish kehilla, it was decided to send a telegram to the League of Nations in Zurich [sic] against the Soviet government's project to reform the calendar.
"He brings greetings from fathers and sons". A new swindling method.

A young man approached Mr. Moshe Akiva Magierkiewicz and passed on greetings from Magierkiewicz's son in Zduńska Wola. At the same time the young man related that he was serving in the Będzin regiment and, since he now had leave, he wanted to travel home to Zduńska Wola.
"What do you want of me?" M. asked the young man.
"I'd like you to lend me 6.30 zł., which I am short for a ticket."
Magierkiewicz gave the loan, and the young man left, leaving his address in Zduńska Wola.
When Magierkiewicz wrote to his son that he should collect the debt from the young man, the son replied that the very same young man had also been to see him, passed on greetings from his father, and borrowed 5 gulden for the travel expenses...
"If the gmina won't support us, we'll ride 'na gapę'".

Three young people came into the kehilla offices and demanded that the gmina give them money for railway tickets to Łódź.
When the secretary, Mr. Lewenhof [?], explained to them that the support could amount to 1.50 per person, the support-seekers came out with abusive language and threatened "sad consequences".
Because of this Mr. L. was forced to call in a policeman, who only then removed the "guests" from the gmina offices.
On leaving, they declared "categorically" to the policeman that, since they were not getting the support they had demanded, they would travel to Łódź "na gapę" (without a ticket) and the "rząd" (government) would bear the loss for it...
Came to visit his parents and shot himself.
On Sucha Street the pupil Gruszczyński shot himself with a revolver. The suicide had come on Friday from Warsaw to Sosnowiec to see his parents, and the next day he committed the terrible deed.
Sensational arrest of an old lecher

For quite some time "the birds on the rooftops" [i.e. the whole town] have been passing on the word that the 48-year-old R. N.[?], a confectioner by trade, engages in forbidden erotic acts.
The police took an interest in the matter and indeed discovered that wild erotic orgies take place at the above-mentioned man's.
The person has been arrested.
From "Hitachdut".

Last Saturday, under the chairmanship of Mr. Fishl, the semi-annual general meeting [of Hitachdut, the Zionist-socialist party] took place in its own premises. The general report was given by Mr. Fridman, the treasury report by Miss Mintsboym, according to which there is a surplus of 200 zł.
Reports were also given by Messrs. Milshteyn (Keren Aliyah), Frommer (Keren Kayemet), Interligator (Hechalutz and Gordonia).
Taking part in the discussion were, among others, Messrs. Kan, Fishel, Kerner, Milshteyn, Interligator, Frommer and others. A new board was elected consisting of the following persons: Frommer, Milshteyn, Mintsboym, Shvartsenshteyn, Kerner, Kupermints, Salna[?].
The meeting was closed with the singing of "Hatikvah".
—o—
At the Last Hour.
Next Monday, on the initiative of the local Revisionist organisation, Dr. Lipman will give a lecture on the subject "At the Last Hour".
The lecture will take place at the "Hotel Polski" in the evening.
—o—
A Baker Punished.
The local baker Eli' Rubin was charged with keeping his bakery in a very poor sanitary condition.
The trial took place these days in the local municipal court, which sentenced him to 5 days' unconditional arrest.
—o—
Visit of Deputy A. Hartglas.
In connection with the present economic crisis in the country, Deputy A. Hartglas will, as we have already reported, lecture next Sunday at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre on "The present situation in the country", in which he will discuss at length the Jewish situation in Poland.
—o—
Czeladź Has a Mayor at Last.
This week the newly elected mayor, Mr. Pitawer[?], began to manage the affairs of Czeladź.
Zawiercie. Dr. Zilbershteyn sentenced to 14 days' arrest for slander.

A few months ago the local surgeon Dr. Levenshteyn operated on a certain Grinboym. Although the operation succeeded, Grinboym died.
In connection with this, various versions circulated in town; above all, the words of Dr. Zilbershteyn spread that "Dr. Levenshteyn cut up the patient like a sheep"...
Dr. Levenshteyn brought a suit against Dr. Zilbershteyn. The trial took place a few weeks ago in the local court, where Dr. Z. was sentenced to 7 days' arrest.
Dr. Levenshteyn was not satisfied with the light penalty and lodged an appeal with the Sosnowiec District Court, where the case was heard this week.
The Sosnowiec District Court sentenced Dr. Zilbershteyn to 14 days' unconditional arrest.
The convicted man has submitted a petition to the Supreme Court.

The "Chelm kehilla" also took part in the conference of kehillot

[Będzin — kehilla; immigration to Palestine. Followed by five short news items: Zagłębie, Dąbrowa, Zawiercie, a PPS meeting, Sosnowiec.]
As is known, a conference of all the Jewish kehillot in Poland took place yesterday in Warsaw, to protest against the aliyah decree for Eretz Israel.
The Będzin kehilla board, which consists of Agudists only, could not decide during the whole week what to do — "take part or not?" After all, it has a "whiff" of Eretz Israel...
Finally the gentlemen realised that one must go, and on Wednesday evening an urgent session of the council[?] and the kehilla board was called.
Because of the "importance" of the meeting, the rabbi too took part in the vote on the delegate who is to represent the "compromise"[?] Jewish kehilla.
After long debates, which had the character of a "Chelm assembly", R' Avraham Lei-Chefer[?] was elected delegate; he received instructions from R' Dovid that "he should be careful and not let himself be caught in Hershel Farbstein's net, but right after the protest he should go off to Ger".
—o—
A terrible storm-rain and hail.
Yesterday around 7 in the evening a storm wind with hail the size of large peas swept over Zagłębie.
The streets were covered with pieces of ice as in winter; many cellar dwellings were flooded.
—o—
Borensztajn's murderer caught.
Yesterday the police arrested a certain Kuszański[?], a resident of Kolonia Reden in Dąbrowa, who was suspected of having murdered the merchant Hershel Borensztajn (the whole story is in the Dąbrowa chronicle).
When the arrested man was interrogated, he confessed to committing the murder. "I didn't want to kill him," he declared, "only to give him a few blows.."
The murderer, a former "halfershchik"[?], is under arrest.
—o—
Tragic accident at the Zawiercie station.
On Wednesday at 9 in the evening the conductor Węcław[?] jumped off at the station before the train had stopped.
The jump was so fatal that the conductor fell under the train and was killed on the spot.
—o—
A PPS meeting dispersed.
Yesterday, Thursday, the PPS held a meeting at the "Korso"[?]. Deputy Czapiel[?] also took part in the meeting.
During his speech he used sharp expressions against the government. Because of this the crowd was dispersed and the police broke up the meeting.

The writer Moshe Stawski in Sosnowiec.
The well-known writer Moshe Stawski, a permanent resident of Eretz Israel, came to Poland a few weeks ago.
The distinguished guest will spend the coming festival of Shavuot in Sosnowiec with his brother Gershon Stawski.
The visit has aroused great interest among the nationalist Jewry of Zagłębie.

English labour leaders against the emigration decree.
Today, Wednesday, the district committee of the PPS in Sosnowiec received a telegram from the English labour leader Cook, who asks that the P.B.[?] delegation be told that he has convened a special session of a number of Labour deputies, whom he informed about the great agitation prevailing in Jewish workers' circles because of the immigration ban to Eretz Israel.

When Father and Mother Quarrel

(From the Polish press).
In the Upper Silesian street paper "Wolne Słowo" we find a very characteristic article about the sadly notorious antisemite Mach, the "editor" of the hate sheet "Do Mszygu"[?]. The paper "Wolne Słowo", which until now was known to us as no great lover of Israel, has suddenly taken courage and comes out openly against the antisemite Mach in particular and against antisemitism in general. The author of the article is not at all afraid even to state at the same time that the Jews in Upper Silesia are loyal and good citizens of the Polish state. In the introduction to his article the author, a certain Dr. Kwiatkowski, writes that the "W. S." has never been a Jew-hating paper; on the contrary, it has always, at every opportunity, defended the powerless Jews.
"This does not prove, however — we read in the article — that we have privileged the Jews. It is possible that among them too there are outcasts and disturbers of society; these we fight and send before the tribunal of public opinion, but there must[?] be equal social justice for every single person. Dealing, out of pure journalistic duty, with the Jewish question in Poland, we have more than once had to expose the immature, illiterate pseudo-public activists who, like the knights of the Middle Ages, wish from time to time to 'run riot' over Jewish society. In fairness we must state here that almost the entire Polish press in Upper Silesia has not come out aggressively against the Jews (! — Ed.)[?]. Only barely two years ago did undeveloped thinker-figures of a 'new order' begin to crawl out of their holes, having sniffed out that one can do good business with the Jewish question.
"We wish to speak of the affair of Editor Mach and his partners. Barely 2 years ago a rumour spread in Katowice, the capital of Upper Silesia, passing from ear to ear, that in order to put an end to the immigration of Jews into Upper Silesia a 'Committee to Fight Jewry' had been created. Not long afterwards the rumour was confirmed, for in the newspaper kiosks there appeared a little paper named 'Do Mszygu'[?], as the organ of the said society. The editor of the paper became Alojzy Mach (we ask that the name not be read backwards. By the way — from the typesetter lad). He was the motor, publisher and organiser of the anti-Jewish action. In the columns of 'Do Mszygu' there appeared articles attacking Jewish firms, denunciatory articles drenched in antisemitic foam. Anyone who can read could read in them a silent prayer: 'If you pay — I'll stop smearing.' And after the articles appeared, special emissaries ran to the Catholic firms so that they would support and distribute the paper."
Describing further the means by which Mach worked, the author points out that he also drew the Catholic clergy into his work, and therefore it is no wonder that he found enough followers.
"It is no wonder — we read further — that after such sermons from a priest many began to believe in Mach's idea. But there were also such, perhaps less 'idealistic' but for that more objective critics, who have known the public activist Mach for a long time and view his idealism from another side — from the right side. Mach (do not read the name backwards) is a great careerist, but he does not feel like working for nothing. He knows that the action will bring him no honour, but money it will surely bring him. And most probably it was money he was after. We say 'most probably' because we do not yet know how much money he extracted for that bit of work, and it is about this that we wish to speak."
Quoting certain passages of the article, we learn with what machinations and swindles Mach operated. Thus, for example, as an attraction he brought down from Warsaw the former tsarist general, the well-known enemy of Israel, the priest Leszno-Brodski[?], with whom he went into partnership. Priest L. held in the Katowice church "Panny Marii" a series of lectures on the role of the Jews in Bolshevism (incidentally, the same lectures were also delivered here by the same priest). Of course the priest carried out his holy mission as it should be done, but when it came to paying, Mach "showed him the fig" [i.e. refused to pay]. Seeing that "they whistle at him" (an expression of the "W. S."), Priest L. tore up the contract. But that is not the end of it, for Mach, fearing a dangerous competitor in the antisemitic field, put some of his followers up to breaking Leszno-Brodski's bones. How the story ended there we do not know, but it is a fact that the leaders of the antisemitic hate campaign in Upper Silesia engaged in deeds that were none too pretty.
Interesting too is the end of the article, which we consider it necessary to quote:
"Would it not be nicer if this holy mission finally came to an end, for in the end nothing will remain of it in the future but the ugly name, which people will later recall with disgust. Sad reflections come to our mind. Why must Mach hide under the cloak of the Catholic clergy, which must not sow hatred and enmity towards another faith — be he a Mohammedan, a Buddhist, a Lutheran or a Jew; this Christ expressly forbade. We therefore ask: does the higher spiritual authority know of these unethical deeds? For God's sake! In all of Poland there is no similar paper which by its content calls for murder, something reminiscent of the 16th and 15th centuries. We are living now, after all, in the 20th century"!
Perhaps this article in the "W. S." will calm the antisemitic hotheads a little, and the Jews in Upper Silesia will be able to breathe more freely?
S. Sztdujk[?].

Protest meetings against the decree restricting [immigration] to the Land of Israel.
Visit of Dr. Gottlieb in Zagłębie.
The restriction of aliyah to the Land of Israel, which so stirred up the Jewish world, naturally also shook Zagłębie Jewry, which expressed its grief and indignation at a number of protest meetings and rallies held in the course of the week.
At the invitation of "WIZO" in Będzin, Dr. Gottlieb spent the Sabbath in Będzin, where he delivered a lecture. The topic was "Impressions of America", but at the demand of the great mass of listeners Dr. Gottlieb spoke with pathos about the emigration decree.
After the lecture Mrs. Ratner read a protest resolution, which was adopted unanimously.
At the same time the Right Poale Zion in Będzin organised in the "Karsa"[?] a protest meeting with the participation of Mr. Y. Ritov, who delivered a sharp speech.
In the courtyard of a meeting-hall, under the open sky, the Left Poale Zion in Będzin held a protest rally. The speakers were Peterzeil (Warsaw), Karnfeler[?] and Councillor Rotenberg (Będzin).
On the Sabbath, in the premises of the Zionist Organisation in Sosnowiec, a meeting of the Revisionists took place. Mr. Klarman gave a detailed lecture on the present situation in Zionism, discussing the latest emigration decree. Afterwards a sharp protest resolution was adopted against the emigration decree as well as against the tactics of the Zionist Executive hitherto.
———
On Saturday night Dr. Gottlieb delivered the same lecture in Sosnowiec, and on Sunday morning in the "Wenus" in Dąbrowa on the topic "The present situation in Zionism". After the lecture a protest resolution was read, which was adopted unanimously.
At the same time the Left Poale Zion in Sosnowiec held a protest rally, at which Mr. Peterzeil poured out his "whole wrath" on the Zionist leaders.
———
On Tuesday evening a grand rally took place in the courtyard of the "Mizrachi" school. Speeches were delivered by Messrs. Cymberknopf (Pabianice), Ganzweich, Klarman, Milsztajn, Chlewicki.
Sharp protest resolutions against the aliyah decree were adopted.
The resolutions were sent to the Labour Party and to the English government.
What's Happening in Upper Silesia?

Opening of the Upper Silesian Sejm.
Last Tuesday the newly elected Upper Silesian (Silesian) Sejm, which holds its sessions in Katowice, was opened with a short speech by Voivode Grażyński.
The chair is taken for the time being by the eldest deputy, Korfanty. Before proceeding to the election of a Marshal, the 2 Communist deputies made an uproar. At the chairman's demand the deputies were carried out of the hall.
Then they proceeded to elect a Sejm Marshal; with an absolute majority of 44 votes the incumbent Marshal, Deputy Wolny, was elected.
———
The Communist deputies arranged [?] demonstrations throughout Upper Silesia, but because of the Voivode's strict orders the demonstrations were not permitted.
Protest meeting in Königshütte.
A large protest meeting was held in Königshütte, at which Rabbi Hager of Sosnowiec appeared with a very fine speech.
Later a banquet was held in the rabbi's honour. Afterwards a large crowd, headed by Rabbi Blumenfeld, escorted the rabbi to Sosnowiec.
Tax distraint for 14 million zł.
The Prince of Pless owes tax arrears for the years 1925 to 1929 amounting to 14 million zł.
Because of this the tax office has ordered distraint on the properties belonging to the Prince.
Visit of Minister Prystor.
In the first days of this week Labour Minister Prystor stayed in Katowice, where he visited [?] a number of economic institutions in Katowice and in Königshütte.

Tend the little branch. (A bookkeeping department and an advisory office have been set up at the “Merchants' Association”.)

A short notice we read in our paper eight days ago[?] — a notice containing all in all a few lines, but it says a great deal. We are told that at the Będzin “Merchants' Association” (Sokhrim-Fareyn) a department for bookkeeping has been founded, and advice will be given on how to keep commercial books.
At first this looks like a trifle not worth dwelling on, but when we consider the matter more deeply we see that it is not as it seems at first glance. We fool ourselves in thinking that every merchant can keep books, that everyone can manage on his own in his business, whereas this is far from so. Why should we fool ourselves? After all, we lose enough strength and courage and money because we are not bold enough to look at the truth and at reality with open eyes and in the right light.
No average merchant is able to keep books for himself that could be certified by the authorities, and not only average merchants cannot persuade themselves of it — even half- and fully-educated merchants will admit it, for however versed[?] they may be in it, however familiar with it, they cannot take such work upon themselves, because they are not bookkeepers but merchants, who must have other things on their minds. First of all they must be modern merchants, who know how to calculate and how to buy goods, when to pay a bill of exchange and how to draw one. Whoever wants to keep books that will be valid for the authorities must therefore have a responsible bookkeeper; otherwise he cannot manage, otherwise he will achieve nothing. And here the question arises: how can a middling merchant commit himself to such great expense? How can a small merchant allow himself to take on a responsible bookkeeper? He has nowhere at all to put him, nowhere to seat him. That is why one cannot even bring oneself to think about such questions, since he has no means to pay the price such a person must charge; often he himself would gladly earn what such a person must charge.
And because of this the small merchant overpays for nothing: he is taxed ten times over, he pays one and the same tax more than once, because he has no means of keeping proper order and of keeping every receipt in its proper place. For he has nobody to speak for him, nobody to defend and protect him, at the moment when someone should fight for him.
The larger firms, those that employ people and have offices — there official books are kept for the authorities, and exactly as much is paid as is due; when even the smallest sum is contested, there is someone to take the matter up and not allow overpayment.
90 percent of those who keep no books become, because of this, [—][?]; but what are they to do when they have no way out? When they cannot persuade themselves that there will be someone to fight for them, someone to intervene for them?
True, there exist associations of merchants and of small traders, and the big merchant does not look for support from his association; he knows he can get nothing from it, and indeed he does not rely on it. His people already do for him what is needed. The small trader, by contrast, has no one to work for him, no one to pay for him and write and run around for him (klapatshen), and having no choice he relies on his association, which he trusts fully; but afterwards he finds out that he had no one to trust and that the whole matter was completely neglected, so that he later had to pay double and twofold.
It goes without saying that things would be quite different if we had professional economic associations that would perform for their members what is due to them, what ought to lie within their competence.
And therefore we are glad when the chronicle tells us that the “Merchants' Association” in Będzin has undertaken to solve what is, in our opinion, the hardest question — for a small merchant cannot engage a bookkeeper, whereas at the “Merchants' Association” such books can indeed be kept, and at worst they can be kept under the supervision of this responsible institution. The legal advice to be given there also plays a great role; but the main thing is that what has been promised be carried out and maintained carefully.
It would do no harm if from time to time lecturers gave various topical talks that would crystallise the merchants who need it. A great, great deal can be done in this field; one need only be willing to deal with and study the painful problems, which simply must be eased with vigour so as not to fall into helplessness.
The “Merchants' Association”, we hold, should in particular take under its supervision and responsibility the keeping of the books of the firms that entrust their books to it, and in that case everything should be under its supervision, so that it would observe all payment deadlines and appeals (recourses), and above all it should be the body that sees to all the formalities and obligations.
One sees plainly that every merchant must now begin to keep formal books if[?] he does not want to come to grief over taxes; one can no longer carry on as in the old days, one must not wait for miracles, for one sees that they bring no great joy...
It is therefore one of the most important questions that the “Merchants' Association” begin to realise what it has undertaken. This would bring a double benefit: first, the institution would have some income, and second, the merchants would know that the association is doing something for them, and so the merchant would gain more trust, more faith, more affection and interest for the institution that was created for him.
Let the board see to tending this little branch, which has every possibility of blossoming out fine and wide and bearing the hoped-for fruit for the members, who need these fruits so badly.
For this work nothing more is needed than a bit of will, devotion and loyalty, and the matter can be settled in the best way.
R. Let.

Shavuot at the Tombs of David and Solomon

[Eretz Israel — Jerusalem; Shavuot.] By M. Emanueli.
Since ancient times it has been a custom among the Jews of Jerusalem to visit the Tombs of David and Solomon on Shavuot; according to tradition they are on Mount Zion, not far from the Zion Gate. Mount Zion is one of the four hills on which the Old City of Jerusalem stands. The Zion Gate, or as the Arabs call it, “Bab Nabi Daud,” is one of the seven open gates in the wall that encloses the Old City. These seven gates of the city are open, and through them passes the traffic between the Old City and the new parts of Jerusalem as well as the surroundings. There are two more gates on the eastern side of the city, at the same time on the eastern side of the Temple site; these two gates are called “Sha'arei Rahamim” [Gates of Mercy] and by the Arabs “Bab al-Rahma”; these gates date from the time of Herod. Among the Arabs there is a legend that these gates are destined for the Messiah son of David, who will enter Jerusalem through them and will liberate the Jews.
When Shavuot comes, masses of Jews stream through all the gates from the Old City and from the new neighbourhoods and go up to Mount Zion, and there, past the Zion Gate, to the tombs of David and Solomon. One can see that the Sephardim all come from the whole country to King David's tomb on the day of his yahrzeit — Shavuot. The Ashkenazim, on the other hand, i.e. the Jews of Eastern Europe, come only the next day after Shavuot (in Eretz Israel Shavuot is celebrated for only one day). The custom — to visit the Tomb of David only after Shavuot — has remained from earlier times, when the owners of the place where the Tomb of David is believed to be did not want to let Jews in and demanded money for it. The place formally belongs to the distinguished Arab family “al-Dahuri” [sic], who pride themselves on descending from King David. Therefore they have the hereditary right to hold the keys of the tomb, and at the same time they look after the religious needs of the mosque built over the Tomb of David. And it was from the eldest of this family that the Sephardi sages obtained that on Shavuot he would open the gates and allow them to visit the Tombs of David and Solomon free of charge. The Ashkenazi rabbis, however, did not obtain anything of the kind, so they had to visit the tombs only the next day, on Isru Chag (for us the second day of the festival), and since then they come to visit the Tombs of David and Solomon only on Isru Chag, even now that access is already free.
At Shavuot Jerusalem has almost its greatest heat, but that does not at all stop the visitors from streaming in camps from all sides to be at the tomb of David King of Israel; it looks like a procession of the Ingathering of the Exiles. One sees here the most varied Jews in the most varied garments; especially conspicuous are the various kinds of Sephardim, from the West African, Egyptian, Balkan and Smyrna Sephardim to the Bukharan, Georgian, Caucasian, Baghdadi and even Afghan ones, who all come in their garments of every kind and settle down on Mount Zion with their wives and children. A large part spend the whole morning here, others the whole afternoon, and they bring here their various national dishes, hold their festive meal here and gladly treat every passer-by.
The Yemenites come here very early and recite many prayers and special chapters of Psalms outside, because inside it is impossible to let the visitors stay long owing to their great number. This is supervised by the police, who let smaller groups in one at a time.
On entering the vestibule, which is an Arab mosque, one must take off one's shoes and remain in one's socks. Here one sees many columns on which the dome of the mosque rests. On the walls and on the round vaulted ceiling there is much mosaic work from ancient times. The columns are marked with various verses from the Koran, as is customary in all Arab historical buildings and places; on the ground carpets [divans] are spread over stone floors, which are also rich in mosaic.
Once inside here, after the noise and crush that reign outside before the entrance, one is overcome by an inner earnestness and a devout mood. Millennia and generations vanish, and we stand at the genesis and cradle of Jewish state independence, which ripened after Jewish spiritual creativity had become firmly established in the people and set about the work of statehood in that spirit and to strengthen its spiritual depth and character — as expressed by the creation of King David as leader of the people and poet, and of Solomon as lawgiver, poet and philosopher, together with the various sublime traditions with which the Jewish national spirit has gratefully woven around them.
From the hall one climbs a few steps and through a small door enters a small room which has on its left a large window with iron bars, through which one sees in the adjoining room a large, long stone, one and a half metres high and entirely covered with a green silk cloth. This is the place where, according to tradition, the tomb of David and Solomon is said to be. There are even Arabs here who say that Joshua's tomb is here too, and of course it is hard to argue with them about it, for he cannot believe otherwise, because that is what his grandfather, who was a famous “sheikh,” handed down to him.
Coming out, we already met new camps of our likeable brethren of those [communities], who with song and dance demonstrated “David King of Israel lives and endures,” and with their enthusiasm and festive mood proved that the Jewish popular instinct still lives and is strong, and that the Jewish hopes for a bright and rich future, on whose foundations the Jewish work of revival in Eretz Israel is being built, are unshaken.
Our Educational System (Haphazardness Is the Outcome of Abnormality. — If Only We Would Want To...)

[Sosnowiec — Education; article.] We have in Sosnowiec one single Jewish secondary school for our daughters. The Jewish girls' gimnazjum is unquestionably a necessary educational institution, and if it did not exist one would have had to create it; so necessary is it to us, so important is this institution for our future mothers, who should also know afterwards how to bring up their children.
The school prospers well, people trust it, the teaching staff is good, and therefore there are pupils, and on the basis of all this the institution has been granted government rights. Nor is this any wonder: after all, a few people simply devoted themselves body and soul to raising this necessary educational institution to the proper level. And here, suddenly, out of the blue, a danger looms; cries of alarm are heard all at once that the institution faces a catastrophe. What happened is that the landlord of the building in which the institution is housed has obtained an eviction against the school, and naturally, at this serious moment everything is in an uproar.
Two things are simply incomprehensible: first, how can things be allowed to come to an eviction at the present moment? How is the school being managed, that the landlord should have the possibility of suing for an eviction? After all, everyone knows how hard it is nowadays to obtain other rooms. Not to mention when it concerns premises of the kind a gimnazjum needs — one does not find so many rooms so quickly, and one is not able to manage it. And secondly, it is also hard to believe that a decent landlord would want to lay waste to such a school, which Jewish Sosnowiec needs so badly.
But all this gives an exact picture of what the most intensive activity, the most energetic work, looks like among us. Now we see clearly that everything among us is a matter of chance: by chance great and lofty things are created among us, and by chance they are lost. Had chance not ruled us from the very start, had it not stood right at the front — something we must not touch — we would not suddenly be faced with such surprises, such shocks, which are simply astonishing when one thinks the matter through, when one begins to analyse it all systematically.
We create schools, we found educational institutions — but what sense does it make, if they exist by chance and by chance can be shut down[?]. The whole disaster is that chance is the main thing among us; it cuts everything down, it creates everything and destroys everything.
What more is needed, when even in our serious problems, such as schools and education, we do not free ourselves from disruptive chance.
Other peoples do not build this way; among decent people such questions are approached with more reverence, with more assurance and planning. And not only among other peoples does one look with a clear eye at what is so important for our future — even among us Jews in other countries things are built in a different way when it is a matter of the future.
Thus, for example, we see abroad quite small Jewish communities which are wonderfully organised. They have everything of their own, and it is a pleasure to view what they create, what they build[?]. How many times are we simply amazed when we look at the grandiose buildings, of whatever type, that have been created by Jews. Such Jews could by no means understand how Jewish communities set up their own schools in other people's houses, which are not suited to the desired purpose; and still less would such Jews understand the haphazard happenings in communities like ours, where there are compact Jewish families numbering several thousand Jews. After all, we see model management among our brethren abroad in communities where there are no more than a mere hundred Jews.
And why should we fool ourselves? Could we not follow their example? True, the crisis is raging in Poland; true, the economic situation is very, very bad; true, the situation in the country is extraordinarily hard, and it is not easy to say that we can work wonders — but one truth must and should be said: with good will we could accomplish a great deal, we would receive much support, all the more so when it concerns such serious problems as the question of education.
Education is surely no luxury; every conscious people must bring up its children, and no person of understanding can remain indifferent to the future of his children. Everyone may have his own standpoint, his own line of thought, his own guideline, but on one thing everyone must agree: children must be educated without any excuses, and for that one must have schools which are not created by chance, do not develop by chance and indeed do not disappear by chance either.
We have a Jewish gimnazjum in Sosnowiec. Who doubts the necessity of such an educational institution? Who doubts that if we do not send our daughters there, we have nowhere to send them? We see, after all, what kind of "Jewish" daughters we get from the general Polish schools: what connection they have to their people, what they know of Jewish history — and apart from the fact that they know nothing of all this, the atmosphere there is often extraordinarily tense.
This means: if we have in Zagłębie no more than this one and only school for girls, then certainly, most certainly, we must see to it that it exists — and not merely for form's sake, but precisely because it is as necessary as life itself.
It is therefore only fair to think more seriously and more sincerely about the existing gimnazjum, to see to rescuing it as long as it exists and is useful. We must bear in mind that we have well-to-do Jews in Sosnowiec who can contribute to the public when it is a matter of consolidating such a necessary educational institution.
One need only approach it with strong will and full awareness that Sosnowiec must have its own building for the "public gimnazjum", and then, step by step, systematically, the project could become a real fact of which Jewish Sosnowiec could be proud.
It is high time that our educational institutions, especially those in public hands, be better situated, and then we shall have the assurance that the education of our children will be normal, crystallised, as it ought to be.
Dr. Pazuri.
