Activity of "Hashomer Hatzair" in Dąbrowa.
[Dąbrowa — Hashomer Hatzair; 15th anniversary.] Last Saturday [24 May 1930] "Hashomer Hatzair" in Dąbrowa [Dąbrowa Górnicza] celebrated its 15th anniversary jubilee, at which its new flag was unveiled. Before the celebration the whole organisation marched through the street. The celebration is opened by the chairman of the patrons' committee, Mr. Nachman Aharon Gutman, who gives the floor to Mr. Y. Bergsztajn, who gives a short survey of the organisation's development over the whole 15 years. A report on the present state of affairs is given by Mr. Isser Leskowicz[?]. After greetings from the KKL [Jewish National Fund], "Frayhayt", P. Ts. [Poale Zion], "Gordonia", the Zionists, "Hechalutz", "Kapai", "Herzliya" and "Hitachdut", the banner of the splendid flag is handed over to the singing of "Hatikvah". Then the invited guests and the representatives of the organisations drive in nails [into the flagstaff], and to the strains of "Hatikvah" and "Anu Olim" the chairman, Mr. N. A. Gutman, closes the celebration. With the flag unfurled and the patrons' committee at the head, the organisation then marches back, singing songs of Eretz Israel, to its premises, where the procession disperses to the singing of Hebrew songs.
Lag BaOmer Outing.
A continuation of the 15th-anniversary celebration was the Lag BaOmer outing with the new flag, which took place the next day, Sunday [25 May], at the "Almes" [unidentified place]. The outing had a very rich programme and was visited by various organisations; various olympiads and games were held for the younger shomrim and shomrot.
The outing ended with an "E.Y. bonfire" ("ע״י מדורה"), at which the orders of the day of the Chief Leadership (Hanhaga Rashit) and of the company leadership were read out. Then several members spoke about the significance of Lag BaOmer and of the "E.Y. bonfire". In a festive manner various distinctions were then awarded, and the passage to the older groups (kvutzot) took place.
An Hour with the Daughter of the Moabite King Eglon

[Shavuot feuilleton — satire; a dream of meeting Ruth the Moabite. By A. Lemech.]
So there I sit at my writing desk, and my head is spinning with worry. Perhaps you think I am pondering how to solve my problem, old today and forever new: "Where does one get [the money] for the holiday?" Or that I am afraid of the bailiff [the tax enforcement officer], who "dunning" me more than if I were [?] to go bankrupt even ten times and annul Korah's treasures — no. It is now twelve at night, and I am sure that His Majesty the Bailiff will not descend on me for a visit. He comes only when I am asleep in my shop, by day... You are still curious what my worry is after all? Then listen: I have not yet finished my Shavuot feuilleton... and there is little time left. What does one do? Help, what does one do? Where does one get a subject? I mean, I have in fact already written plenty of sheets, but although on Shavuot one does not eat meat dishes, dairy one certainly does eat, and my written feuilletons are pareve — neither dairy nor meat.. So I read them again, maybe something decent can be made of them, but they carry me away so much that, that — I fall asleep over them... But everything counts as falling asleep! Just as if I were sitting at a city-council meeting.
Well then, I sleep.
...I hear that a lady has come into the front room and is asking for the journalist Pfeffernotter (that means me). I prick up my ears: a coquettish little voice. I snatch up the little mirror, comb my hairdo (you must not forget that all this is happening in my sleep). At once there stands before me an elegantly dressed lady with traces of former majesty on her face. She introduces herself: Ruth, the daughter of Eglon, the king of Moab. I am filled with joy: now there will be something to write about, no small thing! A meeting with the daughter of a genuine ex-king. It will be very exotic. A thought runs through my brain and I ask her a question:
— Are you not aware, madam, that in the Bible too there is a woman's name Ruth?
— But that is me... Don't you know the midrash that Ruth was a daughter of Eglon king of Moab? That is me. You are evidently a contributor to the Agudah press, if you are such an ignoramus...
I am a little abashed [?] at my ignorance, but my heart very nearly bursts with pride: a ready subject for a Shavuot feuilleton, and how interesting!
— So, you are the daughter of Eglon, the ally of Ammon and Amalek, who together fought the Jews. Be so kind as to explain to me how it came about that you, the daughter of a Jew-hating king, married a Jew, an emigrant, and on top of that fell so passionately in love with a Jewish mother-in-law?..
— You don't know love.. — and she coquettishly tosses back her head, shoots me a sidelong glance, and her eyes look to see [?] what impression her explanation has made on me. I put on a serious face so that she should not notice my disbelief in her words, and say to her:
— An old, mouldy notion, love. Who today brings such a foolish word to his lips? Oh, not modern at all, madam...
I hit the mark. She jumps up as if bitten by a snake. She now changes her tone, and since she possesses "feminine reserve", it is not hard to get out of her at once the whole secret of the so-called love.
— You know, Mr. Journalist, that it was "in the days when the judges ruled", when revolutionary currents were blowing from all sides, and in neighbouring Judah there was "no king in Israel". They had already hurled the king from his throne, and the land was ruled by a Union of Councils [a jibe at the Soviet Union], "in the days when the judges ruled". Well, we knew how shaky things were with our father's throne. Any moment now the people would rise up and make a ruin-heap of our dynasty. Well, tell me yourself, how would we have looked? Just like the Russian Tsar's family. Who would have wanted to make a match with us? With a royal family? Is there anything more shameful in revolutionary times? We would have been left sitting with grey braids. So we made a gesture and promptly married the sons of an emigrant from Judah, and in that way wiped the royal disgrace off ourselves.. That way nothing was done to us, even when Ehud son of Gera stabbed our father; we were spared [?] thanks to our "revolutionary" gesture.
— Yes, in those days revolutionary upheavals really had to take place, because — "there was a famine in the land"... And — I ask further — perhaps you could inform us about your relationship with your mother-in-law? That is interesting.
— A quite nice woman. Especially that a mother-in-law should bear so sweet a name: Naomi [i.e. "pleasant"].. Have you ever heard of such a thing?
— You see, we had the same views and the same character: we both buried our husbands, not they us..
— And Orpah, how did she treat the mother-in-law?
— Quite differently. She kissed her one single time, "and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law", but that was at parting... Ah — she said [?] — how nice it is to kiss when you part from a mother-in-law, and forever at that... You can see my mother-in-law's love for me from her teaching me how to catch rich Boaz in the net, how to flirt with him — you should regard that as something extraordinary. That a mother-in-law should teach her daughter-in-law how to catch a rich bridegroom "on the fishing rod", that a mother-in-law's treacherous heart should help do the toilette — "wash thyself therefore, and anoint thee, and put thy raiment upon thee"? That she should reveal all the feminine secrets of how to fool the bachelor Boaz? And jealousy wouldn't eat her up?..
— Well, about your dealings with Boaz I won't question you. That is your private secret; I only want to remark to you that the custom by which business deals were concluded among you in olden times — to stretch out a foot to everyone ("Now this was the manner in former time in Israel concerning redeeming and concerning changing, for to confirm all things; a man plucked off his shoe and gave it to his neighbour") — has remained today too: after every deal, to stretch out a foot to everyone (pshitat ha-regel [lit. "stretching out the foot"] in Yiddish means: going bankrupt..), and in wedding deals too it is very much in fashion today: right after the wedding to stretch out the foot and give a kick..
She takes her leave, I thank her for the visit and kiss her hand...
— — — — —
At that "kiss" my wife woke up angrily: "What kind of kissing is this with you? Just look what he dreams in his sleep... Whom are you kissing? — "you've got no other worries""..
I rubbed my eyes and decided, instead of a feuilleton, to tell you the dream.
Klara Michelson. A Hasidic girl, a heroine of the uprising of 1863.

[History — Jews in the January Uprising of 1863; portrait: Klara Michelson.]
Moshe Feinkind.
In all the uprisings that took place against tsarist oppression, our Jews too took part in great numbers, both materially and physically.
But the Jews distinguished themselves above all in the last, unfortunate "powstanie" of the year 1863.
In this "powstanie" Poland no longer made the mistake it had committed in 1831, when it would not let the Jews take an active part in the ranks of the revolution. This time Poland stretched out its hands to the Jews, begging that the Jews should fight alongside for a free Poland, for a better tomorrow, and promising the Jews, in the event of victory, equal rights and other blessings.
And as is the way in such cases, our Jews indeed did not let themselves be begged for long, and volunteered for the ranks, and in solidarity with Poland's finest sons they shed no little blood on the Polish fields for Poland's honour and freedom.
Quite especially in this "powstanie" the "fair Jewish sex", the "min ha-yafeh", distinguished itself [?]. With self-sacrifice our Jewish daughters too took part in the bloody uprising and fought heroically against the cruel enemy — tsarism.
And one of those women heroes was the Hasidic girl Klara Michelson, who occupies a very important place in the history of the January Uprising, and who, remarkably, has not yet been mentioned by anyone.
Only thanks to the fact that the gates of the official archives now stand open has one also learned about her.
* * *
Our Klara Michelson came from a wealthy Hasidic house, and the green fields of Kałuszyn were her home.
Already as a child the Hasidic girl would listen, at her father's, the timber merchant, at home, to the stories of the squires, who used to converse with him about the sufferings of the "powstańcy" [insurgents], who had to uproot themselves from Poland, abandoning all their goods and property.
And already in her childhood years there flared up in Klara's young soul a love for the tormented land and compassion for its heroes, who fell as victims for Poland's freedom in the fields and forests where her father raised [?] his cattle and sheep and felled "poręby" [forest clearings]...
Her only dream was Poland's liberation. These thoughts hammered [?] day and night in her young brain, and as soon as the January Uprising of 1863 broke out, delicate, slender Klara threw herself with all her fiery soul and impetus into the waves of the revolution, and, taking her place in the ranks of Poland's finest sons, she drew more than one Jewish life along with her and sacrificed it for her beloved fatherland.
Klara Michelson wins the trust of the revolutionary authority; she becomes the leader of a so-called "stiletto detachment" [oddział sztyletników] in the Maków and Przasnysz districts. On her white mare, armed from head to foot, she rides at the head of her detachment from town to town, from village to village, through the Przasnysz fields and the Maków forests, spying on the movements of the tsarist army, agitating for the uprising, collecting money, weapons, horses, recruiting conscripts, etc. On these dangerous missions her young life was threatened more than once by the enemy, who lay in wait for her keenly.
The Jewish daughter was also a terror to the population; wherever she came with her "sztyletnicy" [dagger-men] she would carry out large requisitions for the "powstańcy", and she also carried out executions of traitors, of those condemned to death, etc.
The Russian general Schmidt, who operated in that area with his artillery and a detachment of Cossacks, wanted at any price to get the young lady "horsewoman", as they called her there, into his hands alive; he pursued her everywhere with great doggedness, searched for her in the Jewish houses, and in the peasant huts, in the thick forests and in the dark caves. And therefore indeed [?], where Klara Michelson spent one night she could no longer spend a second night; she always had to wander with her band, and the energetic General Schmidt did not succeed in catching her; she always managed to slip away on her mare out of his bloody hands and to hide from his spies...
*
The people's strength fails, the unfortunate uprising is liquidated, the "myatezhniki" [rebels] are hunted, a manhunt is organised, and among others the Jewish heroine too falls into the hands of the tsarist gendarmes, together with several more of her "sztyletnicy", and they were all interned in the Warsaw Citadel.
According to the court records that have been found, their trial took place in the Citadel on 12 January 1866. They were tried by the so-called "Field Auditoriat", which consisted solely of generals and had the task of punishing Poland's freedom heroes with death.
Her band is accused of carrying out death sentences in the year 1864 on the Jews Gutenberg of Maków and Lejzer Oszerow [?] of Przasnysz, and of extorting money from the population for revolutionary purposes. The "Żydówka" Karolina Michelson — so she is called in the court records — is accused of having been in contact with the "powstańcy", passing on orders from them which she carried out, and also of persuading the Polish gendarmes to carry out the death sentence on the Przasnysz merchant Lejzer Ożerow, among others.
Fortunately none of her co-defendants gave her away, and whereas they were sentenced to 12 years of katorga, the military court sentenced Klara Michelson to deportation to Siberia for life.
The military court did not wish to apply mitigating circumstances to the idealistic fighter for her holy fatherland, and passed such a heavy sentence on her.
The namiestnik Count Berg, to whom Klara's parents had turned for a pardon, confirmed this sentence on 15 January 1866, and on a certain grey morning one could see in the streets of Warsaw how the beautiful "Żydówka" Klara Michelson was led, in her coarse pink [?] prisoner's clothes, forged in chains, with a black square patch sewn on her back, among dozens of other freedom fighters, being sent to Siberia, where after a certain time, on the snowfields there, she breathed out her tender patriotic soul.
A Little Feuilleton — “Vuzkes” [Prams]: Help, the “Vuzkes”!

We live in a period of tremendous development of wheeled transport. In America almost every citizen already has at least one automobile. In Europe it goes a bit more slowly. In Zagłębie we have more people run over, killed and crippled by automobiles than automobiles themselves — but it is progressing!
Meanwhile we are in the midst of a noisy[?] development of another kind of wheeled transport.
Baby carriages.
Instead of the days of the old-fashioned cradle, instead of the sweet, dear lullaby, today one sings a little “vuzek” song [wózek — pram].
The “vuzkes”, however, are made more for the street than for the child. When buying a “vuzek”, the mother’s first worry is that the colour of the carriage should match her costume, her hat. If such a mother has several costumes, she must have several carriages matched to the colour.
A young wife who wants to keep up with fashion will not go out into the street today without a “vuzek”. A wife without a “vuzek” is like a door without a handle, a government without a Sejm, a merchant without a bankruptcy and a squire without a “żydek” [little Jew].
By rights, the “vuzek” requires a nanny to push the wheels. If one has no nanny or maid, it is a mitzvah to bestow this honour upon the old mother; a really modern lady harnesses her husband, and walking with him and with the “vuzek” in the street she must not stop squealing, getting angry and shouting that he does not push well, steers crookedly, shakes it too hard; and if one wants to show oneself a true woman of valour, one must not forget to give the husband, every few steps — at least at the end of every street — a few jabs in the side and to shout out loud, so that the whole street hears:
— My shlimazl, move a bit faster already!.. You look[?] just like the horse!..
I know a few young wives who are not at all long after their wedding. They have no desire for little children; this honour they gladly leave to their mothers-in-law. But what does one do with the “vuzkes”?! Without a child one cannot go out with a “vuzek”, after all!...
These little wives are living through a real tragedy.
Other little wives find a way. If they have no little ones, they pack a 12-year-old lad into the “vuzek” and off they go. Jokers tell that at the “vuzek” market — on Third of May Square [Plac 3 Maja] — they saw wives driving “vuzkes” in which no little ones were lying. It will come to the point that the wives will pack their own husbands into the “vuzkes” and off — away to the Old Market.
You are toying with fashion
Yankele.
The Golden-Calf Affair (A Shavuot Feuilleton)

By “Peters” [pseudonym].
— If all the forests became quills and all the seas — ink, it would not be possible to describe the delight brought by the charming holiday of Shavuot. Something of a trifle, such a holiday, which doesn’t get into your bones; a holiday which, because of its shortness, always leaves you feeling as after a beautiful little story not quite told to the end.
Take, for example, the holiday of Passover. It seems a holiday, too, that is not to be waved away. You have in it every[?] good thing: fat and salt and good dishes — and yet you are treated to a hefty portion of maror. And the maror doesn’t begin only at the seder; its true beginning is way, way before Passover; and if this short little, but oh-so-tasty, sun-dipped, greenery-decked Shavuot did not suddenly arrive, one could not forget the terrible, merciless Passover for a long, long time...
A cold spring, a rainy spring, but before the holiday of Shavuot it learns its manners, becomes bright and cheerful in every corner.
For example, I cannot imagine that, sitting at the seder, anyone would have in mind to go off to a dacha for chol ha-moed; but at Shavuot, at a table served with dairy food, I am sure that many a Passover “king” sits in a cheerful mood, as seven weeks ago at the seder, and more than one of them thinks: now, when I send my queen off to the dacha, I shall feel like a king, and not just like a king, but like a liberated man, like one who has come out of prison... And when such cheerful “perspectives” come into one’s thoughts, the soul becomes bright, like the Shavuot sun...
So it is good, eh? For truly, what better holiday can there be than Shavuot? Yet something is not entirely in order. This bright Shavuot sun has spots in it. I mean precisely the affair of the golden calf — the calf of gold, that is — which came about just at Shavuot.
It would seem: a fine, a great leader, Moses our teacher; a Torah — an antique, too; and Moses our teacher risked his life, did not eat and did not drink and probably did not sleep either, all in order to make us into Jews, into an “Thou hast chosen us” people — into the People of the Book; and suddenly this generation of the desert goes and acts foolish, childish, and in a hurry makes itself a calf. This generation of knowledge, those who had seen so many miracles, cannot hold out until Moses comes back — it would have suited a present-day impatient, nervous generation. No, I cannot understand it.
Talk to someone of the older generation and he will always reproach you that we, the young generation, do everything in haste: worked in a hurry, ate in a hurry, married in a hurry and even divorced in a hurry...
Let us think for a while and check who was more impatient, “they” or “we”. When I say “they”, I mean not only the menfolk of that generation, the generation of the desert, but precisely the women.
Let us go in order.
Who of you, for example, can imagine that if nowadays a “mobilisation” of jewellery were proclaimed among the women, and they were promised that a golden calf would be made of it, they would just like that[?] throw off all their bit of feminine finery and give it away with no use for themselves? We picture it quite differently. It would rather be possible in today’s generation of women that they would sacrifice their jewellery for the invention[?] of a new[?] means of becoming younger, or at worst — for an automatic device[?] for painting the lips and the like. In such a case, you see, I do not believe our wives would withstand the temptation; but for a calf? Only “those” desert women could do that..
And what about the menfolk of that generation? You see, one cannot entirely blame them either. No small share of the guilt in the golden-calf affair lies with Moses himself. This great Moses, who saw everything and knew everything, did not foresee what everyone of today’s generation knows.
Nowadays, for example, what kehilla or congregation is not organised? Had Moses then, before he went up Mount Sinai, put through a kehilla law and seen to it that a kehilla council be elected at once, with a board, with various committees, with the whole hullabaloo as is done nowadays, we are sure it would never have come to such foolishness — he would not have found any golden calf on his return.
Imagine: had the Jews then been run by a kehilla board, the golden-calf affair would first have been submitted to the board as a project; a committee would have been created; in the committee factions with opposing opinions would again have formed, and at best it would only after some time have been presented to the board; the latter would have sent it on to the council for approval; the kehilla council would have elected a new committee, which would have worked on it and had[?] to present it to the plenum — and only here would the real “fun” have begun: how big the calf should be, where the calf should be made, how much to assign for it, in what language to speak about it, and simply a bit of obstruction and exchanges of abuse, etc.
I guarantee you that in the course of the 40 days Moses tarried on Mount Sinai the calf would not yet have been finished at all, and even had Moses lived Methuselah’s years they would still be debating this question — and the proof: the Będzin mikveh..
Truth be told, the greatest benefit would yet have come of it — when Moses came back to his congregation he would not have found such an upheaval there. The men could have looked him in the face, the women would have kept their jewellery, and no calf idol would have remained.
Only now do we see that our generation is the cleverest, the most practical and the most patient. Even making a calf would not have come so easily to us.
But what comes of it all? The golden-calf affair remains a stain, and this very stain spoils my Shavuot a little!
Soul-Pangs

[Literature — poetry (sonnet); "Zangen", the literary supplement.] A. M. Wertheim (Radom).
(Sonnet)
To R. Sh. — a gift.

Ah, many waves have already passed over my head,
Rinsed away by the foam of life;
Yet my heart grows ever sadder and more troubled,
And old dreams of wounds [?] awaken in it...

I never possessed a heart that would feel for me,
I always only longed, and received but little;
And when your hand wished to still my pain,
Stretched out to me in friendship — then I kept silent..

Now my glances wander along all the roads,
My hand now seeks yours, the one stretched out to me,
In my heart feelings gather, awakened —

You! You have swum off into the sea of life, into the distance,
And dropped anchor at another shore,
And now my heart bleeds, when I have met you..
Purity and Sin

[Literature — drama criticism; "Zangen", the literary supplement.] "Reverend Silver" — a drama in 3 acts and 4 scenes by Sholem Asch.

Broad and expansive stretches [?] Sholem Asch's field of creation. Upon it shimmers a profusion of colours from the most varied blossoms [?] of all kinds of poetic plants. Some sparkle with the golden gleam of youth and the heavenly blue of love, breathing an intoxicating scent of happiness. Others, by contrast, darken with the sad, grimacing face of the reality of want. There is not a single place in Jewish life that has not been ploughed and sown in Sholem Asch's field of poetry. And that means a great deal, because the life of a people is too rich in colour and too varied for [?] one single poet to be able to embrace it, master it and give it the fullest expression. Every poet therefore chooses one domain to which he feels himself most called. And only the most varied instruments of the most varied artists together play out the life-symphony of a people. And it goes without saying that if someone commands such an unnaturally broad sweep as to embrace the whole of Jewish life, which is so scattered and dispersed among the most varied peoples and the most varied conditions of life — that means a great deal, because in fact it also means singing out the many life-melodies of many peoples — — — wherever a Jewish life has sprouted, in whatever most forsaken corner, the bee has come, absorbed the nectar — be it sweetish or bitterish, it makes no difference at all — then poured it out and handed it to the world. To form a picture of Jewish life in all its shadings one can only achieve by getting to know all of Sholem Asch's works. And in the Jewish past, too, his imagination has swum about and drawn up from there many precious pearls, which glitter in the crown of Jewish poetry.

And this breadth has not harmed the depth in the least. Each of his works is in and of itself a piece of Jewish life rendered with brilliant simplicity, naturalness — that is the quality of Sholem Asch's virtuosity.

* * *

Unceasingly gushes the inexhaustible spring of Sholem Asch's creation. Time and again he showers us with masterpieces, each of which is in itself an event in Jewish literature. And of the many masterpieces with which he has lately presented us, his new drama "Reverend Silver" deserves special treatment, because in it he shows himself in a new light, little noticed in him before. The great majority of his works consist of portrayals, descriptions and poetic re-creation of Jewish life in all its variety. In the new drama, however, he takes as his canvas a highly interesting, out-of-the-way mode of life in itself — the life of the reverends in America — and winds upon it a problem, a problem reaching to the heavens. And the canvas — that is, the peculiar life of the reverends — is so masterfully woven, so interesting and vivid, but the great problem wound upon it amazes and dazzles. We know that Sholem Asch can take a hidden, little-known side of life and unfold and reveal it so broadly. But here he has taken a broad and great problem and pressed it tightly into a few dozen pages and not many incidents, and the novelty of the theme brought him also a novelty of form — towards concentration, because just this compression of word and action suits such a theme as: God and Sin.

———

A young reverend, who occupies his father's inherited chair and carries on himself the dusty burden of generations. He preaches in his synagogue about the sanctity of family life and about the greatness of honour, which is "the divine flame that burns in man". But at the same time his wife Clara spends her time in the company of a young musician, playfully and "immorally", and this happens at the very time when her husband is preaching in the synagogue, ablaze with fervour, about the sanctity of family purity. The reverend's mother, however, the old, stiff Rebecca, knows about it, and when her son goes to carry out a [?] reverend's duty — to give spiritual help and advice to a woman of his synagogue — the mother takes him away and prevents him from carrying out his duty, because "the pillar on which you stand is itself rotted through by the very disease you want to heal with your words"; and she demands that he keep to his own duty, grown out of himself, that "words have weight only when deeds stand behind them". For words are like bills of exchange drawn on feelings, thoughts and sensations, and whoever has issued them must always be ready to redeem the bill. She wants him to drive away his sinful wife.

Silver calls Clara in. He is agitated. Can there really be such a flaw in his calling? He speaks to her as a reverend. It does not upset him what feelings his wife has for her beloved; he only wants to know from her whether there has not occurred between them such a relationship as would undermine his reverend's pillar. She may love Rubinstein, that is no concern of his; he only wants to know whether sinful relations do not exist between them. And when he succeeds in getting from his Clara the answer that no such sinful relations have occurred, he is the happiest of men and demands of his mother that she beg forgiveness of his "pure", innocent wife.

But it was not the reverend who here overcame [?] the man; it was not his office and calling that had dulled in him the feelings of a man, and that is why he made nothing of Clara's love affair with Rubinstein. His indifference stems not from dullness but from a noble source. He knows that it is not her fault. "It is not you who sinned against me, but I against you. Yes, I know it, I did nothing to win your love." And out of this very feeling springs such a big-hearted forgiveness. He pleads that the musician Rubinstein should go on being a frequent visitor in his house; he offers him his readiness to help him build a conservatory where Rubinstein would work together with Clara. He sees nothing bad in it. Why should she not enjoy happiness?...

So noble, so lofty, so far from low human jealousy. He knows that because "he had neglected her, she had to seek joy and love elsewhere".. And this seems so natural to him that he feels guilty and seeks some way to repair his fault.

Clara has left him, spent a year with Rubinstein, and in the end Rubinstein abandoned her. Silver learns that she has come back to his town, where she is staying in a dubious hotel. He runs to her to bring her back to his house. She does not want to return, because "she has already looked the night in the face, her body has been wind-beaten [?] by the cold of the night". She knows that she is now so impure, so sinful, that she is not worthy of the holy and pure Silver.

But Silver argues to her: "You are lovelier, purer, better than I, because you have been tossed [?] by the winds of the night, you have seen people in their pain and want, you tormented and purified wife of mine. Clara weeps: "I went to look elsewhere for that which shone like a sun in my home, I, an unworthy wife."

The mother runs to call the members of the synagogue. Such a scandal — a reverend to live with a treacherous woman, a sinner who has already sold her body. But the reverend pours out the light of truth [?] of his new faith.

"What is sin? What is right? Who can say it? Have you been in a person's heart and ached with his ache? You see a person lying in a pit and you, like foolish boys, stand around holding your sides with laughter."

"It is an idol, a foolish idolatry which people have made for themselves, and on whose altar whole nations are brought as sacrifices."

"And precisely because I believe that there is a great God, because I believe in a just, logical Ruler of the world — I believe that there is no sin. If I did not believe in God, I would believe in sin."

And while the mother and the synagogue leaders speak to him in the name of God and demand that he drive the sinner out of his home, and never let God's name out of their mouths and preach morality — Clara has been found dead; the preachers of morality have killed a human being..

* * *

Avrom Reyzen, in his memoirs "War Years" ("Tsukunft", February 9130 [sic, = 1930]), relates that Sholem Asch once said to him: "One must [?] say something, a word to the world... I want to say it"...

In his latest works one does indeed feel the urge to say a new word to the world, a "word"... One hears the knocking of the approaching new word, and when it arrives, the world will hear the Jewish poet — Sholem Asch...

S. Elida.
The Sick in May

[Literature — poetry.] Leyzer Shikman (Sosnowiec).

The sick grow glad in white, full-blossomed May:
The ever-gloomy winter has died once again —
They sing out a song, soaked full of joy,
Though their suffering is not lessened by it...

In fragrant May the sick are always so cheerful,
And in their fading eyes bright little fires flicker;
— If one has already made it this far,
Then every danger is already past the border...

In May the sick laugh as merrily as any healthy man,
Their ever-darkened spirits grow clear.
Yet the sick often turn sad in the middle of bright May,
When the thought comes to them of the first snowfall.

The world-famous French writer Romain Rolland has published in "Monde" an article against the campaign of the various religions over the religious persecutions in Soviet Russia. The activity of the American Culture Society.
The American Jewish Culture Society, which recently held its first conference, has entered the phase of productive work. A commission has been created for the coordination of the Jewish secular schools in America. The committee includes Dr. Chaim Zhitlowsky, S. Niger and others. At the end of May a large popular conference is also to be convened.

* * *

Where a blessing and where a curse.
It is worth noting that precisely at the congress of the American Jewish Culture Society two resolutions were adopted: one — a greeting to Soviet Russia, where a new Jewish "culture" is being "built", and the second — a "protest" against the "persecutions" of Yiddish in the Land of Israel. Something with which to protest against the Yevsektsiya, and something with which to greet the Land of Israel — that the conference no longer had...

Nahum Sokolow's 70th jubilee.
In America, on the 11th of this month, Nahum Sokolow's 70th jubilee was celebrated. The “Green” Shavuot

[Humour — “Der Kokh-Lefl”, Shavuot humour page; satirical poem on taxes.]
(Dedicated to the tax offices of all Poland).

Green the businesses, green the fields,
green the people, green the woods,
wherever you cast your glance,
green today is all of life,
wherever you take a step —
green, oh green, oh green..

In these green times of ours
Jews are shutting their shops,
for trade is shattered
and the head is badly cracked;
they turn this way and that;
everything, alas, yellow and green...

Jews sit, consult, ponder,
and weep with bitter tears:
where to get a bite of bread
so as not to suffer hunger's need?
Gevalt, where does one go now,
when all around is black and green...

And the children cry and scream:
Daddy, Mummy, give us something to chew —
stones, bones, anything at all!
It pounds in the heart as if with flails [?],
God! where can one turn,
when all around is pale and green...

Oh green the meadows, oh green the woods,
oh green the people, oh green the fields,
wherever you cast your glance,
green today is all of life,
wherever you take a step —
green, oh green, oh green..
Yosef Perlberger.

A Great Event in Bielitz.

Last Sunday, during the outing of the Będzin “Hakoach” to Bielitz [Bielsko], a “great event” took place on the way.
The car in which the “father” Yaakov (Jakub) and his “eldest son” Reuven (Romek) were riding suddenly stopped, and a “little angel” in the shape of a woman took them by the arms and went strolling...
The power of the little angel was so strong that both of them, the “father” and the “son”, shook hands...
The little birds in the trees, who were watching this scene of peace, played along and whispered:
— May it last for long years...

Why Don't the Express Trains Stop?

As our readers already know, the railway directorate in its new timetable abolished the stopping of the express trains at the Będzin railway station.
On this question our Warsaw correspondent had a conversation with the president of the railway directorate, who explained that the ban on the express trains was issued so that the antiques found in Będzin should not be able to get out quickly into other towns.

"He Does Not Agree"...

[Humour — Dąbrowa; a Zionist meeting against the restriction of immigration.] They tell of a yishuvnik [village Jew], a great ignoramus, who longed to become famous "in the whole world". Once he came into the synagogue and heard the shammes bang on the table and call out:
— Ya'aleh ve-yavo!
At this the yishuvnik shouts: No, lo ya'aleh ve-lo yavo [it shall not go up and shall not come].
Why do I tell this? On Sunday morning I was in Dąbrowa, where Dr. Gotlib lectured on the present situation in Eretz Israel.
After the lecture a resolution in this spirit was read out, expressing a protest against the restriction decree.
— Who is against? And as luck would have it, there was indeed a hero like that yishuvnik, and he shouts:
— Lo ya'aleh! I am against....

[Satirical poem — Eretz Israel: the restriction of immigration and the Wailing Wall.]
It is dark in Palestine,
The Philistines have as if awoken,
Ishmael torments Israel
And the Englishman laughs..

A great laughter seizes him,
And the Grand Mufti rubs his hands:
Should this mean that the decree
Is still because of the old Wall..

England gives "according to capacity" [economic absorptive capacity]
And ... [?] the Jew;
The Jew does have brains in his head —
Let him shoot with them..

Jews lament, Jews groan,
And workers ... [?]
And over everything flutters
Proudly the British flag..

Oh, what shall we say, what shall we speak?
It grows bitter in the land,
The devil laughs mightily [?]
And the old Wall weeps...

[Humour — Będzin; the Zionist Organisation and Agudat Israel.] The committee of the Zionist Organisation in Będzin held a meeting in connection with the emigration decree, at which a report was given on the intervention with the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel], which had not permitted speaking in the synagogue.

Ławnik Goldsztajn at a Session of the League of Nations

[Humour — Będzin; satire on municipal figures.] From Geneva we are informed:
In the middle of a session of the League of Nations news arrived that the ławnik [alderman, member of the municipal executive] of the Będzin magistrate, Mr. Goldsztajn, is travelling to Paris. The session was immediately interrupted, and the presidium of the League of Nations went off to the railway station to welcome the statesman.
The welcome was a hearty one. After much effort and labour Mr. Goldsztajn agreed to take part in the session, at which the economic situation in Europe was discussed.
The floor on the question was taken by ławnik Goldsztajn, who reported on the situation in Zagłębie and especially in Będzin, a town that grows and develops like a true Garden of Eden. Będzin — he said — will become a second Tel Aviv; in place of stones and rocks [?] flowers will grow...
The speech was received with strong applause.

In Honour of Shavuot

[Holidays — Shavuot: Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes; followed by a political interview with Deputy Hartglas in Sosnowiec.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes relating to Shavuot and the receiving of the Torah.
Collected and adapted by Y. L.

a) The Time of the Giving of Our Torah.
Why is Shavuot called "the time of the giving of our Torah" and not "the time of the receiving of our Torah"?
— Because the Torah was indeed given on Mount Sinai, when the Jews came out of Egypt; at that time a Torah was given to the world. But the receiving — the accepting of the Torah — is not limited to that time; in all later times, whoever wishes can receive the Torah. Therefore the receiving of the Torah cannot be tied to a particular time; only the giving of the Torah took place then.
The Rim of Ger.

b) "I will betroth thee unto Me for ever."
In Talmudic and Kabbalistic literature (with traces of it in the Bible too) the act of the giving of the Torah is described and compared to a betrothal, or a marriage of the Shekhinah with the Community of Israel. Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berdichev once said, in his own manner:
Master of the Universe! You made a pedigree match in us — we are of such distinguished lineage, sons of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. We, on the other hand, bought ourselves no pedigree from You, since You, so to speak, have no father... So what then? We made a money match in You. You do say "Mine is the silver and Mine is the gold, saith the Lord." If so, then keep Your word and give us the rich dowry...
• • •
The Gaon of Sanz married four times. The fourth time his children did not like it; his son Rabbi Baruch of Gorlice came in to him and said: "Does Father know that when Rabbi Reb Baruch became a widower he said he would not marry any more, but would marry the Torah"...
— Well, — his father answers him, — do you want me to marry the Torah too? She is already a married woman — Rabbi Reb Baruch's...

c) "We will do and we will hear."
All the Jews at the giving of the Torah called out "We will do and we will hear"! But in fact each one cried "I will do and hear", so the Torah should have said "I will do and I will hear", in the singular.
— So dear and precious was the Torah to them that each one took upon himself the responsibility and surety for the other. The exaltation of the moment called forth such solidarity in them.
Siach Sarfei Kodesh.

d) "And there Israel encamped."
When the Jews were to receive the Torah beneath Mount Sinai, the verse describes their encampment in the singular — "vayichan", not "vayachanu", because — says the homily — they rested there with one heart and one will. And only in this way could they receive the Torah.
And that is why we celebrate Shavuot only after the days of the Omer count, because the days of the count symbolise disunity and fragmentation. At that time the disciples of Rabbi Akiva died because of their intrigues and groundless hatred. And so, when we pass through the days of the count, when we overcome the days of disunity, we can attain the receiving of the Torah, which happened only through unity.
Kedushat Levi.

e) Why is he glad about the receiving of the Torah?
An apikoros (unbeliever) was very glad on Shavuot about the giving of the Torah. He was asked: Why are you glad about the giving of the Torah? You commit every sin in the world!
— That is exactly my joy, that they gave the Torah to us — we do with it what we like... Had they given it to the police, it would have been very bitter: for every little sin — a fine, a police report...

f) Oath and Shavuot.
When the famous philosopher Moses Mendelssohn arrived in Berlin he behaved in a very Jewish manner: he kept all the Jewish traditions and on Shavuot decorated the house with greenery, according to the old Jewish custom. Later, when his house became a meeting place for the greatest German thinkers and aristocrats too, he abolished the custom at home. When this was told to the Berlin rabbi of the day, Reb Hershele Halberstadt, he made the following sarcastic remark: Before, he was one who admits part of a claim (— a half-believer), so he was liable to an oath (— "shevuah", and Shavuot); now he denies everything (— a complete unbeliever), so he is exempt from oaths ("shevuot")...

The Scroll of Ruth.
a) "There was a famine in the land — and a man went" (1:1)
Avimelech [sic; read: Elimelech] was one of the leaders of the generation, an important statesman and a very rich man; so when a famine broke out in the land he thought to himself: from all sides people will come for support, each with his beggar's bag — so he took counsel with himself and went away...
b) "And a man went.. he, and his wife, and his two sons"
One by one the wealthy family slipped out of famine-stricken Eretz Israel. First Avimelech himself, and he went as "a man", as a simple person, dressed in plain clothes, so that the people would not recognise him; then "his wife", and only after that "his two sons" — so that no one would see them fleeing, so as not to have to help the poor...
Yichus Dor.
c) "Whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge" (1:16)
Ruth knew that to take up a Jewish life means to live through a night.. So she said figuratively [?]: "Whither thou goest, I will go" — I will go along with the Jewish people; "and where thou lodgest, I will lodge" — though it will be dark there for me as the night, I will stay the night.
Revid HaZahav.
d) "And she beat out that she had gleaned" (2:17)
Why did Ruth thresh and beat out the ears? She was afraid that on her way home a young man would meet her and out of [?] politeness would want to help her carry the bundle; but she knew that such politeness borders on lewdness... And because she was modest, she threshed the ears right there in the field, so that she would have a small bundle and no young man would need to "help" her...
Beit Avraham [?], citing [?] the Alshich.

—o—

[Interview — Polish politics and Zionism; Sosnowiec.]
Over a Glass of Black Coffee with Deputy Hartglas
(A special conversation for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung").
As is known, Deputy Hartglas visited Sosnowiec on Sunday. The writer of these lines had a conversation with the distinguished guest about various current questions in the country and in Zionism.
— What is of most interest today, — Deputy Hartglas begins, — is the closing of the extraordinary session of the Sejm, a thing which in my opinion is an absurdity, for if the constitution provides that an ordinary Sejm session can be closed, this certainly cannot be applied to an extraordinary session, since its very extraordinariness already closes [?] the matter by itself.
Will the Sejm be dissolved? I think not, because the Sanacja is now afraid of elections, and for that reason it actually withdrew its lists in the Volhynia and Lida electoral districts. Besides, there is not a person in Poland today, not even the Prime Minister himself, who knows what will be tomorrow, or even what the government will say tomorrow... What is known is this: the economic situation grows worse from day to day, and the Jews suffer from it most of all. And therefore we, the Jewish "Koło", have no reason whatsoever to change the oppositional tactics we have followed until now.
— And what is your opinion, Mr. Deputy, about the decree against immigration to Palestine?
— One must not deny that the situation is serious. But there is no reason for despair. First of all, England will abolish this decree, because she must have Palestine, and Eretz Israel without Jews is out of the question. England must have us there. It is only a question of tempo. The greatest influence at the present moment can be exercised by American Jewry; its voice now carries weight [?].
What should be done in the Zionist ranks? Strengthen our forces, for we have shown over the last 10 years that more than 70 thousand people immigrated to Eretz Israel, although according to the official immigration regulations it is an impossible thing... This happened thanks to faith in our only hope — to build our national home, Eretz Israel."
Sh.

Antisemitic Outburst by an "Agudah-ławik" / Sensational "News" from Zagłębie in Haynt / A Health-Fund Outpatient Clinic in Będzin / What Isn't Good for the Health Gets Cut Out... / Will the Shops Be Open Next Sunday? The City President Confers with the Starosta Today / Reading of the Eretz-Israel Poet Papiernikov / An Incident with a Torah Scroll / They Protest, Poor Things... / Secular Studies at the Talmud Torah / The Matura Examinations / Artisans' Meeting / A Second Lecture by Mr. Israel Ritov

[Będzin — City Council.] The municipal budget is being debated in its second reading. At Monday's session a number of budget items were adopted, such as schooling, cultural purposes, etc.
As always, all the non-Jewish factions put forward motions to allocate thousands of złoty for paving the streets in the outskirts. From the Jewish councillors, too, the following motions were made: 1) by Mr. Erlich, to increase the subsidies for the ḥadarim "Yesodei Torah" and "Mizrachi"; 2) by Mr. Kleinman, that the subsidy for the artisans' courses be increased; and 3) by Mr. Feiger, that 2 thousand zł. be allocated as a subsidy for the Yiddish secular school that is to open at the beginning of the new school year.
In the "Jewish" debate the Jewish councillors behaved like that false mother who agreed that "the child should be cut in two"... "it shall be neither mine nor thine". The first signal was given by the councillors of the Left Poalei Zion. They by no means "could" agree to vote for increasing the subsidy for the above-mentioned schools and for subsidising "Tarbut"... that would indeed have been a real "assault" on their principles.
The bourgeois Jewish councillors answered "as was fitting" and voted against Feiger's motion to allocate a subsidy for the future Yiddish folk school; thanks to this the motion failed.
———
The session is chaired by the president [of the council] Mr. Fürstenberg. During the discussion of expenditure and subsidies for educational purposes, councillor Erlich (Poalei Agudas Yisroel) reads from a paper a motion that the subsidy for "Yesodei Torah" and "Mizrachi", amounting to 3,500 zł., be raised to 17,500 zł.
Councillor Dr. Rechtman speaks about the lack of order in the field of the evening courses for adults. For this purpose an apparatus of engineers[?], directors and administrators has been engaged, but qualified teaching staff are lacking. Dr. Rechtman proposes that 15 thousand zł. of the projected sum be allocated to the evening courses.
Councillor Kleinman, citing a review of the evening courses in our paper, proposes that the subsidy for the artisans' courses, amounting to 500 zł., be increased to a thousand zł.
Councillor Feiger expounds at length on the importance of the Jewish child learning secular subjects in Yiddish, and puts forward a motion that 2 thousand zł. be allocated for such a Jewish folk school, which is opening in Będzin for the new school year.
The first to speak in the debate is the [city] president Michał. He comes out against the sums requested, arguing that private institutions must be maintained by their own members. "I would still have understood — he says — if councillor Erlich had demanded a subsidy for the Talmud Torah, where poor children study" (alas and alack, that a non-Jew must draw attention to this.) "But toward private schools the magistrate has 'no obligation at all'"...
An extremely antisemitic speech was delivered by the "Agudah-ławik" Hetmańczyk, who this time "forgot" the promises they give their Jewish allies. "We — he says — live in Poland, and the letter that a Jewish grandchild writes to his grandfather must be written in Polish," etc.
Replies were made by: Dr. Rechtman, Jakubowicz, Rechnitz, Feiger and Gitler.
The "Jewish" debate was finally closed, and in a tense atmosphere the vote on the motions submitted took place. The result:
The motion of councillor Erlich (PAY) fails. On the other hand, Mr. Gitler's amendment is adopted, that the subsidy for "Yesodei Torah" and "Mizrachi" be increased to 10 thousand zł.
The artisans' courses receive 1000 zł.
Dr. Rechtman's motion that "Tarbut" receive 500 zł. fails.
Mr. Feiger's motion receives 2 votes...

[Będzin — Press.] Lately Haynt [the Warsaw Yiddish daily] has been carrying sensational "news" from Zagłębie, which strikes "terror" into the inhabitants of Zagłębie.
The first item from "the accurate correspondent" was that 14 (read: fourteen) sportsmen from Będzin had been seriously injured.

Will the Shops Be Open Next Sunday? The City President Confers with the Starosta Today.
[Będzin — Commerce.] In connection with the fact that next Sunday is the eve of Shavuot, and the population is unable to provide itself with foodstuffs and other articles for the holiday, the local merchants' institutions have approached the starosta and the city administration with a proposal that on this Sunday the shops be open from 1 at midday until 6 o'clock.

Reading of the Eretz-Israel Poet Papiernikov.
[Będzin — Culture.] On Saturday the 31st of this month, at 2.30, a collective literary reading devoted to the Eretz-Israel poet Y. Papiernikov will take place in the City Council hall. The poet himself will also take part in the collective reading.
The same reading will also take place in Sosnowiec on Saturday at 8 in the evening at the "Hotel Polski".
The readings promise to be interesting.
—o—
An Incident with a Torah Scroll.
[Będzin — Religion.] On Wednesday morning, while a Torah scroll was being taken out in the Amshinov shtibl, a second scroll fell out through carelessness.
Because of this, the worshippers who had been present fasted yesterday.
—o—
They Protest, Poor Things...
[Będzin — Merchants.] The traders in the local market halls held a meeting at which they discussed their bitter situation: there is no turnover, and the tax office shouts "give!"...
It was resolved to intervene with the authorities so that the tax burden of the poor traders be eased.
—o—
Secular Studies at the Talmud Torah.
[Będzin — Education.] After much effort it was obtained from the school authorities that the Talmud Torah be recognised as a general public school [szkoła powszechna].
The secular studies already began on the 15th of this month.
—o—
The Matura Examinations.
[Będzin — Education.] At the "Fürstenberg" gymnasium they begin on Wednesday, Isru Chag of Shavuot. 9 pupils are sitting the examination.
—o—
Artisans' Meeting.
[Będzin — Artisans.] On Tuesday, the 2nd day of Shavuot, a general meeting of artisans will take place, at which the following will be dealt with: combating illegal artisan workshops; registration of artisans; a levy on artisan workshops for the benefit of the artisans' fund; tax matters: exempting small workshops from purchasing [trade] patents; exempting home workers (chałupnicy) from purchasing patents; reducing the turnover tax for artisans producing articles of primary necessity to 1 per cent.
—o—
A Second Lecture by Mr. Israel Ritov.
[Będzin — Zionism.] Israel Ritov's lecture last Saturday at "Karsa" attracted a large audience; in a 2-hour lecture he described the present situation in Zionism.
At the request of the public the organisers, the Right Poalei Zion, succeeded in keeping the talented speaker for another lecture, which will take place this Saturday afternoon at "Karsa" on the topic: "The new winds around our life's work in Eretz Israel" (the Bund, the Yevsektsia, the Left; the MOPSists, effendis, antisemites of every kind).
The same lecture will take place the same evening in Sosnowiec at the "Hotel Polski".
Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — local news: municipality and transport, schools, press, crime, politics, kehilla, Zionism.]
The tunnel will be finished this year.
This week a commission of the Railway Ministry stayed here and acquainted itself with the work around the tunnel.
The commission held a conference with the town administration, which pointed out a series of difficulties because of which the tunnel cannot be completed.
At the conference the commission declared that the railway directorate will see to it that the tunnel is completed this year.
Enrolment in the public schools.
On 16, 17 and 18 czerwiec [June] the enrolment will take place in the public schools for children born in the year 1923.
"Kurier Zachodni" is afraid...
The organ of the N.D. [National Democrats, Endecja] this week devoted a special article to the restriction [of immigration] to the Land of Israel.
The gist of the article is that the main body of emigrants are from Poland, and because of the restriction the emigration will be stopped...
A suicide — a stubborn one.
The 23-year-old Sobala of Przechodnia [?] Street cut his veins with the aim of committing suicide.
A few weeks ago the same man had thrown himself under the tram.
A brawl of debtors.
On Dekerta Street a brawl broke out between the Lederman family and Dwora Fiszel. The brawl took on a serious character. Only the police put an end to the "war" and handed the guilty parties over to the investigation office.
Lecture by Deputy A. Hartglas.
On Sunday, at the invitation of "Herzliya" in Sosnowiec, the former president of the Jewish "Koło" [Jewish Club in the Sejm], Deputy A. Hartglas, gave a lecture in the Municipal Theatre on the topic: "The present situation in the country". In a successful two-hour lecture the speaker pointed to the bad economic situation of the country, from which the Jewish population suffers most of all.
For his successful lecture Deputy Hartglas was rewarded with long-lasting applause.
To the conference of kehillot.
Which took place yesterday in Warsaw, the member of the kehilla board Mr. J. S. Wajgreb [?] was delegated by the Sosnowiec kehilla.
The League for Labour Palestine
is holding a protest meeting on Saturday night against the aliyah decree.
From the town administration.
At its last meeting the town administration decided to buy from Count Renard the "Steiner-Boden" [the stony ground; ?].
Thanks to this several hundred workers will be employed.
A members' meeting.
This Saturday afternoon a larger members' meeting will take place in the premises of "Hitachdut", devoted to the question of the emigration decree for the Land of Israel.
Dąbrowa

[Dąbrowa Górnicza — crime: murder of a Jewish merchant; fire; accident.]
A Jewish merchant murdered.
On Monday at about 10 in the evening the local iron and rag dealer, the 44-year-old Herszel Bergsztejn, was murdered on the railway bridge.
The murder, as people recount, took place in the following way:
Herszel Bergsztejn was at that time walking home to Limanowskiego Street. Coming onto the iron railway bridge, he was attacked by several persons who, as it turns out, had been standing on the lookout and waiting for their victim.
When Bergsztejn was in the middle of the bridge, he was struck from behind with a hammer on the head, from which he fell unconscious. After the "job" the murderer calmly walked away.
When the railway watchman saw blood pouring down from above, he raised the alarm; people came running, and also a policeman, who gave help to the unconscious man. Later Bergsztejn was taken to the Będzin hospital, where an operation was performed.
The operation unfortunately did not succeed, and the next day, Tuesday, he died.
According to conjecture it was an act of revenge by Christians who hated the murdered man.
A fire at the station.
On Monday a wagon with straw burned at the local station.
Horses "get angry"...
In Reden a horse pushed its cart into a tram car, as a result of which several window-panes were smashed.

Budget debate at the plenum of the City Council

[Będzin — City Council.] At Wednesday's session of the Będzin City Council the continuation of the expenditure budget for the year 1920/31 [sic; read 1930/31] was considered.
Under the item „social welfare“ the following proposals and resolutions[?] were submitted: from Klejnman, that the Magistrate should build an asylum for the insane; a proposal from Lewin that out of the item 5 thousand zł. for evicted families be given to the Tenants' Association and to „Dobroczynność“ [the charity society] — a thousand zł. each; from Goldfeld, to assign 2 thousand zł. for coal for the poor and 2 thousand zł. for sick children not of school age.
Councillor Fajner dealt out „with a generous hand“ and proposed that 10 thousand zł. be allocated to build an institution for undernourished children, 10 thousand zł. for health-cure purposes, etc.
Erlich (Poale Zion): that the Jewish children who are sent to Busko for a cure should receive kosher food.
After a lengthy discussion about the votes that had taken place: Lewin's proposal was rejected, Goldfeld's coal proposal — adopted, and Fajner's proposals too were „adopted“.
The total sum for social welfare amounts to 489 thousand zł.
Those who wish to benefit from the 1 percent turnover rate.

[Będzin — taxes.] The Będzin tax office (urząd) has sent out a circular to all those who wish to benefit from the relief[?] of paying 1 percent of turnover (those who do not keep books): by the 11th of this month they must submit a series of certificates from merchants proving that the merchants in question conduct wholesale trade.
District conference of „Hitachdut“.

[Będzin — Zionism.] Next Sunday a district conference of „Hitachdut“ will take place in its own premises in Będzin. The conference will be attended by the guests Gershon Geller and Aharon Berski (Eretz Israel), Moshe Tacza (Warsaw) and Yosef Lewi (Łódź).
In connection with the conference a members' meeting is taking place this Sabbath.
A theft.

[Strzemieszyce — crime.] Unknown thieves got in through the back door into Yehoshua Grin's paper and stationery shop in Strzemieszyce[?], from where they carried off various goods worth 4 thousand zł.
—o—
A „hooligan“ attack on Jewish schoolchildren.
[Będzin — antisemitism.] Yesterday at noon a large number of children, accompanied by two teachers from Public School no. 8 in Będzin, went out on an excursion to the „Żelaga“[?]. But when the children arrived at the spot, they were attacked by several Christian hooligans, who began beating the teachers.
The children ran home in great fright.
This is already the second case in which Jewish children receive such a „welcome“ when they want to enjoy a few hours in the open air.
Who received the matura?

[Będzin — education.] Yesterday the matura (school-leaving) examinations were completed at Fürstenberg's „Yavne“ gymnasium and at the Polish boys' gymnasium.
At „Yavne“ 9 pupils sat the examination and all of them received the matura.
The pupils are: Arysz Felsensztajn, Gershon Frajberg, Yitzhak Nachum Grundman[?], Zalman Ber Rechnic, Chaim Yosef Sztajer, Zbiham[?] Wajnrajch, Natan Zborowski, Moshe Zabrame[?], Tuvia Ajnwald.
At the Polish gymnasium: Eli Flachner, Adolf Bursztyn, Yitzhak Szer, Adolf Lewin, Leon Sprzarosz[?], Moshe Półtorak, Kalman Rotenberg.
At this gymnasium 8 Jewish pupils sat the examination
From craftsmen's life in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — craftsmen.] This Saturday night the culture committee of the Sosnowiec Craftsmen's Association is holding a large artistic evening in the Municipal Theatre with the participation of the well-known artistic reciter Herman Lewensztajn.
On Sunday afternoon a mass meeting of craftsmen will take place. The meeting will deal with the question of the forthcoming examinations and other important questions.
—o—
Draft of the 1909 class.
[Zagłębie — army.] Yesterday the draft (pobór) began of those born in 1909, and also of the classes of 1907 and 1908 who had received a deferment (odroczenie) at the previous commissions.
Of this year 1,720 men are registered on the draft list.
—o—
A death sentence for a mother-murderess.
[Kraków — court.] The jury court in Kraków has sentenced to death the woman Zofia Furdyn, who murdered her 5-month-old child. The murderous mother stuffed sand into the child's mouth and thus suffocated it.
—o—
The Sosnowiec city budget on the agenda.
[Sosnowiec — City Council.] Yesterday a City Council session took place in Sosnowiec, at which the new municipal budget was dealt with.
After settling a series of urgent proposals concerning relief and work for the unemployed, the general debate on the budget began. The BB and ND clubs proposed sending the budget back to the budget committee.
On behalf of the Jewish councillors' club, Dr. G. Mladiska[?] declared that the Jewish club would vote for the budget.
On behalf of the Left Poale Zion, councillor Hamburger declared that they would vote against.
Finally the proposal of councillor Michel, that the budget be sent back to the budget committee, was put to the vote.
By a majority of votes the proposal was defeated.

From Last Shavuot

Last Shavuot as it were "announced" that the cucumber season (the silly season) is approaching. All parties and organisations "sat" quietly and organised no events whatsoever.
—o—
The holiday season was exploited by the Messrs. fish and meat sellers. In honour of the holiday the price of fish was raised by no less than 2 zł. per kilo, and meat by 1 zł. per kg.
—o—
The weather too was suited to the holiday. Not hot and not cold, only sultry, cramped like all of life...
—o—
On the eve of Shavuot the "Mizrachi" in Będzin also wanted to protest against England, but so that the "Torah"[?] should suffer no distress on the festival of the Giving of the Torah, the protest was called off..
—o—
The Jewish vagrants (17 men in number) were provided with... distress. Only thanks to Szmuel Dawid Perigs did the vagrants get a lunch, and only on the second day of the holiday.
The same "provision" was also enjoyed by the Jewish prisoners in the Będzin jail. Only when the prayer leader raised an alarm in the town that Jews were starving there was a little food collected for them.

A Bibliographical Note

[Bibliography — press and health.] "Folksgezunt" ["People's Health"], a fortnightly illustrated popular-scientific journal for hygiene and medicine, published by "TOZ" — "OZE" [the Jewish health-protection societies], edited by Dr. Tsemakh Shabad [Cemach Szabad].
Although "Folksgezunt" has already been appearing for 8 years and is very popular with the broad public, it is still desirable from time to time to give a survey of this important journal, so as thereby to help bring about the still wider circulation it truly deserves.
For 8 years now the Jewish population has had the privilege of a popular organ that discusses the hardest subjects of hygiene and medicine so clearly that even the simplest reader can get an idea of the most practical questions bearing on his own health and on the health and upbringing of children, and the like.
The articles in the "F.G." are written in a simple style, yet at the same time strictly scientifically. The delicate questions of sexual life are treated decently and scientifically, and the journal strives to avoid any taint that might excite the imagination, and in the sharpest way every medical sensation that might blackmail and mislead the credulous public.
Among the important sections of the "F.G." the following are worth noting: 1) the structure[?] and functioning of the human organs; 2) hygiene and upbringing of the child; 3) children's diseases; 4) hygiene of the woman; 5) personal hygiene; 6) hygiene among Jews; 7) occupational hygiene; 8) food hygiene; 6) [sic, for 9] contagious diseases; 10) hygiene of sexual life; 11) venereal diseases; 12) eye diseases; 13) first aid; 14) scientific questions; 15) social medicine; 16) bibliography; 17) letter-box (answers to inquiries), etc. In addition, interesting illustrations are given.
"Folksgezunt" thus deserves the widest circulation, and it is a duty of every Jewish family to subscribe to it, especially as the price is so affordable: 30 groszy a month.
The greatest duty regarding circulation, however, lies on all organisations engaged in educational work, in particular on all the boards of Jewish schools, Talmud Torahs and orphanages. In the "F.G." these organisations have an invaluable means of showing the broad strata within their sphere of activity the way to observe the foundations of hygiene, in order to attain a healthy life.
It is also worth mentioning the valuable premiums that the "F.G." gives from time to time. Thus, for example, readers receive a "Hygienic Library" consisting of 18 very useful popular-scientific booklets, "The Life of the Woman" — a good handbook for every woman, and so on. In 1930 a home medicine cabinet with the most necessary medical supplies for first aid in accidents is being given as a premium. This is certainly a very useful thing, which ought to be found in every Jewish home.
In conclusion we must still say a great "yasher koach" — both to the health-protection organisations "TOZ" — "OZE" and to the tireless Dr. Ts. Shabad — for the great effort and love they devote to the journal "Folksgezunt", which is an ornament of Yiddish literature.
Dr. S. Ostrzon[?].
