Oyneg Shabes — Torah sayings for Parshat Toldot

[Torah.] Regular feature: Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the weekly portion, collected and styled by Y. L. Parshat Toldot.

(a) "Abraham begot Isaac" (25:19). Rashi notes that the verse repeats "Abraham begot Isaac," though "Isaac son of Abraham" was already said, because the scoffers of the generation claimed Isaac was really fathered by Abimelech; so God shaped Isaac's face like Abraham's, to confirm to all: Abraham begot Isaac. [—] Those who spread the slander that Isaac came from Abimelech are not outright jesters; [—] the term "scoffers of the generation" includes the "vertl"-tellers who joked: this is why Sarah was held [captive] by Abimelech [—]. [—] That Isaac was born is what the true Sages meant by "she shall be cleared and bear seed." [—] Not by Abimelech's merit was Sarah preserved. Abraham begot Isaac.

(b) "The children struggled within her" (25:22). Granted, Esau pushed to get out, drawn to idolatry; but Jacob — what had he done, wanting to come out? [—] It is said that in the mother's womb an angel teaches the child Torah; so why "struggle to leave" when the mother passes the study-house of Shem and Ever? Is it not better to learn from an angel? He found the learning pleasant even from an angel, while sitting in his chamber together with Esau... By Rabbi Moshe Sofer.

(c) "Two nations are in your womb" (25:23). The Talmud (Avodah Zarah 11) expounds this of Antoninus and Rabbi, of whom it is said their table never lacked horseradish or radish. And what is the "rum" (greatness)? [—] The ample hospitality at their table. By Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin.

(d) "A wholesome man" (25:27). [—] No one was so "tam." To Laban he said "I sojourned with Laban... [and did not learn] trickery." Jacob was wholesome only when he need not use guile — "a wholesome man"; he mastered his innocence and did not need to exploit it, but when dealing with a trickster he knew how to tuck cunning up his sleeve. By Rabbi Yaakov Yitzchak of Lublin (the "Seer").

(e) "Let me gulp from this red stuff" (25:30). Once the Maggid of Dubno asked a rich man for a donation [—] at a table bearing various coins, and the man handed him a [small one]. Said the Maggid: "Let me gulp from this 'adom' (red)" — meaning the money, not the small red coin the rich man gave ... The clever Maggid adds: "and the mind of the 'adom' settled once he found his pretext" ... (in his wealth — another small coin, not a ruble) ...

(f) "He sold his birthright to Jacob" (25:33). How could Esau sell the birthright, [being] doubly rich? For the taste [of a stew]? [—] that Isaac was [—] and Esau feared the inheritance would grieve [him], and so [—] "the game of his son." Many verses show Isaac was [right] in this, though he was righteous, since [—] hold that for the righteous wealth is a virtue. Ibn Ezra.

* * * [—] Of those who hold to the Torah the verse says "days are in her right hand," long life; and one asks: [—] length of days, but not wealth and honor? The answer: [—] wealth and honor are in the left hand — i.e. responsibility. Rabbi Nachman said on this: indeed a true a-fortiori, that the upholders of Torah [renounce] wealth and honor; [—] in reality they have not a penny [—]. Sichot HaRan (sec. 4). [—] they rely only on his spiritual "adherents"... Rabbi Nachman of Breslov.

(g) "Perhaps my father will feel me" (27:12). [Rabbi Elimelech] was very strict that [his hasidim] not dress in modern fashion ... In comes a hasid wearing a starched collar, which in those days was deemed a great "progress." [R. Elimelech] clasps him round the neck; the hasid asks a blunt question: how does the Rebbe know the Patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob wore starched collars? Rabbi David (then still a small boy), son of [—], answered on the spot: Rebecca covered [Jacob's neck] with a kerchief so Isaac would not recognize; and had Isaac's sons worn starched collars, Isaac anyway could not have told whether the neck was hairy or smooth — the collar hid it.

(h) "Be lord over your brothers" (27:29). Such "luck" Jacob has, that even when blessed with "be lord over your brothers" — you shall be a lord [gvir] over your brothers, they shall deem you a "man" [and give you] "big cuts," but may you possess a [—]. A folk joke.

(i) "And Isaac trembled a great trembling" (27:36). Once — says the Midrash — Isaac trembled when [he rebuked] Esau the second time he came to him. The second time is "a great trembling," for this time the fear is [greater]. [—] the meaning of the old preacher's saying is thus: sad moments befall Jews in exile: once [—] them by force [—], and the second time when Esau comes with "smooth talk" and sweet words — and thus he [leads astray] the [Jews]; the second moment is far more dangerous... [Yalkut Margaliot].

(j) "And when you grow restless you shall break his yoke off your neck" (27:40). There are 613 commandments; but [the Sages] like to add a mitzvah: "one mitzvah draws another." On Panaska(?) Street a Jewish woman suddenly fell ill. The sick-fund's doctor, who was called out, established that the woman was ill with appendicitis (blinde-kishke) and had to be operated on.
The husband, wishing to make sure whether his wife was really so seriously ill, demanded a second doctor from the fund; but the second doctor too declared the same — that the woman must be operated on at once — and sent her to the hospital (the 'gur. rewir' — surgical ward).
At the hospital all the [preparations] for the operation were made, despite [the fact] that the woman [—] 40 groszy[?]...

At the Senate elections one saw a great deal; for generations the 'mischievous deeds' done in the name of the 'guardians of Torah and faith' will be recorded. Fine bearded Jews were seen shaking hands with the worst dregs of Jewish society, and the vilest libels were read out on the opposing side. The method is nothing new to us: it is well known that the 'Torah-true' hold a monopoly on Jewishness, and a rabbi (even like Rabbi Rubinstein) who is not harnessed to the Agudah's wagon is a 'transgressor of Israel' who eats carrion and treyf; whereas yesterday's sinners, betrayers of Israel, are 'honest Jews, true tzaddikim'... We also saw a document printed in the Agudah organ 'HaMevaser' in the Land of Israel, carrying a 'good tidings' (in Hebrew): 'Since today news has been received that the Zionist and national [enterprise] has been annulled and the National Home — the source of licentiousness, insolence, Sabbath desecration and eating carrion and treyf in our Holy Land — destroyed, therefore all who fear God, take part... This is the day the Lord has made, let us rejoice.' In the Yiddish rendering: since news has come that the English government is annulling and destroying the promised creation of a Jewish national home — the source of licentiousness and insolence, Sabbath desecration and eating carrion and treyf — all the pious and upright should share in the great joy and praise the Almighty...
Then a series of election-day vignettes: (1) A Jew from Piaski who came to vote and stepped in to buy goods from an Agudah merchant; asked which list — '17'; he explains he does not want to live in Poland but in Palestine, and if he does not vote for the Zionists, how will he be able to emigrate. (2) 'He prays every day' — a leftist young man meets an Agudah 'editor': he wanted to vote 17 but read that Rabbi Rubinstein is a 'transgressor of Israel' who eats treyf; the 'editor' answers 'so it is' — and is Reb Rafael a fine Jew? — 'Our Rafael prays every day and lays tefillin.' (3) An old blind Jew is brought in a droshky by two young men, his hand trembling as he votes — what number could the cripple have put in? Who took a blind, sick Jew out of his home? When he left, he was put back in the droshky that rides with 'customers' among the polling stations — that is number 18. (4) '17 and 1' — a modern young woman lost the number her (Hasidic) neighbor gave her, who had explained that list 17 is the symbol of the [—], and that a rabbi figures there as a candidate; as a 'proletarian', a roll-baker, she wants to support the 'candidate of the progressives' — number 18; by the polling building she found a 17 slip and a 1 slip, rolled both together and voted 18. (5) 'The World to Come with a piece of Leviathan' — the wife of a Ger Hasid on Third-of-May Square agitates for 18 and showers pitch and brimstone on 17 and all the Zionists; a supporter of 17 remarks that the well-known rabbi issued a proclamation calling all the pious to vote for 'one', and whoever votes for 'one' is assured of the World to Come and the privilege of enjoying the Leviathan; and a God-fearing woman tries to persuade her friend: 'Yente-Dvoyre, have mercy, vote for one, for man is sinful, and if we vote as the holy rabbi commands it will atone for our sins and we will merit the World to Come and taste the Leviathan a hundred years hence'...
Man and His Wonder-Filled Secrets

[Essay/reflection; by L. Spiegelman; sub-heading: “Such a Conversation.”] In the last two decades circumstances have flung us across a distance of many generations. People could never have imagined that in so short a time such transformations could occur. The wonders happening in our day cannot be grasped by the ordinary mind; they rush past before our eyes with the speed of cinema pictures, as though through a telescope, so that we cannot even pause, observe, and form an opinion about one problem or another. Formerly life was one long, uniform chain: every day, week, month and year resembled one another like two drops of water, everything calculated in advance to the minute and the second, no one hurried and no one was ever late. The leisurely chats between afternoon and evening prayers, sitting before the house on the benches, sitting on the steps of the shop — all took place at the exact time; even nature was obedient and never rebelled. One knew when the frost, the snow or the mild weather would come, and knew by the months and the date how to dress and how to conduct oneself. No one imagined that nature could show wonders, or that new conditions could change the world. But suddenly revolutions broke out that shattered everything from beginning to end: an entirely new world was revealed before our eyes — people are different, the world different, conditions different, the gods different. Gods are burned, ideals annihilated, dreams smashed, and in the place of sacred ideals modern views are exalted, views that shift with the time and the climate. And who knows — perhaps time will show us that problems, views and ideals too can be changed like a fashionable lady’s wardrobe, and perhaps that is even more practical, durable, lively and beautiful; perhaps modern philosophy too must be studied differently. In our day one no longer studies for its own sake to become a scholar or a great mind; learning is perfected more from a practical standpoint, because of the prevailing conditions of existence in which we live. Once there was more time to investigate thoroughly; today we are in another world, among other people. No one is allowed any longer to settle in one place and research and philosophize — not the scholar, not the chemist, [—] nor the idealist. Today’s world cannot permit itself such a luxury; we live in a time when one thing chases another, and the rush is so great that one cannot stop, and whoever tries slips, falls off the magic wheel and breaks his neck and nose. In the modern world people are greatly enamored of inventive medicine. The technicians, chemists and artists cry out: we achieve so much, we invent the new and improve the old, we simply overturn worlds, we show wonder upon wonder, and humanity trembles and marvels at the giant works we have given the world — and we have not yet said the last word. And we doctors, we professors, we who are the mechanics around the mechanism called man — what have we invented for human life? What have we done [—] for the life of man, or at least so as not to shorten it? [—] to prolong human life or to steady it as in former generations? Our Answer

[Poem; by B. Sternberg (Warsaw); sub-heading: “To the English Verdict”[?] — most likely a response to the Passfield White Paper of October 1930.] The blow has fallen, the struggle begins / Hey brother, hold firmer our blue-and-white flag, / With sweat they were hammered, with blood put to use, / We all as one stand ready for the fight! Our breast is like steel, our hands are strong, / We must show the world our power, / And let it feel the blow of the hand, / Together with all those who fight side by side in the ranks. Enough of being trodden by the robber’s hand, / We gathered the crumbs from the robbers’ feet, / The land is ours! We create and build a life in the land / With bloody sweat of generations long past. And what shall become of whoever stands in our way — / We will show with hammers, with scythes, with axes, / We will tear up and destroy the robber’s field, / Together with those who block our life. The blow has fallen, the struggle begins (first stanza repeated).
„The Ghosts” (Gengangere)

[Theatre review; signed Sh. Ratshberg[?]. “The Ghosts” — a drama in three acts by Henrik Ibsen, from the guest performances of the [Lemberg?] theatre in Zagłębie.] Just as in Norway, Ibsen’s homeland, the skies are always clouded over and cold, stormy winds blow, so too it is in his dramas: there too a cold wind blows and one feels in them the harsh chill of [—] Scandinavian nature. In Ibsen’s dramas psychological conflicts find expression against a social background. His worldview is pessimistic, suffused with tragedy and a critical mood. [—] For Ibsen attainment is not the goal but rather the struggle itself, which may be regarded as the true life, in which a person’s character is hardened and defined. In “The Ghosts” it is Mrs. Alving who stands in struggle with the two forces. Soon after her marriage she returns to her husband and stays with him until his death, despite terrible sufferings and humiliations, yet she resolves to suffer and to conceal everything from human eyes, for the sake of her son Oswald, in whom she sees her only consolation in life. She sends her son away from home when he is barely 7 years old, so that he not be poisoned by the spiritual atmosphere prevailing in her house; but the remedy is ineffective, for Oswald is sick in his blood — inherited from his father. Our 'Declassed' Youth

[Social essay.] It has already become a constant[?] phenomenon that the door of our editorial office opens and on the threshold remains standing, embarrassed and not bold, a young man whose mustache is only beginning to sprout, who in a quiet, barely audible voice turns to us: — Perhaps you know of some work for me? When you talk things through with these youths who seek work, you become aware of an abyss of tragic circumstances and neglect. Most are children of specifically middle-class (balebatish) parents, who in normal times would perhaps have settled into their parents' enterprises, or into a private, communal or state post. But in the present conditions in Poland, [while] their parents' businesses [—], they have no entry, and they find themselves as a 'declassed' element, i.e. an element that has no ground under its feet and no place in society. And precisely they are capable[?] young people, with education and abilities, who under other circumstances would surely not have been wasted — graduates (abiturientn)[?] of schools, some even with professions, but.. there is no work. [...] For after all a Jewish editorial office is no labor-exchange and can hardly help them. It has even happened that such a one, after convincing himself that the editorial office could not provide him work, barely uttered: — I have not eaten for two days. This you hear from a young man's mouth not seldom in these times. When we think more deeply about how it stands with our Jewish youth, we reach sad conclusions. One notices such a phenomenon: the declassing of our youth is not a natural one, as happens in certain social processes, but a torn-out[?] one, through the policy of those who lead and [run] the government machine in the country. Our youth is declassed not because of a change in the social milieu, as we see for example in the Soviet Union, but because of the blocked[?] social-economic possibilities of integration, precisely under capitalist conditions, directed straight against that part of the population which does not belong to the ruling nation. The suppression of Jewish commerce and entrepreneurial initiative, the rightlessness of the Jewish schools, the rightlessness regarding work in the monopolies, factories, government offices, administrative and municipal institutions and so on — force our youth, [—] and able-bodied youth, to be seemingly declassed, when in truth they are not; and [democ]racy[?] pushes such youth out beyond the borders of Poland, and we soon receive greetings that so-and-so has settled here or there [—]. But how many such young emigrants can there be? The youngest remain on the spot and must have a livelihood; one cannot let them starve in — [sub-head:] Lumpenproletariat. Do our decisive governing spheres notice[?] the harm of this declassing-policy, which brings the youth of a whole people to beggar's bread merely because it does not belong to the ruling nation[?].
Living Corpses... — Light Chats on Serious Political Themes

[Satirical feuilleton; by 'Felitis'.] [...] that you must push yourself[?] down into the earth, and why exactly [—]? — For, they say, there is already water, and even bitterer water; and however bad a person may feel at heart, he would still want to remain on dry land, on the dry yet blessed[?] dry land with its borders and border-posts, with its states and little-states, with its institutions founded (supposedly) for the good of mankind, and with its parliaments. An institution for which people once gave their lives, brought sacrifices, made revolutions, beheaded kings[?], until it was established. And then, in the democracy, came the ban (cherem). And the ban, as it says in the verse, was traded in power; and power is a sweet tidbit, whose nature it is that one spoils oneself with it if one takes too much. Indeed, they say, many parliaments ruined their stomach and began to ail so long and so wide, that a part of them have now died and others — have become... living corpses. [...] like all other [things], like a human, and is not a human, but some such ugly thing that just drags along like the blind gut (kishke) in the belly? Who needs it, this gut? Can one not live without it? The spiteful[?] Creator planted it in our innards and said: here, whoever bursts with it — bursts; and what, don't people burst? One simply gets torn[?] to pieces. Ask them [—], they'll tell you, they'll lament and sing with tears the old Jewish couplet: 'On a stomach one must not rely, for one can still be left without a pair of pants.' And if I am mistaken, and in the Jewish [—] repertoire there is no such couplet — one must put it in, even if the rhyme limps a bit. And who today isn't limping — the whole world walks about on crutches, and that is because among the 15 million cripples that the World War bequeathed to us, [...] the greatest war-cripple[?]... is the world itself. And it seems it has already remained an eternal cripple, hapless, and even the eternal pillars of the League of Nations will, it seems, no longer be able to sustain it. And perhaps precisely because the world has become such a cripple, our whole life has become so flawed, and there is not one thing in the world that does not limp. [...] in truth — one sees it from how people crawl there so [—] and slowly, as if they had no legs at all. And peace[—] too limps; its legs, they say, were promptly chopped off so it couldn't move in the Sodom-bed of all kinds of [—], peace-accords and confe[rences] [—]. But the greatest cripple is democracy. A lame democratism[?] and a paralyzed people's-will. A paralytic[?] who cannot move from the spot, and if he does lift a foot and by luck makes a step, it is out of a fall — from the party[?], the organization, the program, the leader, the [—], but by no means of his own will. The people's will has long been dead, deceased, and they forgot to bury it; it drags itself around the world like a living corpse (bar-minan), just so, without any intent, without any goal, without body and life. And this living corpse goes round in a dance with the second living corpse — with parliamentarism... Two dead ones dance, and in the middle stands the lame-crooked[?] democracy and whistles. And the one who piped them to their 'luck' in Poland was the P.P.S... — Felitis.
Napoleon's Romance with the Young Widow Joséphine — 4

[Historical-literary essay; by M. Aszerowicz.] 4. The fact that she set no great store[?] by it made no difference to her. It was all the same to her what to put on — such a famous general, marching with an army from victory to victory, taking so many cities, when everything is laid at his feet and all are ready to obey his command — well, it is only fitting that he should not forbid love-affairs here and there[?]; it is after all impossible... He must tell himself the truth! How many women has he already loved? Since he left[?] home? With how many women has he already been intimate?... With this she shut his mouth, and he could no longer speak of what he suspected her of — that she was not faithful to him... In the two days in which [he] was wholly absorbed in Milan with his new beloved Joséphine, the situation on the battlefield became very critical, and the army of the Austrian king nearly[?] smashed the French at the siege of Mantua. Then [Napoleon] could no longer remain alone in Milan with Joséphine, and he went off to the battlefield. The moment was very serious, the danger very great; [—] that the enemy [—] and the French would have to abandon the positions they had taken, after losing many casualties. [...] in order to defeat the enemy — and despite being so occupied, despite having then such heavy duties upon him, he nevertheless found time to write letters to Joséphine, and what letters! Full of love, full of tenderness, full of devotion! One of the letters to Joséphine from that time is very characteristic, and we reproduce it as it is: — Since I left you — he writes to her — I am terribly sad at heart. I can be cheerful only when I am beside you. All the time I do not cease to think of your kisses, of your tears and of your enchanting jealousy. The charm of Joséphine [—] has no equal, and does not cease to fan the flames that burn in my heart and in my senses. If only I were already free for a longer while, free of worries, free of duties, free [—] the whole time for you, free — to do no other thing in life but love you... The more I come to know you, the more respect I have for you, and this proves that what people say — that love comes suddenly — is not true. Nothing in all of nature comes suddenly; everything develops by stages... Be less beautiful, less tender, and above all — less jealous. Your tears ignite my blood... Come back to me, [but] quicker, so that if we go strolling, we may say: 'Yes, we have had many happy days'! A million kisses even for your [—]. Such a letter to a beloved woman [Napoleon] could write from the battlefield at a time when all [—] of the war hung in the balance, and the whole army under his command was in danger of being annihilated. The last remark about Joséphine's [little dog] is very characteristic. The little dog — 'Fortuné' it was called — lay well in the bones[?] and gave him a fair bit of grief in love... Joséphine always kept the little dog with her, and every time Napoleon took her[?], the little dog could not bear it and rose against him: it barked and bit his hands and feet. And perhaps Joséphine kept the little dog with her only then, when Napoleon [was] with her... perhaps it was for her a means [—] the stormy passion he felt for her? Napoleon himself complained more than once about the troubles he had to endure from the little dog. He recounted that even on the wedding night Joséphine kept the little dog with her when she went to sleep... Joséphine cared little that Napoleon pined so strongly for her. Only from time to time did she write him, for form's sake, a short little letter, and from the letter breathed such coldness, 'just as if we had already been [married] fifty[?] years [—]. Napoleon himself expressed [—]. And here, in the army too, the courage of the soldiers and also of the officers began to fall; all were under the impression that they stood on the threshold of a terrible defeat. All looked Napoleon in the eyes and turned to him for help, and Napoleon himself felt that his mind[?] was being deranged, for besides holding in his hand[?] the lives of so many thousands of people, besides having to work out plans how to overcome the enemies all around, he must also think about Joséphine not letting him [—], and about her not being faithful to him. Then he grew angry and sharply [reproached] her in a letter. 'I no longer love you — he wrote to her. — I hate you, you are repulsive to me, you are [—] and impossible, you do not write to me, you no longer love your husband. Tell me just, madam, what do you do all day long? With what important matters are you so occupied that you have no time to write a few words to the husband who loves you?.. And tell me indeed, who is he there, the handsome young man who takes up so much of your time that you cannot even write a letter to your husband? Remember, Joséphine! [—] one fine night the door will suddenly open and I shall come in!.. Yes, yes, in all seriousness, I am very uneasy, my beautiful little wife. Write me a letter at least from [—], full of [—] words, [to] warm[?] my heart [—] happiness. [...] Then I will embrace you tightly and cover your body with a million hot and burning kisses.' In this letter Napoleon's relationship to Joséphine is very accurately reflected: he begins with hate and ends with a million kisses... It is clear that he would want[?] to hate her, but he cannot; he would want to loathe her, but it comes hard[?] to him against her, he cannot help himself at all, his reason[?] indeed suffers from her not being faithful to him, he is indeed burning[?] with jealousy, but he still loves her. A thought [comes] to him, that perhaps he has no [complaint] against her at all for not loving him... He seeks the cause and finds it. [...] 'Yes — he writes to her — it is after all my fault, for nature did not give me the charm that should bind you to me.' And he, the man who [achieved] everything or else nothing at all — brought himself to the point that in his love for Joséphine he would demand of her less — 'just a bit of attention, a bit of respect, because I love her to madness, her and only her.' He was truly faithful to her and devoted with his whole heart; the first while he really took no interest in any other women, but [—] later he did look about him and realize that one must [—] pay faithfulness for faithfulness. Oyneg Shabes

[Torah.]
Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around this week's portion. Arranged and styled by Y. Y. — Parshas Vayetze.

a) "And Jacob went out from Beer-Sheva and went to Haran" (28:10). Though it could have been written "vayelekh le-Haran," instead of the 'lamed' of the first word the 'he' of the last word can serve — so it is expounded. Seemingly this changes nothing, for what difference does it make whether the letter comes at the start or end of the word? — It teaches: as long as one can hold back and spare a word, one should not bring it out; as long as it can be kept in, keep it. So sparing must a person be with words. — From Rabbi Mendel[?] of Vorki.
*  *  * Rabbi Hershele of Halbersta[dt][?] had a pupil who bore hatred for his rebbe but feared to voice it. On Purim the pupil was chosen 'Purim-rav,' got thoroughly drunk at the feast, and in his drunkenness poured out everything in his heart against his rebbe. An uproar arose among the pupils. When he sobered, R. Hershele told him: the rule 'what is on a sober man's lung is on a drunk's tongue' would seem to apply, and you would deserve a verdict; but that rule does not hold for an animal — for if it did, one would not need to toil to inspect the lung; one would simply get the animal drunk and all the adhesions would show on the tongue. Since the rule does not hold for an animal, I have nothing to hold against you...

b) "And he lay down in that place" (28:11). The Midrash: there he slept, but all the years he studied with Shem and Ever he did not sleep. Another saying: there he slept, but all the years he worked for Lavan he did not sleep. Jacob cannot rest. He went into the study-house and learned; studying only Torah, he was reproached for isolating himself from life and living apart from his neighbors, drawing their hatred. And when he became a worker for Lavan and became productive, he was reproached for taking over everything and exploiting society too much.. Jacob has no rest. Yalkut Marganiyot (RM"H).

c) "And he ran to meet him" (29:13). It is said: why did he run and for what. One who runs — the heart in time senses the deceit; one asks: why did Lavan run? The answer: "he set his eyes on money" — though the running comes from the eyes, it was worth it to him for the money he reckoned to swindle out of him. Siftei Torah (R. Yosef Landau of Jassy[?]).

d) "Is it because you are my brother that you should serve me for nothing?" (29:15). Suddenly Lavan became a man of fairness, unable to bear Jacob working for free — whence fairness in a miser? Hearing Jacob wanted nothing for his labor, Lavan thought: "he is my brother" — Jacob showed me he knows the art of trickery just as I do. "Serve me for nothing"? Would he serve for free? A trickster like me — would he let himself be cheated? Surely, Yankele, you have some speculation in it... Ohel Yaakov.

e) "And Rachel was of beautiful form and fair appearance" (29:17). Solomon says "Grace is false and beauty vain — a God-fearing woman shall be praised," yet here Scripture praises beauty? The answer: grace is false and beauty vain only in the licentious; in a God-fearing woman beauty too becomes her. Derekh Tzvi (the Gaon of Miron/Vilna). *  *  * Another reading: when falsehood wins grace and vain beauty is taken for beauty — "a God-fearing woman shall be praised" — a God-fearing one will be praised; it will be exceptional praise. Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa.

f) "And Lavan gathered all the men of the place and made a feast." Therefore he gathered them and then made the feast. He assembled the men of the place, and when they [—]

g) "And it was in the morning, and behold it was Leah" (29:25). The Midrash: "all that night he called her: Rachel! and she answered him. In the morning — behold it was Leah; he said: deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Did I not call you Rachel in the night and you answered?!" There is a way to test whether a stranger presenting himself as a certain person is genuine: invite him to sleep and suddenly call his name — if he truly answers, that is his name. Jacob, who knew Lavan's tricks, feared being cheated and used that very device: he waited until Lavan fell asleep and began calling: Rachel! Rachel! She answered — so he was sure it was Rachel. In the morning — it was Leah.. He cried: deceiver, daughter of a deceiver! Even in sleep you deceive.." Sfas Hayeria.

h) "And she said, this time I will thank the Lord . and she ceased bearing." Why, once she thanked God, did she cease to bear? When one already has enough of the good another gives and wants no more — one thanks him, and the thanks means: enough now. When Leah thanked God for the children it meant she had enough, hence "she ceased bearing." Maor VaShemesh.

i) "And Lavan said: I have divined that the Lord blessed me for your sake. And he said: you know how I have served you" (30:27-29). Lavan persuaded Jacob that he grew rich not by Jacob's abilities, loyalty and toil, but by the merit of keeping an idler in the house: "the Lord blessed me for your sake" — God blessed me for keeping a pious good-for-nothing. So the thanks go to God, not to you. Jacob replied: who suddenly gives a righteous man a fur coat? Your wealth came "as I served you" — by my toil; "the Lord blessed you at my feet" — by my feet that ran, God blessed you with riches; so pay me for it... The Maggid of Dubno.

j) "The wrapped ones to Lavan and the bound ones to Jacob" (30:42). A father-in-law buys the groom a tallis, while the groom himself buys tefillin; whence is it derived that it should be so? "Wrapped" — a tallis to wrap in (atifah) belongs to Lavan (ye[—]
The Electoral Campaign for the Senate in Zagłębie.

[Local.]
The battle over the senate elections could already be seen [?]. After the attack on the List 17 meeting, the "street" got a "tongue" (began talking). One told another that the "Mizrahi" meeting had been disrupted, while at the "Agudah" and "Beys Yakov" meetings they say what the most abominable enemies of Israel once allowed themselves: eyes rolled up to heaven, sidelocks tucked behind the ears, dressed in Sabbath clothes, the most pious souls preached that "the Zionists are not citizens of Israel... and above all, that whoever votes for List 18 is exempt from the commandment of tefillin.."
The general campaign was staged on the Sabbath, from early morning; crowds of cheder-boys, Beys Yakov schoolgirls and young men were dispersed, going house to house and calling to "sanctify the Name" for the righteous R. Rafael...
Their work was wide-ranging, within and without; in the shtiblekh and prayer-houses they campaigned for number 18, and outside, in the streets, posters were pasted up. For the great "rabbis" sanctioned even desecrating the Sabbath, so long as the honor of the Torah be saved — namely, that R. Rafael become a senator...
In all the "shtiblekh" and study-houses, the passionate agitation led to brawls. The fight arose chiefly from the pretexts and means used by the agitators of the Agudah list, who waged the "rescue action" under the sign of the honor of the Torah, yet in fact disgraced the Torah.
Thus we know[?] that in certain "shtiblekh" the rescue-number 18 was pasted on the holy ark, and after reciting Psalms in the study-house it was proclaimed that one should "go the straight path and vote for the holy list number 18."
The true "fire of holiness" first flared up in the course of [the campaign], echoing an agitation the "Agudah" had years earlier in the rabbinic elections, with the phrase "neither mine nor yours shall it be"; and they went out into the Jewish street aiming to bring down the mandate of the hitherto senator, Rabbi Rubinstein.
Young and old were mobilized, from the cheder-boy to grey-haired elders with their pious wives, for the sake of the "holy war"; in the "Yesodei Torah" cheder and in "Beys Yakov" studies were suspended, and the pupils with their teachers, cheder-boys and schoolgirls worked from morning to the last moment with every tool and every means.
For the work the "Agudah" had mobilized nearly all the porters and carriers, with a whole lexicon of bans and curses.
Several times a day, List 18 circulated lampoons against the "luckless" senator Rubinstein, who [—]
In the streets, especially on the 3rd of May Square, large groups of people stood debating; in the process they paid one another "honor" with the coarsest abuse and curses. Despite the heavy rai[n] [—]

In Sosnowiec a conference of the railway directorate (ban-direktsye) was held about the new timetable. [—] Representatives of the Chamber of Commerce (handls-kamer) also took part, [—] the authorities and the press.

Among other things the question was raised that the express trains should stop in Będzin, and we received a reassuring answer that it would be taken into consideration. Of course this does not yet mean the matter is finally settled and that the trains will indeed stop in Będzin; in our view one must still press the case.

It is ridiculous [—] the new timetable is already at the printer, and if Będzin is not included in it, nothing more can be done — it will be a lost cause until next year. [—] What shall we do then? The matter would be put off automatically[?] [—] for further years [—].

[—] Będzin demands that the express trains (kurirn) go on stopping as always, because the station is called Będzin, and because the town's residents and its economic and communal institutions demand it.

We must do everything possible so that the express trains stop with us again. It is enough that a town like Będzin has had to endure a whole year; we are simply amazed that the population has remained so patient — and that only because we have lived in the hope that any day everything would return to how it was.

The new railway station is already being completed and next year it will open to passengers; it is the newest in Poland. [—] Shall the express train really not stop at the very newest station?

The economic and communal institutions, together with the merchants' associations, must intervene at the ministry; and for that one should call on the local authorities to help — the starostwo, the commandant's office[?], the military, the police, and so on.

We have the right to demand that one can reach Będzin by every train, because Będzin is a city and not a village, an old established place and not some small shtetl. The railway administration draws much revenue from Będzin; many goods and products are dispatched (ekspedirt) from here, [—] that we not be treated worse than far smaller towns.

Let us therefore remember that this is a civic matter that must be resolved as quickly as possible.

The town of Będzin is forever made famous by the "fine" deeds of its leaders. Things happen in this town that no community in Poland has to this day been "privileged" to experience. But what took place on Shabbat Vayetze, at Kabbalat Shabbat in the Będzin synagogue, surpasses everything.
By way of preamble — begins one of the synagogue's worshippers, giving his "impressions" of last Friday night — what happened, he says, crosses every bound of lawlessness and demoralization. Was it ever heard that, when a cantor steps up to Kabbalat Shabbat, a worker from the slaughterhouse should run to the lectern and shout:
— "Get away, cantor! If not, I'll skin you like a calf"...
And then the congregation, in the lit synagogue, saw sharp knives and gleaming revolvers flashing...
Later the police came and led the present community leaders off to the commissariat, where the commissar delivered a moralizing sermon to them. You should have heard it — says [—] — the truth is, such [—] ought rather to have been spoken by one of our own spiritual "leaders," lehavdil.
— "How dare you — shouted the commissar — profane the holiest of holies? Among what nation could such a scandal occur, that as the officiant steps up to conduct the divine service he is disrupted so brutally?"...
And the man who had come to the synagogue to "fulfill the holy mission" of not letting the cantor pray bowed his head in shame and declared with remorse:
— "I am not guilty at all, I was told to do so, I truly repent"...

A Topical Matter
— You haven't met him yet? You can see him on Kołłątaja Street or on Małachowskiego Street. — A young man, slim, wearing a hard hat; and when he begins to speak to you, it soon becomes clear that the young man is mentally ill, out of his mind, or in plain Yiddish: — a madman!
But laugh — only not when he talks nonsense, for when his father spoke people also laughed, yet a different laughter. — Laughter! from the humor of fine couplets. — Yeshai Goldzweig was his name. Będzin ought to be grateful to him, who by his word drew tears and laughter from hundreds of people.
Should not the pious camp remember the "whoever sustains one soul of Israel" and the "postępowe" [the 'progressives']? They surely ought to seek means so that the young man not sink ever deeper, for it is a matter of saving a young life — and no stranger's, at that.
— A native son, a Będziner indeed...

Piety Down to the Pocket...
— I want to tell you a thing about a Będzin householder, a Ger Hasid, who — when it comes to money matters forgets everything, even his Hasidism, but I beg you not to name me explicitly, for I too — as you know — am a Ger Hasid, yet it boils in me like a kettle, and I cannot allow such a scandal to be hushed up.
— Now, a bit less preamble; to the point.
— All right, all right, only promise me not to publish my name?
— I promise you...
The scandal occurred last Friday night, after Kabbalat Shabbat, at the minyan of the local rabbi. After prayers, R' Berish the shochet went up to the rabbi and asked him to intervene with R' Dod, to hold back the eksmisja (eviction/execution of judgment) against a certain haberdashery merchant on Kołłątaja Street. First, that merchant is also one of 'our own folk'; and second, how can one, in such hard times, even think of evictions?
R' Berish, who with truly no self-interest wished to do a Jew a kindness, never imagined that for this he would get a "verse with a stick" from R' Dod:
— "You, and you too — shouted R' Dod, and finally "ruled" that "one may not eat from R' Berish's shechita"...
The next morning there was an uproar in the shtibl: how can it be?! Because Berish the shochet wanted a Jew, and a decent man at that, not to be utterly ruined — he should be reviled in public?...
— You will know — the Jew tells me — how to write up the story, only I beg you: "don't give me away"...

A "Satisfaction"
The "Vayakhel-Pekudei" crowd, the well-known brazen-faced ones, the sold souls, do not cease barking at and besmirching those who refuse to pay monthly dues for their "cheating."
Among the "fallen" is also the former vice-president, who is "insulted" by them because he stopped paying — guilders...
But the abuse is so repulsive that even the Ger Hasidim were greatly outraged by it; and besides the "editors" getting their due "verdict" in the "shtibl," a delegation was sent to Mr. Rubinlicht with the question: what satisfaction does Mr. R. want for the insults?
Mr. R. explained the following to the delegation: — The best satisfaction would be to slap the snouts of those lowly creatures, but I don't want to soil my hands"...

Religion on the Sabbath...
A Będzin Jew, a father of children, comes into the editorial office and puts the question to us:
— What is one to do?
— What do you think? — we ask.
— My daughter — he says — "goes to the Kołłątaja [school]," she studies in the fourth grade, and by the program the Jewish children are taught religion in class on the Sabbath... And since I — he says — do not let my daughter go to school on the Sabbath, she learns no Jewish religion at all"...
We heard the Jew's complaint out and thought to ourselves:
— A foolish Jew, no doubt; our "upholders of the faith" have more important problems to deal with — to stand guard and watch that, God forbid, no goose be sold without a "kvitl" (certificate) on its leg. — That is more "important" than a Jewish education...

The Grave Housing Question

(The difficulty of the tenants' question — how can the matter be solved?)

Lately there has again been much vigorous talk about introducing reforms in the housing sector, and it is telling that the reforms are calculated precisely on the intention to raise the price of dwellings.

The housing shortage in Poland is dreadful; the population is suffocating in overcrowding. In no cultured country is the housing situation as terrible as it is here in Poland. At a time when elsewhere so much is being done in the field of building modern, hygienic, well-arranged houses, among us nothing has yet been done in this field, and it is therefore no wonder that the situation is terrible and the predicament unbearable.

Here people in our larger towns still live in unheard-of anti-sanitary conditions; whole families live in cramped, tiny little rooms. And when we occasionally come into such families and meet face to face the people of these "holes," we are astonished; we simply cannot grasp how the people live there, how they manage — to raise the children, work, earn a living, run a household and get along with others all at once. At times, when we end up there, we are beside ourselves, contemplating the hard plight of people whose fate it is to bear so heavily the yoke of existence.

There is thus no doubt that our government must seriously begin to think how to ease the hunger for dwellings; and as an expression of that, the plan is to raise the rents and from the increase to create a fund for building new houses. Of course, in that case the increase would have to be large, high — otherwise nothing would be accomplished, otherwise it would amount to illusions and unworkable projects.

And so the question arises: are there possibilities of burdening the population with increases of 50, 75 or 100 percent? One must not forget in what a difficult position the country now finds itself; one must give an accounting of where we stand. One must not close one's eyes to reality. The country is in a terrible crisis that makes it impossible to carry on the already difficult conditions of existence of the present time. The housing question is now, for us, like a dangerously ill patient whom it hurts wherever you touch him.

To leave the question standing unsolved like this is unheard of — it is simply catastrophic, for very many troubles, ruin, illnesses and arrested development arise because of the housing question. Yet to solve the question on the scale that is needed would mean, on the other hand, making the citizens miserable. For one must reckon: is the average population in Poland capable of taking on itself the heavy burden of carrying on its shoulders the building of large networks of houses? Can it be burdened with such high increases? Even now, when dwellings are in fact not dear, one hears that people do not pay the rent because of the serious critical situation; so what would it be then, when a small shopkeeper or an artisan had to raise 75 percent for his little shop or workshop? How heavily would that fall upon the masses and upon the worker, who today lives in modest enough conditions — how could he undertake such a sum to enlarge his budget?

But we would say this: it is indeed bad and bitter and there is no other way out, and if the lower strata of the population will have to and be able to meet it, then it is understandable that in that case conditions of existence would worsen considerably, becoming hard, unheard-of harder than they were, for earnings would then have to be raised significantly, a higher reckoning would have to come into play, so that everything would once again be forced to change for the worse.

It is possible that in time the housing situation would be eased — and that because people would not have had the means to come by dwellings, as we see even now, which was not caused by the rise in rents, since that has not yet come, but merely the crisis has already given a push, so that today, for example, it is easier to obtain dwellings than two years ago.

Yes, one must ponder this problem seriously, one must treat the question from all sides and honestly, one must not after all forget that this is not a matter of a luxury article that whoever wants it should pay for. In short, a roof over the head must be had by every living person, so that no one will doubt that this is a strictly first-class article, without which none of us can get by.

Because of the gravity of this problem and because of the hard situation and the prevailing crisis, it is absolutely necessary that the community not be isolated: everything and everyone — the population and the institutions, the communal activists and the representatives — must occupy themselves intensively with the question. We do have tenants' associations whose task is to stand guard and protect tenants' interests, but that is still not enough, it is far too little. True, as a professional association the tenants' associations ought to take the place of honor; possibly they would have something to say that no other institution would say, but still the question is too generally social and too serious to entrust it to them alone.

We would go even further and say that even the house-owners' associations ought to occupy themselves with the question too, for one must understand that the owners of the houses will gain nothing from the present worsening, and as soon as they gain nothing from it they will, without doubt, be the first "sacrificial chicken." For at the time when the tenant has to enlarge his budget considerably because of his housing expenses and cannot sustain it, there is no doubt that first of all he will have nothing with which to pay the monthly or quarterly rent, so that, willing or not, it will fall also on the shoulders of his landlord; and precisely from this standpoint the house-owners too ought to think seriously about the future of the housing question.

As we have already said above, there is no doubt that the housing question cannot and must not remain standing as it is today, for that would mean non-solution; but just as it must be solved — which we need very, very much — so it can by no means be done at the expense and burden of the average citizens. And therefore it is precisely important that one take it up seriously, with all the sharpness of the situation, so that it is absolutely necessary to carry out consistent [measures][?] with all the economic associations in the country, which should find a modus by which the question may be solved and not so heavily burden the citizens of the land — something that would still many times over make the situation worse.

We are therefore of the opinion that already now, while it is not too late, the question should be taken up by the tenants' associations, the house-owners' associations, the artisans, the small traders and the commercial societies[?], the workers' associations — and all together should form one chain of a single coordinated[?] activity, which, together with the authorities and the Sejm deputies, would find an eased[?] modus to solve the painful housing question in such a way that it will not burden the poor and average strata of the population.

We too, the inhabitants of Zagłębie, ought to take part in this serious question; let Zagłębie too [say][?] its word — it has the right and the responsibility not to remain indifferent to this cardinal matter.

— The question is serious and topical enough, so that it must not be neglected[?] for a single minute.

R. Let.

[History.] By Rabbi S. Assaf [Jerusalem]. (Special for the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".)
The love and bond between the Jewish people and Eretz Yisrael may be called eternal. In all times the people carried "Zion and Jerusalem" in its heart and never forgot its former splendor and glory. Wherever it was exiled[?], it always carried with it this holy love, and the striving for redemption, for "the comforting of Zion and the rebuilding of Jerusalem," was expressed[?] in the language[?] of the dark[?] exile of Israel itself, which gave hope for the times to come. In every generation there were among the people chosen ones, "yechidei segulah," who could not reconcile themselves to the exile and its troubles[?], and who with self-sacrifice set out on the road to the Holy Land; many[?] were the obstacles, great was the danger on the roads, but the eternal love between people and land prevailed.
These [sole][?] roads became the emissaries of the whole people, who were "upon the Torah and upon the service" and prayed at the holy places on behalf of the whole people scattered among the nations. Should a misfortune, God forbid, occur, the Jews in Eretz Yisrael were at once notified to pray and annul the evil decree. For this reason the exile exerted itself, as far as it could, to support the Yishuv in the Holy Land. Whoever possibly could took part in this mitzvah, and through it felt bound to the land and to the Jewish spirit[?] and hope. And not only individuals took part in it, but also the communities. The masses in exile saw to all communal affairs, and used to elect each year [representatives] such as parnasim, dayanim and various gabaim[?].
In Lithuania the Jewish Council of the Land ordained[?] in the year 5406 (ת"ו) that every community and settlement set aside special sums at the time of the chalukah, so that money be found for the poor of Eretz Yisrael. In the year 5440 (ת"ם) a takkanah was made whereby all communities were obliged to send the "Eretz Yisrael money" each year to the Lublin fair and not to withhold it, so as not to nullify the Eretz Yisrael money through "bal te'acher" (do not delay). And since a single community may[?] lend from this money to communities that were at times hard-pressed for money, the rabbis decided that one should lend only with care, even on the surest promissory note, except on a silver pledge, which must be worth one-and-a-half times the loan.
In most of the Italian communities there were separate special societies under the community's supervision, which dealt with all matters concerning Eretz Yisrael and called themselves "Chevrot Eretz Yisrael." The gabaim and [heads] of these societies occupied themselves chiefly with collecting the donations for the needs of the Eretz Yisrael Yishuv. The Campaign in Zagłębie for the Yiddish Scientific Institute Begins!

[Culture/YIVO.] Disheartened(?) by the difficult economic situation, harried and worried by the cares of making a living, the Jew has no opportunity all year long — especially lately — to take an interest in higher questions, spiritual questions, cultural questions. That is a fact; but from this sad fact one must not draw the conclusion that one can live by bread alone. It is a long-known rule that a people whose culture does not develop gradually dies out.
Therefore it must be a joy and an encouragement for us Jews that, despite the stormy(?) times, our culture is nonetheless moving(?) forward. Yiddish literature, the Yiddish press, the Yiddish theatre, the Yiddish school are growing stronger. An intensive, many-sided activity is being developed by the highest form of our cultural movement — the Yiddish Scientific Institute [YIVO].
The Institute was founded 6 years ago — only 6 years in all, yet in this time an enormous amount has been accomplished. Even before YIVO there were Jewish scholars who wrote scholarly works, but what was missing was the world centre that would organize scholarship in Yiddish, give scholarly work planning, order and system, encourage scholarly work and help train new scholarly forces. Precisely this is what YIVO had to fulfil(?).
The world must increasingly base itself on scientific foundations. Scholarship therefore ceases to be the affair of individuals only, of a chosen few; on the contrary, ever broader strata must begin to take an interest in scholarly questions.
The sympathy YIVO arouses among the Jewish population all over the world results from the fact that its activity is of great importance for our culture. In various countries, wherever there is a living Jewish community, loyal and devoted friends work for the Institute.
The Institute has 4 scholarly sections and a bibliographic centre that registers the entire printed output in Yiddish, Hebrew and also in other languages, insofar as periodicals and books in foreign languages concern Jews or Jewish problems.
The Institute has an archive holding many very important materials, documents, pinkasim (communal registers), etc.
The Institute has a library holding over 25 thousand books, many of them rarities.
The Institute's work is branching out more and more. From January 1931 the Institute's monthly, 'YIVO Bleter', begins to appear.
YIVO's first world conference, held last year at Sukkot(?) in Vilna [Wilno], resolved to build a building for the Institute where all branches of YIVO would be able to work.
Today the building is already finished on the outside; in the coming half-year the interior work must be completed and the necessary equipment acquired.
In order to acquaint the broad public with YIVO's achievements and to collect larger funds for the Institute, YIVO is now conducting a campaign across the whole country. In a number of places the campaign has already been carried out and has brought satisfactory results. People of various tendencies take part in the work for the Institute. Owing to its purely scholarly, objective work, YIVO arouses great sympathy among persons of differing world-views.
Now the YIVO campaign in Zagłębie begins.
Everyone must take an active part in it!
M. Shur.
